title: Third person dies from malaria in cluster near Germany’s Frankfurt Airport
author: Anadolu; DPA; Reuters
content:
![female anopheles mosquite](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/AP22301698582716-1707372046.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
A third person has died from malaria after a recent cluster of cases linked to Frankfurt Airport, in what German officials have described as an extremely rare air-traffic-related outbreak of the tropical disease.
In a statement on Thursday, city administration said the person died at Frankfurt hospital and was one of two infected residents living in the Schwanheim district, in the immediate vicinity of the airport.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
The two new malaria cases in the neighbourhood had been reported on Tuesday.
“Both individuals had become infected with the malaria-causing parasite Plasmodium falciparum, even though they had not travelled to a malaria-endemic region and had not worked at the airport,” the statement said.
According to the city’s public health department, the two newly infected people contracted the disease from a mosquito flown into Germany on an aircraft or in luggage.
Six Frankfurt airport workers had contracted malaria tropica, the most dangerous form of the disease, in July, authorities said. Two later died.
Malaria is a potentially life-threatening mosquito-borne disease that is extremely rare in Germany.
The malaria parasite is spread between humans by some types of mosquitoes, but not through direct human-to-human contact.
Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport said it set up traps to catch mosquitoes and sent the insects to a laboratory in Antwerp in Belgium in July and August, but results were not available yet.
Health authorities have warned doctors near the airport to consider malaria in patients who come in with a fever.
Airport workers and residents have been urged to seek medical advice in case they display symptoms including fever, chills, headaches, confusion, seizures and breathing difficulties.
An airport spokesperson said local public health authorities had the power in principle to order airlines to disinfect aircraft.
summary: A third person has died in Germany from a rare malaria cluster linked to Frankfurt Airport. The victims, including local residents and airport workers, were infected with the parasite Plasmodium falciparum without traveling to endemic regions. Health authorities believe the mosquitoes were transported into the country via aircraft or luggage.
key_points: A third fatality has been reported in a rare malaria cluster near Frankfurt Airport.
Two newly infected residents living near the airport had no history of travel to malaria-endemic regions.
Six airport workers previously contracted malaria tropica in July, resulting in two deaths.
Health authorities and airport operators are taking precautions, including setting traps and warning local doctors and residents.

title: Bournemouth University study aims to cut veterans' dementia risk
author: Stuart Rust
content:
![A group of people gathered around a table with a yellow table cloth turn towards the camera and pose for a picture.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/565e/live/974a1920-b1c7-11f1-8493-1910d79d53eb.jpg)
Veterans with dementia were invited to workshops to share their experiences
- Published
A new study could help reduce the risk of veterans developing dementia.
The SERVED project, run by Bournemouth University's Ageing and Dementia Research Centre, is working with veterans to raise awareness of brain health risks and improve support.
Associate Professor Michele Board, who is leading the research, said veterans could be at greater risk due to their exposure to dangerous environments and traumatic events.
Previous research suggests about 45% of dementia cases worldwide could potentially be prevented or delayed through lifestyle changes.
Through a series of workshops, veterans with dementia were invited to talk about their experiences in the military and their lives since leaving service.
The research found many were at risk of being isolated later in life due to the impact of their work on relationships.
The study also found there was a stigma around discussing early symptoms of memory loss, which affected their ability to access support.
"I think in being pushed to be strong and self-sufficient it does not encourage sharing, especially of areas that may be perceived as a weakness," one participant said.
Board said the research also found veterans from poorer backgrounds, or with unhealthy habits like smoking and drinking, were at greater risk.
Bruce, a former member of the Queen's Royal Hussars who is living with dementia, is among those who took part in the research.
![An old photograph showing Bruce, a man with short dark hair, pose for a picture in his military uniform, which includes a hat, jacket and tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/552/cpsprodpb/fd51/live/a7e29a50-b1c7-11f1-8493-1910d79d53eb.jpg)
Bruce, who served with the Queen's Royal Hussars, said veterans affected by dementia needed a "champion"
He said: "I would suggest that we need a champion across all the services who acts for us.
"In the meantime, it is really important for my fellow veterans to understand where they can get support."
As part of the project, researchers worked with veterans to create an animated film sharing their experiences, which was launched at an event at the Tower of London on Wednesday.
It is hoped the event, which was supported by Dementia Research UK, will encourage other veterans to open up about brain health.
summary: Bournemouth University's Ageing and Dementia Research Centre is leading the SERVED project to help reduce dementia risks and improve support for military veterans. Through workshops, researchers found that veterans face increased risks due to military trauma, social isolation, unhealthy lifestyle habits, and a cultural stigma around discussing memory loss. The project culminated in an animated film launched at the Tower of London to raise awareness and encourage veterans to seek help.
key_points: The SERVED project by Bournemouth University aims to cut veterans' dementia risk and improve support.
Researchers found that exposure to dangerous environments, trauma, poverty, and unhealthy habits increase dementia risks.
A cultural stigma of being strong and self-sufficient prevents many veterans from discussing early memory loss symptoms.
The study revealed that many veterans are at risk of late-life isolation due to the impact of their service on relationships.
An animated film sharing veterans' experiences was launched at the Tower of London to encourage others to discuss brain health.

title: Brynna mum's Facebook kidney plea prompts stranger to donate
author: Matt Murray
content:
![Gary is bald and wears a burgundy and white checked shirt and sit nexts to Karen who has her hair in a ponytail is wearing a camel coloured jumper.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/66b0/live/f6d8bbf0-b1fc-11f1-a4a7-291ff3d1006b.jpg)
Gary Summerfield told his family "this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them"
- Published
A woman who shared a desperate plea for a kidney on Facebook has undergone a lifesaving transplant after a stranger offered to be her donor.
Karen Davey, 41, had exhausted every avenue before turning to social media, where she said she did not "want to leave her family without a mother".
Gary Summerfield saw the mum-of-four's post and, after learning he was a match, donated one of his kidneys via an operation in July.
"I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them," said Gary.
Karen's family said they would never be able to repay Gary for his generosity, adding that it had given her "another chance to be a mum".
The average wait for a deceased donor kidney transplant in the UK is two to three years, according to NHS Blood and Transplant, but if you have a living donor it can be about three to six months.
![Karen is pictured in a hospital gown, lying in a hospital bed with tubes from her nose and other monitoring equipment](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/95b8/live/22676640-b1fd-11f1-a4a7-291ff3d1006b.jpg)
Karen says she feels "100 times better" following the transplant in July
This was Karen's second lifesaving transplant. She underwent a heart transplant 10 years ago, after having a heart attack aged 31 while watching her son play football.
A transplant increases the risk of infection because of the medication patients need to take following the procedure, and complications led to Karen developing kidney failure.
"I knew the tablets I was taking following the heart transplant would damage the kidneys so they try and keep the dose as low as possible, but we always knew when I had the heart transplant that I would probably need a kidney transplant at some point, and that is hard to deal with mentally."
Karen, from Brynna, Rhondda Cynon Taf, was in stage three kidney failure when she discovered her friends and family were not matches and decided to put a plea on Facebook.
She explained in her post that she has a relatively rare blood type and described the kidney failure as putting her life on hold.
"My main thing is the kids, I want to be around for them."
Karen's eldest is now 22, and she is also grandmother to a one-year-old.
"The kids were 10 years younger when I had the heart transplant, and they've been through a lot since then and the kidney was just the next hurdle," she added.
![Gary has a closely shaved head and wears a burgundy and white checked shirt and hugs Karen who has her hair in a ponytail is wearing a camel coloured jumper and has her back to the camera](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/440/cpsprodpb/e859/live/458eba60-b1fd-11f1-a4a7-291ff3d1006b.jpg)
Gary seeing Karen for the first time after he donated his kidney to the mother-of-four
Gary, a security guard from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, stumbled upon Karen's post by chance and felt he had to help.
"I saw Karen's appeal and she mentioned the children, and I thought 'Karen's a similar age to my daughter and her youngest child is the same age as my grandson', and I just thought it's terrible for the children," he said.
"If It was my daughter, I would be searching everywhere if we had exhausted all avenues through the family and friends, I would want a stranger to come forward. And I thought it would be selfish not to."
He added: "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them."
Although, Gary, 60, had never met Karen, he immediately volunteered to be tested.
He underwent extensive assessments, including compatibility testing, psychological evaluations, blood tests, cholesterol checks and other medical examinations.
The pair then underwent the six-hour procedure on 15 July at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff.
Gary said he never had any second thoughts.
He added: "It's amazing seeing Karen today, the first time since the transplant and looking so well.
"For me, donating a kidney is simply up there with getting married and having my children, it's one of the top three things in my life.
"And she's a very deserving lady and a deserving family."
![Karen's is pictured with her husband, Matthew, who has black hair and a beard and wears shorts and striped black and white t-shirt and her 17 year old son, Brandon, wears a grey hoody and has a mop of dark hair](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/8914/live/7f274bc0-b1fd-11f1-a4a7-291ff3d1006b.jpg)
Karen, pictured with husband Matthew and son Brandon, who say Gary has given her the "gift of life"
Karen said she felt "100 times better" and her husband Matthew said they would always be grateful to Gary.
"Everyone knows what's going on in the world at the moment, it's a horrible place at times, but it really does give you hope that there is kindness in the world," he said.
"We'll never, ever be able to repay Gary and the family for what they've done, and to give Karen another chance, another chance of being able to be the mother to our children and just live a life that she deserves.
"He has given that gift of life."
Karen added: "The fact that somebody came forward and has gone through all the testing, because it's a lot of testing. For somebody to put their body through that and having a kidney taken out for somebody that they don't know, it's mind-blowing, I'm just so grateful."
The couple's son Brandon, 17, said it was "amazing" to see his mum on the road to recovery after the transplant.
He said: "She's looked better now than she has in a long while.
"It can be scary, obviously, when she's going into surgeries, but you just have to have hope. It's just amazing there's still good people out there."
summary: Karen Davey, a mother-of-four from Wales who suffered from kidney failure following medication for a previous heart transplant, has undergone a successful lifesaving transplant. After her friends and family were not matches, she posted a desperate plea on Facebook that was answered by a complete stranger, Gary Summerfield. Following extensive medical testing, Summerfield donated his kidney to Davey during a six-hour procedure in July at the University Hospital of Wales.
key_points: Karen Davey turned to Facebook for a kidney donor after exhausting all options with family and friends.
Gary Summerfield, a stranger from Tredegar, saw the post, found he was a compatible match, and decided to donate his kidney.
Davey previously underwent a heart transplant 10 years prior, and the necessary post-transplant medications eventually led to kidney failure.
The successful transplant surgery took place on July 15 at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff.

title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target
author: Joshua Nevett
content:
![Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham attends a meeting with Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney (not pictured) ahead of the Everton v Wolverhampton Wanderers English League Cup football match at Hill Dickson Stadium in Liverpool, Britain, 16 September 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney visits Britain, Liverpool, United Kingdom - 16 Sep 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/fef0/live/bdc56440-b2b9-11f1-ad9d-efc12ace03e0.jpg)
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to reform adult social care in England
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.
An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.
In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".
In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report, external.
She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on."
The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".
She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives."
The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year.
McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".
Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.
In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.
Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target for dementia patients was achievable.
He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding.
"All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.
The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.
In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target".
Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.
She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now."
Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer.
About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040.
Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease.
Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make".
In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.
Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls from the Alzheimer's Society, former officials, and Baroness Louise Casey to establish an 18-week referral-to-treatment waiting-time target for dementia care in England. Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the proposal, noting that dementia has been neglected for too long. The government has already committed to appointing a dementia tsar and publishing a new modern service framework by the end of the year.
key_points: The Alzheimer's Society proposed an 18-week referral-to-treatment waiting-time target for dementia care, similar to targets used for cancer.
The proposal is backed by England's former national cancer director, Professor Sir Mike Richards, and social care reviewer Baroness Louise Casey.
Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report at an Alzheimer's Society conference.
The government plans to appoint a dementia tsar and release a new service framework by the end of the year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to reform adult social care in England, influenced in part by his late father's experience with Alzheimer's.

title: Plan to limit NHS diagnoses of ADHD attacked as ‘rationing’ healthcare
author: Anna Bawden
content:
Proposals to limit the number of patients being formally diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder have been attacked as “rationing” healthcare and pushing children and adults to self-diagnosis via social media.
The comments came before a government review due next week, which is expected to say that patients with ADHD symptoms should not automatically be formally diagnosed, but should be “triaged” and offered support without the need for a formal diagnosis.
Details of this “needs-based” system, first revealed in the Times, would mean NHS services target those most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those at risk of self-harm or unable to work.
Less severely affected people may not be referred for a formal diagnosis to NHS clinics but would be offered help according to a “holistic” assessment of their needs, the report will say.
The government’s independent review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD was commissioned in December by the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, amid concerns over the sharp rise of people making sickness benefit claims due to mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses.
Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support.
Official figures show that patients are waiting years to be assessed, with 800,000 on NHS waiting lists. Meanwhile, complaints about autism and ADHD services in England have more than tripled in five years.
As a result, growing numbers of adults and young people with ADHD are not in education, training or work, of whom about 100,000 are on health-related benefits due to their condition. The ADHD taskforce calculated that the cost of undiagnosed, untreated ADHD was £17bn.
Fonagy’s review will recommend that only patients who would benefit from a formal diagnosis, such as those needing medication, would be referred to ADHD clinics.
Under the proposed holistic needs-based assessment, patients would be triaged according to their difficulties and ability to cope at school, college, work or other settings. They would be offered targeted early support, regardless of whether they had a diagnosis or not.
Such support could include one-to-one help for children to cope with lessons, quiet rooms in schools, classes to help parents support children with ADHD symptoms, and encouraging employers to offer staff with ADHD flexible hours.
after newsletter promotion
The final report is expected to propose a similarly holistic approach to supporting people with autism, and to mental health more widely.
But experts said the proposals would in effect introduce rationing of health services and that schools and workplaces were already able to offer early support without a formal diagnosis.
Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK, said the review proposed “rationing”.
“There is no ‘mild’ ADHD. Diagnosis requires evidence of a debilitating impact on your life. We already have a clinically drawn line of need.
“Without a formal diagnosis, it appears we will be left to self-diagnose via social media. Schools and businesses shouldn’t be forced to rely on TikTok to know when to put in adjustments and support.”
Shelford said that, on average, a woman with ADHD would die nine years younger than her peers and a man seven years younger.
“In almost any other area, those numbers would have this treated as a health emergency, but the stigma and misunderstanding around ADHD means instead we’re treated as an inconvenience and proposed to be ‘disappeared’, untreated, from the waiting lists.
“Diagnosis means people turning their lives around, more people in employment and succeeding in careers.”
Investing in ADHD services, he said, offered a high return on investment to the country, noting that last year, the NHS spent £574m on a single weight-loss drug because treating people meant they could get back to work. “The same is true of ADHD, with cheaper medication and better evidence.”
Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Denying people a diagnosis will only worsen inequalities experienced.”
A government spokesperson would not comment on the forthcoming report, but said: “Last December, we asked clinical psychologist Prof Peter Fonagy to lead an independent review, examining the prevalence of – and support for – ADHD, autism, and mental health conditions. Prof Fonagy’s final report will be published shortly and will inform our new national approach in this area.”
summary: An upcoming government review is expected to propose a needs-based triage system for NHS ADHD patients, offering support without requiring a formal diagnosis unless medication or acute intervention is needed. Critics have attacked the proposals as healthcare rationing that could force people to self-diagnose via social media and worsen inequalities. The review was commissioned amid rising sickness benefit claims and lengthy NHS waiting lists affecting hundreds of thousands of people.
key_points: An upcoming government review recommends that patients with ADHD symptoms be triaged and offered holistic support without an automatic formal diagnosis.
Only patients most acutely affected or needing medication, such as those at risk of self-harm or unable to work, would be referred to NHS clinics for a formal diagnosis.
Critics, including ADHD UK and the National Autistic Society, have condemned the plans as healthcare rationing that will lead to self-diagnosis via social media.
The independent review was led by Prof Peter Fonagy to address sharp rises in sickness benefit claims and years-long NHS waiting lists for ADHD, autism, and mental health services.

title: Ferritin face: the new health scare taking social media by storm
author: Guardian Staff; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Name: Ferritin face.
Age: The name is new, but the symptoms are old.
Symptoms: Pallor, dull skin, dark circles under your eyes. Looking washed out, basically.
What are you, a mirror? Oh no, does this describe you? Do you also have ferritin face?
Aren’t those just symptoms for “looking tired”? Is this one of those social media health scares with little to no scientific basis? No! I mean, yes, the term has recently become very popular on social media, as reported in the Washington Post. Ferritin face is not a real medical term (nor are there consistent criteria that define it) – but ferritin at least is definitely a thing.
Tell me about ferritin, then. It’s a complex globular protein that stores iron in the body in its inactive form. If you have low ferritin levels, it could indicate an iron deficiency.
And what happens if I have an iron deficiency? If it is severe and goes untreated for long enough, it could lead to tachycardia, breathlessness, chest pain and heart complications.
This is terrible! How can I cure myself? Well, earlier this summer, Allure magazine wrote a long piece entitled What It Means to Have “Ferritin Face”, calling iron deficiency an epidemic that women are prone to. It had plenty of advice.
Like what? Tell me now, before my dark circles kill me! It can often be overcome with a change of diet, as meat and green leafy vegetables are a good source. But you can also just go and have an intravenous iron infusion.
An IV it is! Be warned that, according to a leading iron infusion clinic, it could cost you in the region of £800.
Cabbage! Someone get me a cabbage! Alternatively, you could stop crapping your pants at every social media health scare. You should never diagnose and treat yourself via TikTok clips.
OK, fine. Think it about it sensibly. There is a vast difference between ferritin face and actual anaemia. Anaemia doesn’t just make you pale and tired-looking; it can leave you fatigued and breathless, with headaches, dizziness, palpitations and a loss of concentration being common symptoms.
Oh, I don’t have any of those. Good. But if you do, the NHS recommends that you see a GP, who will try to discover the underlying reason for your iron deficiency – which could be anything from heavy periods to cancer – and put you on a course of iron tablets.
So I don’t need to worry about ferritin. Probably not, no. But get an early night tonight. You look dreadful.
Do say: “You do not have ferritin face.”
Don’t say: “But you do have ferreting face, which is far worse.”
summary: "Ferritin face" is a viral social media term describing a washed-out appearance with pale skin and dark circles, though it is not a recognized medical diagnosis. While the term lacks scientific backing, it relates to ferritin, a protein that stores iron, and low levels can indicate an iron deficiency. Severe iron deficiencies or true anaemia can cause serious symptoms like fatigue, breathlessness, and heart complications, which should be evaluated by a medical professional rather than self-diagnosed via social media.
key_points: Ferritin face is a popular social media health scare but not a real medical term.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, and low levels can indicate an iron deficiency.
Treatments for iron deficiency range from dietary changes to expensive intravenous iron infusions.
True anaemia involves more severe symptoms than just looking tired and requires a GP's diagnosis.

title: Why coffee makes some people buzz and others barely notice
author: Jim Reed
content:
![A portrait shot of Emily staring at the camera. She is wearing dark glasses and a black jacket, and has light brown hair. She us holding a cup of coffee in front of her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/875/cpsprodpb/eda0/live/8c2f59a0-ac5f-11f1-be57-03729df1d736.jpg)
Emily, out with her friends in London, says that coffee and caffeinated energy drinks don't have much effect on body or her sleep
- Published
"Coffee just doesn't have much effect on me," says 20-year-old Emily, who is leaving a cafe in central London at 18:00 BST.
"I'll normally have two cups a day and then maybe an energy drink too. And then I can drink coke all night and feel completely fine."
We've all got a friend like Emily. The one who can knock back a double espresso or even an energy drink in the evening and still drift off to sleep an hour or so later.
For many people, though, the effects of caffeine can linger for far longer.
Why then can some people drink coffee before bed and sleep like a baby, while others lie awake staring at the ceiling?
What exactly is caffeine?
Caffeine is by far the most used psychoactive substance in the world.
More than two billion cups of coffee are drunk each day and that's before we start talking about cola, energy drinks, plus some chocolate, chewing gum and sports supplements, which also contain the chemical.
It can make us feel more alert, improve concentration and stave off tiredness. Too much can cause headaches, jitters, a racing heart and restless nights.
Caffeine doesn't give your body extra energy, it helps mask tiredness, experts say.
It does this by blocking the action of adenosine, a chemical that builds up in the brain throughout the day and makes us feel sleepy.
Why does it affect people differently?
One key factor is how long caffeine stays in the body.
After drinking a cup of coffee, it is absorbed into the bloodstream, where it quickly reaches the brain.
All this time it's also being broken down â or metabolised â by an enzyme in the liver and then flushed out in our urine.
That clean-up process can take between six and 20 hours depending on the individual, says Dr Marilyn Cornelis, an associate professor of nutrition at Northwestern University in Chicago.
"It's possible to have a first cup of coffee and maybe not feel the effects," she says.
"But then two or three hours later, the caffeine is still lingering in the system, and, if you add a second cup, that might be enough to tip the scales and you start feeling a little anxious."
Why caffeine makes some people buzz
How quickly the liver can processes the caffeine depends on a single gene â known as CYP1A2.
Intriguingly it might be influenced, at least to some extent, by your ancestry.
A study published this year, external found that Europeans and South Americans tend to break down caffeine more quickly on average.
What other factors are at play?
Your DNA is far from the whole story. Smoking, but probably not vaping, appears to stimulate the liver to break down caffeine much more quickly, speeding up the process by as much as 65%.
That may help explain why smokers tend to drink more coffee and why people who quit can suddenly find their usual cup feels much stronger than before.
Some antibiotics, contraceptive pills and other prescription medicines can have the opposite effect, allowing caffeine to stay trapped in the body for longer and prolonging the effects.
![A male shopper in a jacket and hoodie looks at a selection of energy drinks stacked up in a fridge in a supermarket.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/54d4/live/5e3edf80-ab78-11f1-9823-01a7469535d5.jpg)
Energy drinks typically contain around 80mg of caffeine per bottle, a bit less than a cup of filter coffee, although there are big variations between brands
That's also the case during pregnancy, when hormonal changes suppress the liver enzyme that breaks down caffeine.
Then there is the question of tolerance.
Regular coffee drinkers become less sensitive to caffeine as the body adapts to the presence of the chemical.
If you then go without the drink for a few weeks, those adaptions in the brain begin to reverse, meaning the first coffee back might leave you feeling unusually wired or jittery.
What do experts advise?
Sleep researchers often recommend avoiding caffeine for at least six hours before bedtime.
Dr Lindsay Browning, a psychologist and sleep expert, says the evidence suggests caffeine might not just stop you dozing off but can affect the quality of sleep as well.
"I'll suggest to people that they might want to avoid caffeine after about 2pm if they are going to bed around 10pm," she says.
"But a blanket hard-and-fast rule isn't helpful, because it doesn't really allow for the intricacies and the individualisation of what's really going on."
The NHS advises pregnant women, external to keep caffeine intake below 200mg a day, about two mugs of filter coffee, as studies have linked it to low birth weight and other complications.
For other adults the key message is moderation, as sensitivity to caffeine varies so much from person to person.
"Caffeine is relatively safe," says Peter Rogers, emeritus professor of nutrition at the University of Bristol.
"If you consume a great deal of it, you just start feeling jittery and unpleasant and you start realising, 'I need to stop this, there's no point taking any more'."
Caffeine overdoses are very rare and severe poisonings almost always involve concentrated caffeine products, where several grams can be swallowed in a matter of minutes.
For coffee lovers the good news is that, if anything, that regular (if expensive) morning habit is linked to better health outcomes.
While researchers cannot prove that coffee is the only reason, decades of studies suggest that people who drink it in moderation tend to have lower risks of several major diseases and may even live slightly longer than non-drinkers.
summary: Caffeine affects individuals differently based on how quickly their bodies break down the substance, a process influenced by genetics, smoking, medications, and tolerance. While some people can consume caffeine late in the day and sleep easily, others experience prolonged alertness, jitters, or sleep disruption. Experts generally recommend moderation and avoiding caffeine several hours before bedtime.
key_points: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine, a brain chemical that makes people feel sleepy.
The liver breaks down caffeine over a period lasting between six and 20 hours depending on the individual.
Genetics, smoking, certain medications, pregnancy, and regular tolerance levels all alter how the body processes caffeine.
Sleep experts suggest avoiding caffeine for at least six hours before going to bed.
Moderate coffee consumption is linked to better health outcomes and lower risks of several major diseases.

title: I don’t care if science has vindicated literary slop. Not all reading is equal
author: Lara Brown
content:
![Reading the latest ghost-written celeb tome is good for you, apparently](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/15/TELEMMGLPICT000003513405_17894845142130_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqXNzwmV2URyi_Ke1zCpKeyvFwAoVatUYeaMo7rAJTZz8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Reading the latest ghost-written celeb tome is good for you, apparently](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/15/TELEMMGLPICT000003513405_17894845142130_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqXNzwmV2URyi_Ke1zCpKeyvFwAoVatUYeaMo7rAJTZz8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Every now and again scientists prove a hypothesis so self-evidently obvious that I’m left questioning how they ever secured the funding for their study.
The latest finding is that reading for pleasure can substantially lower the risk of dementia. Researchers followed almost 5,500 adults aged 55 and older and concluded that those who read regularly were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment over a five-year period.
The most shocking revelation to come out of this work, however, is that apparently it doesn’t matter what you read. Science has finally vindicated bad taste.
If you want to spend your days reading the latest ghost-written celebrity memoir, romantasy or scrawl of One Direction fan fiction, apparently you’re doing yourself some good.
Whatever scientists may or may not have discovered, I’m really not convinced that all reading is good reading. Conversations about literature increasingly treat books like broccoli. Anti-taste indoctrination starts young.
We impose the ghastly Biff, Chip and Kipper on children just as they’re learning to read. Who cares that nothing interesting has ever happened in one of these as long as you can learn about “magic e” and “ing words”.
Then, once you’ve got phonics nailed down, you graduate on to such masterpieces as The fart that changed the world (by the comedian Stephen Mangan) and the Rainbow Magic books (there are more than 300 of these).
Once you’ve churned through all that, adulthood now culminates in a series of 400-page memoirs by former Love Island contestants who are yet to hit 30.
Due to a packing mishap, I recently found myself scouring an airport WH Smiths for something to read on the plane. Most of the options offered versions of my truth, my journey, finding my voice or learning to love myself by reality TV personalities I’d never heard of, interspersed with the odd self-help book on stoicism.
Of course, given that any of these could have warded off Alzheimer’s, I had no reason to despair. But there is something rather depressing about reducing reading to a workout for the brain. Why bother with the novel when you could do a crossword, learn the capitals of the former Soviet republics or memorise the periodic table?
The written word has a claim on us far beyond the promise of keeping one compos mentis for a few more years.
Some books reach deep into our souls; others tell the story of a Strictly Come Dancing dancer’s rise to fame. It seems perverse to lump both into the same category.
If we don’t prove this point, then the study is pointless anyway. The number of adults who read for pleasure is falling dramatically. More than a third of Britons now describe themselves as “lapsed readers”.
For many in this group, publishing has left them behind. We’ve homogenised and overproduced literature – relying on TikTok influencers to do marketing while the big houses are increasingly cautious to commission anyone without a large, pre-established following.
Meanwhile, it is almost impossible to find pleasure in reading the same iterative nonsense that sold well last summer.
Content matters, even if the hippocampus doesn’t care. No one should read Tolstoy, Wodehouse and Austen because they’re good for the brain. These works aren’t preventative medicine, they’re simply wonderful.
I promise that your life will be enriched by them, even if scientists can’t prove it.
summary: Recent scientific research suggests that reading for pleasure, regardless of the material, can lower the risk of cognitive impairment in older adults. However, the author argues that reducing reading to a mere brain workout is depressing and that content genuinely matters. Classics and literary works offer deep enrichment that goes beyond the preventative health benefits attributed to low-brow books.
key_points: A study of adults aged 55 and older found that reading regularly for pleasure helps lower the risk of dementia.
The research indicates that the specific genre or quality of reading material does not matter for cognitive benefits.
The author criticizes the homogenization of literature, the reliance on pre-established influencers, and the rise of celebrity memoirs.
Great works of literature should be read for their intrinsic wonderfulness and enrichment rather than as preventative medicine for the brain.

title: Women with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’
author: Anna Bawden
content:
Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found.
A review of global research found that for several health problems, including cardiovascular conditions, kidney disease and Parkinson’s, women were less likely to receive the same treatment as men, revealing the extent to which women have significantly unequal care.
Researchers at the University of St Andrews analysed 38 studies and found that in 33 of them women were less likely to be offered active treatment. Women with myocardial infarction, heart failure or an irregular heart beat were more likely to be given medication, whereas men were more likely to receive a coronary bypass, stent or other surgical treatment. Women were also less likely to be prescribed statins, according to the analysis, which was published in the journal Plos One.
Men with Parkinson’s were more likely to be referred for deep brain stimulation, while those with liver failure were more likely to receive a transplant than women. Female kidney patients requiring dialysis were less likely to be given permanent access and had to spend longer using a catheter. And women were also less likely to be given opioids for pain management.
For stroke and diabetes, however, there was no significant difference between the sexes in treatment. And women were more likely to be treated for dementia.
The findings come amid growing concern about the gender health gap. In March, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, said women were being let down by “medical misogyny”. The previous Conservative government appointed Lesley Regan as England’s first women’s health ambassador, to help tackle the gender gap.
The analysis concluded the discrepancy was not a result of the need for different clinical approaches to women’s health. It found that none of the studies identified any guideline recommending different treatment by sex, raising the question of whether unequal care was a factor.
Dr Andrew O’Malley, who co-led the study, said: “For clinicians, the findings are a prompt to check whether treatment is being offered on clinical grounds rather than assumption.”
He said studies showed doctors more often attributed women’s symptoms to anxiety and made more diagnostic errors with female patients, even when test results were positive.
Dr Miriam Veenhuizen, an honorary lecturer in the School of Medicine at St Andrews, said: “While the direction of the findings was not a surprise, the consistency was. The same pattern appeared in cardiology, surgery, transplant medicine and emergency care, and it survived statistical adjustment in most studies.”
summary: Research from the University of St Andrews reveals that women with the same medical conditions as men are less likely to be offered active treatments such as surgery, stents, and strong painkillers. Analyzing 38 global studies, researchers found disparities across various fields, including cardiovascular disease, Parkinson's, and kidney disease, even though clinical guidelines do not recommend different treatments by sex. Experts suggest these discrepancies may stem from assumptions and diagnostic errors by doctors, such as attributing female symptoms to anxiety.
key_points: Women are less likely than men to receive active treatments like surgery, stents, and organ transplants for identical health conditions.
The University of St Andrews analysis reviewed 38 global studies and found unequal care in 33 of them.
Disparities were identified across multiple areas, including cardiology, kidney disease, Parkinson's, and pain management.
Researchers found no clinical guidelines that recommend different treatments based on sex.
Studies indicate that doctors more frequently attribute women's symptoms to anxiety and make more diagnostic errors regarding female patients.

title: Scientists create mice with part-human brains
author: Ian Sample
content:
Researchers have created mice with half-human brains in an effort to understand and develop new treatments for disorders such as schizophrenia, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and rare forms of dementia.
The scientists transplanted lab-grown human brain cells into animals that were engineered to be born without a cortex or hippocampus. This made space for the human tissue to grow inside the rodents’ skulls.
The procedure means scientists can now take cells from patients with brain disorders, turn them into brain tissue in the laboratory, and grow that tissue in living animals. The animals can then be studied to see how the disorder takes hold in human brain tissue, and how drugs might treat the conditions.
“We’ve been trying really hard as a community to find therapeutic solutions for these conditions, but the reality is that in psychiatry and neurology we’ve been left behind [by] every single branch of medicine and we have fewer therapeutics than, again, every single branch of medicine,” said Sergiu Pașca, a professor of psychiatry who led the research at Stanford University.
“That could be because the human brain is very complex, but it’s also because the human brain is inaccessible,” he added. “To a large extent, our goal has been to make aspects of human brain development and function accessible for investigation.”
The work is the latest from the field of neural organoids, where human brain cells, grown in the lab, assemble into tiny but complex structures that mimic some of the features of real brains.
While potentially transformative for brain medicine, organoids have sparked a wave of ethical concerns, not least around whether the clumps of tissue could become conscious or feel pain, and the welfare of animals implanted with organoids.
Pașca said the work had received extensive ethical oversight from the start.
Experts said this would need to continue. Emily Jackson, professor of law at London School of Economics and chair of a recent report on neural organoids for the Nuffield Council on Bioethics, said: “Animal welfare is a really important concern, and it will be necessary to closely monitor these animals in order to evaluate the impact on them.”
In previous work, the Stanford team transplanted human neurons into rat brains. The tissue took root and wired into the animals’ brain circuits, but there was too little room for the human tissue to grow very much.
To solve the problem, the researchers genetically engineered mice to stunt the growth of key brain regions, the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. Surprisingly, the mice survived because the remaining parts of the brain took on new roles. While the mice look normal, they are cautious on their feet and more forgetful.
Writing in Nature, Paşca describes how the mice were injected with human brain organoids that were themselves created by reprogramming donated skin cells. The newborn mice received several injections, each containing about 100,000 human brain cells, into the space where their own brain tissue was missing. In total, the rodents lacked about 14m mouse brain cells and ended up with about 4m human ones – half the brain by volume.
Three months after surgery, the human tissue had hooked up to the mouse’s blood supply and almost entirely filled the cavity, taking up about half the size of the rodent’s brain. Some of the human neurons formed connections with mouse brain cells and spinal cord.
The human neurons were not structured or wired up in the same way as in people, and the brain tissue was immature, equivalent to that found halfway through human pregnancy. Tests on the “xenocortical” mice showed the animals were not enhanced by the transplants, but their shaky gait and cognitive problems did improve a little.
To demonstrate how the mice could shed light on human brain disorders, the researchers exposed some of the animals to five hours of low oxygen. This showed how vulnerable human nerve cells are to oxygen deprivation, which in pregnancy and birth can cause cerebral palsy.
The researchers found that human brain tissue in the mice contained rare cells known as von Economo neurons, which have only been seen in postmortem examinations. The cells are among the first to die in frontotemporal dementia, a rare form of the disease, which Paşca now hopes to study in xenocortical mice.
Prof Madeline Lancaster, group leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, said the approach was best suited to questions about disorders and treatments where a whole animal was needed. “It’s less clear to me how this will inform our understanding of human brain development since it is rather artificial, and not at all like how the brain develops naturally,” she said.
Many researchers working on brain organoids are growing them in vitro, or in dishes. The hope is they help to reduce the number of animals used in research. “It’s obviously ethically sensitive and there needs to be a very good reason to do this type of animal experimentation, which most scientific avenues do not require,” Lancaster added. “The field is still aiming for fully in vitro solutions, but this work can also inform on what may be needed to improve those in vitro models to reach more mature stages.”
summary: Stanford University researchers have created mice with part-human brains by transplanting lab-grown human brain tissue into rodents engineered without a cerebral cortex or hippocampus. This technique allows scientists to study human brain disorders, such as cerebral palsy and dementia, and test potential new treatments in living animals. While the research offers a potentially transformative approach for neurology, it also raises ethical concerns regarding animal welfare and the complexity of the tissue.
key_points: Researchers transplanted lab-grown human brain cells into mice engineered with stunted cortices and hippocampi, allowing human tissue to make up about half the rodent brain volume.
The method aims to help scientists better understand human brain disorders and develop treatments, as demonstrated by testing oxygen deprivation related to cerebral palsy.
The human neurons connected to the mice's blood supply and spinal cord, though the tissue remained immature and did not enhance the animals' intelligence.
The work has sparked ethical oversight concerns surrounding animal welfare and the potential consciousness of the implanted human tissue.

title: NHS latest Covid symptoms and what to do if you have it - AOL
author: Kate Lally
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Man with a sore throat feeling unwell](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/09/16/1c061f24-6f7c-3c4a-84a8-d4410ecdab5a/3b23af9b-17d6-4fab-a216-988b1696e214.jpg)
The NHS provides guidance on Covid symptoms to watch for, along with advice on what to do if you contract the virus.
With pupils having returned to school and the seasons changing, many people are already experiencing runny noses, sniffles and coughs. As many symptoms overlap, distinguishing between a cold, flu and Covid can be challenging. However, according to the NHS, the most common indicators of Covid are a high temperature, a new and continuous cough, and a loss or change to your sense of taste or smell.
Those with Covid may also suffer from fatigue, shortness of breath, headaches, body aches, a sore throat, a runny nose, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Most people feel better within a few weeks, though recovery can take longer.
For some, it can be a more severe illness with symptoms persisting for an extended period.
Do I need to take a Covid test?
Previously, the public was encouraged to take Covid tests when showing symptoms. However, current guidance states this is no longer necessary for most people.
If you decide to take a test and the result is positive, the NHS recommends you try to stay at home and avoid contact with others for:
- three days after the day the test was taken if you (or the child who took the test) is under 18 years old
- five days after the day you took your test if you are 18 years old or over
You should also "avoid meeting people who are more likely to get seriously ill from infections, such as people with a weakened immune system, for 10 days after the day you took your test".
What should I do if I have Covid symptoms?
NHS guidance advises that you should try to remain at home and limit contact with others if you or your child are experiencing symptoms, have a high temperature and/or feel too unwell to attend work, school, or childcare.
You may return to your usual routine once you feel better or your temperature has returned to normal. If your child is experiencing mild symptoms such as a runny nose, sore throat or mild cough, and feels well enough, they are able to attend school or childcare.
What can I do to recover from Covid?
The steps you can take to help yourself recover from Covid are much the same as those you would follow when dealing with a cold or flu. Ensure you get plenty of rest, keep yourself well hydrated, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen to relieve any aches and pains.
A teaspoon of honey may help ease a cough, however honey should never be given to babies under one. If breathlessness is an issue, turning down the heating or opening a window may provide relief - as can sitting upright in a chair and relaxing your shoulders.
Refrain from lying on your back if you have a cough, and try to stay calm if you feel breathless as anxiety can make it worse. It is also inadvisable to use a fan to cool your room, as this could potentially spread the virus.
In the week to August 31, there were 261 patients admitted to healthcare settings in England with Covid. This was up 15%, from 227, in the previous week.
summary: The NHS has outlined current Covid-19 symptoms, noting that distinguishing the virus from colds and flu can be difficult due to overlapping signs. While routine testing is no longer necessary for most people, the NHS recommends staying home and limiting contact with others if you have symptoms and a high temperature or feel too unwell. Recovery steps mirror those for colds and flu, including rest, hydration, and over-the-counter pain relief.
key_points: Common Covid-19 indicators include a high temperature, a new and continuous cough, and a loss or change to taste or smell.
Most people no longer need to take a Covid test, but those who test positive should try to stay home for three days (under 18) or five days (18 and over).
Individuals with mild symptoms like a runny nose or mild cough who feel well enough can still attend school or childcare.
Recovery methods include resting, staying hydrated, taking paracetamol or ibuprofen, and using honey to ease coughs in those over one year old.
In the week leading up to August 31, healthcare admissions for Covid in England rose by 15% to 261 patients.

title: Eye scans detect signs of atrial fibrillation years before diagnosis
author: University College London Reviewed
content:
People with atrial fibrillation have signs of the condition in the retinas of their eyes that can be detected as early as four years before diagnosis, finds a new study led by University College London (UCL) and Moorfields researchers.
The authors of the PLOS Digital Health paper analysed retinal imaging data from more than 90,000 people and discovered differences in the structure of the retina in people with atrial fibrillation, compared with those who do not have the condition.
Atrial fibrillation, the most common heart rhythm disorder, affects more than 1.5 million people in the UK, and substantially raises the risk of stroke, heart failure and death. Because atrial fibrillation often occurs intermittently, it can be missed on a standard electrocardiogram (ECG). As a consequence, many cases remain undiagnosed until a serious or life-threatening complication occurs.
The team set out to establish whether retinal imaging, already used routinely in community optometry practices and hospital eye clinics, could offer a non-invasive way to flag people with atrial fibrillation before they have a stroke or heart attack.
Researchers analysed optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans and colour retinal photographs from two datasets. In the AlzEye dataset, a Moorfields Eye Hospital cohort with over 50,000 patients, 5,735 already had atrial fibrillation. In the UK Biobank cohort of around 40,000 participants, 526 had atrial fibrillation. Across both datasets, people with atrial fibrillation consistently had thinner macular ganglion cells and inner plexiform layer (mGCIPL), which is a retinal layer at the back of the eye made up of nerve cells that connect the eye to the brain. The thinner this particular layer was, the more likely the person was to be diagnosed with atrial fibrillation.
Notably, among patients who did not have atrial fibrillation when their retinal images were taken, those who went on to develop atrial fibrillation had thinner mGCIPL layers on average four years before presenting to hospital with the condition, even after accounting for age, sex, ethnicity, hypertension, diabetes, smoking and alcohol use. This indicates that retinal changes may be detectable before a clinical diagnosis of atrial fibrillation is made, at a stage when the condition has no symptoms.
The authors propose that the thinning they observed in people who developed or had atrial fibrillation could indicate mini strokes in the brain that typically occur as a result of atrial fibrillation before its diagnosis. The thinning could happen because blood flow to the retinal nerve cells is reduced by these strokes, they say.
This large-scale analysis shows that retinal imaging can pick up on structural changes within the eye that are clearly linked to atrial fibrillation. For patients, the value of this kind of eye imaging is that it is easy to access, quick and doesn't involve any invasive procedures. Although not intended to replace ECG-based diagnosis, retinal imaging could act as a complementary tool, catching those most at risk of atrial fibrillation before it causes real harm."
Dr. Siegfried Wagner, senior author, UCL Institute of Ophthalmology and Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
John's story
Moorfields patient John Brewer first discovered he had atrial fibrillation in the operating theatre, while undergoing a cataract operation under sedation, earlier this year. The surgical team noticed John was experiencing heart arrhythmia and paused the procedure to hook up an ECG, which indicated that John did have atrial fibrillation. Medication was then provided so the operation could be safely completed. John was given an immediate referral to see a cardiologist who has since confirmed the atrial fibrillation diagnosis.
John said: "It would have been so much easier if my atrial fibrillation had been detected earlier through a routine retinal scan at one of my regular appointments, rather than on the operating table, which was a very distressing experience for my wife and I."
Oculomics: Eye tests predicting systemic disease
Lead author Dr Josef Huemer (UCL Institute of Ophthalmology and Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust) commented: "If confirmed in further research, our findings raise the possibility that routine eye examinations could, in future, help identify people who would benefit from closer cardiac assessment, potentially enabling earlier treatment with therapies known to reduce the risk of stroke."
This study adds to growing evidence that high-resolution images of the eye can be used for early detection of systemic disease, a scientific field known as oculomics. The UCL and Moorfields team has been able to identify early signs and predict progression risk of eye conditions including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. The same team has also found markers for Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, cardiovascular disease and stroke.
Oculomics has been made possible by the INSIGHT Eye and Oculomics Health Data Research Hub at Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and UCL Institute of Ophthalmology, the world's largest ophthalmic imaging bioresource, with over 30 million eye images linked to medical records.
The research was supported by: Moorfields Eye Charity; NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Moorfields; NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: University College London Hospitals; NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Great Ormond Street Hospital; NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Barts; and NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Birmingham.
Source:
Journal reference:
Huemer, J., et al. (2026). Atrial fibrillation and retinal imaging-based oculomics: A cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of two large cohorts. PLOS Digital Health. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pdig.0001661. https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article?id=10.1371/journal.pdig.0001661
summary: A new study led by University College London and Moorfields researchers reveals that signs of atrial fibrillation can be detected in the retinas of patients up to four years before a formal diagnosis. By analyzing retinal imaging data from over 90,000 people, researchers found that individuals with the heart condition consistently exhibited a thinner macular ganglion cells and inner plexiform layer. While not replacing standard ECG tests, routine eye scans could serve as a non-invasive complementary tool to identify at-risk patients early.
key_points: Researchers analyzed retinal imaging data from more than 90,000 people across two major datasets.
Individuals with atrial fibrillation consistently showed a thinner mGCIPL retinal layer.
Retinal thinning was detectable up to four years before patients were diagnosed with atrial fibrillation.
The structural changes in the eye may be caused by reduced blood flow from silent mini strokes associated with the condition.
Routine eye examinations could potentially become a non-invasive tool to flag individuals at risk for early cardiac assessment.

title: Bio-warfare is now a clear and present threat, as dangerous as nukes
author: Hamish de Bretton-Gordon
content:
![A British Army practices chemical warfare drills in the Brecon Beacons](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/15/TELEMMGLPICT000143559874_17894851524680_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A British Army practices chemical warfare drills in the Brecon Beacons](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/15/TELEMMGLPICT000143559874_17894851524680_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
As Parliament debates the security risks posed by artificial intelligence this week, there is one threat that deserves far more attention than it is receiving: the possibility that AI could make biological warfare terrifyingly accessible, even if President Trump believes the only thing the planet needs to protect itself from AI is his massive intellect.
For decades, we have treated nuclear weapons as the ultimate weapon of mass destruction. Governments spend billions maintaining deterrents, monitoring proliferation and trying to prevent nuclear technology falling into the wrong hands. Chemical weapons are subject to a similarly rigorous international verification regime.
Biological weapons are different. They remain the poor relation among weapons of mass destruction, frighteningly powerful, comparatively cheap and, most worryingly, inadequately regulated. Now AI is beginning to change the equation.
Anthropic, the American AI company, has reported identifying and disrupting attempts to use its models for malicious activity that could support the development of biological weapons. Its warning is part of a growing chorus from AI researchers that the technology could dramatically lower the expertise and resources required to conduct dangerous biological research. That should set alarm bells ringing in every government.
The nightmare is not simply that AI might become super-intelligent and somehow decide to destroy humanity. A much more plausible danger is that humans use increasingly capable AI systems to design something that nature never intended to exist.
Annie Jacobsen’s recent brilliant book Biological Warfare paints a chilling picture of what could happen if a deliberately engineered pathogen escaped into the world. The nightmare scenario is not difficult to imagine: a highly contagious, highly lethal disease deliberately designed to spread faster than governments can contain it.
![Al-Hakam, an Iraqi facility used to produce biological weapons, destroyed by the UN in 1996](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/15/TELEMMGLPICT000004542311_17894750913230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQUzIfGpr0fw9kIH6pu_3XVzl6B3R2tC_OSh_9z6T9_w.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
AI could accelerate that process by helping bad actors navigate biological science that would previously have required years of specialist knowledge. At the same time, precisely the same technology could transform humanity’s ability to detect outbreaks, model transmission and develop vaccines and treatments. This is, therefore, a race between good and evil.
The uncomfortable truth is that biological weapons are probably the least regulated of the major categories of weapons of mass destruction. The Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention is an important international instrument, but it lacks the verification machinery, resources and political weight enjoyed by the Chemical Weapons Convention. That is a dangerous weakness at precisely the moment biotechnology is advancing at extraordinary speed.
I learnt the psychological power of biological warfare first-hand in Iraq in 2005, when I was commanding British Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) defence forces. On one occasion, we received indications that Al-Qaeda might be attempting to attack British and American forces in southern Iraq with anthrax.
Our detectors indicated a possible biological threat. At the time, only a handful of personnel in theatre were known to be vaccinated against anthrax. Normal military operations had to be halted while we established whether we were facing an attack. For almost 36 hours, the possibility of anthrax hung over our operations.
Thankfully, it was a false alarm. Naturally occurring anthrax had triggered our detection system. But the consequences of those readings were profound. An invisible biological threat, whether real or imagined, can paralyse a military force remarkably quickly.
That experience first brought home to me the extraordinary power of biological warfare, not merely to kill, but to create fear, uncertainty and operational paralysis.
![Hamish de Bretton-Gordon and the Secure Bio team visit the Kurdish city of Halabja in Northern Iraq, 2011](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/15/TELEMMGLPICT000022352639_17894737951430_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf9FFn1uV5BWyM-ZKgzsDfSU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Covid-19 should have been the defining wake-up call for biological security in the 21st century. It demonstrated how quickly a novel pathogen can cross borders, overwhelm health systems and disrupt economies and societies. Whether or not one accepts every theory about the origins of Covid, its consequences demonstrated beyond doubt how vulnerable the modern world is to biological catastrophe.
During my visiting fellowship at Magdalene College Cambridge between 2021 and 2023, I studied some of the emerging dangers from synthetic biology. The extraordinary expansion of genetic engineering should be one of the great achievements of our age. But every powerful technology has a dark side. The question is whether our regulation is keeping pace. At present, I fear it is not and the US president is not helping.
Thousands of laboratories and scientists around the world are working with increasingly sophisticated biological tools. Much of this research is entirely legitimate and potentially transformative. But the distinction between beneficial and malign biological research could become increasingly difficult to police as AI becomes embedded in the process. We must not wait for the first catastrophe before taking this seriously.
Indeed, I am increasingly more worried about biological warfare than nuclear war. That may sound alarmist. It is not. A nuclear weapon remains extraordinarily difficult and expensive to acquire. A biological weapon, particularly one enhanced by AI, could potentially require far fewer resources, and its perpetrators could remain invisible until the damage was already done.
The answer is not to stop AI or biotechnology. That would be both impossible and profoundly damaging. The answer is to regulate the dangerous edges of these technologies internationally, strengthen the Biological Weapons Convention, improve laboratory oversight and invest massively in detection, vaccines and rapid-response capabilities.
Britain can be leading that effort and should be, most especially with Donald Trump talking such utter rubbish to the effect that only he can stem the dangers of AI with his massive intellect, which hitherto has not been evident! We have spent decades preparing for the possibility of nuclear Armageddon. We now need to prepare with equal determination for biological Armageddon.
The most frightening weapon of the future may not be a missile launched from a silo. It may be a microscopic organism designed by a machine, released by a human being, and discovered only when it is already too late.
Col Hamish de Bretton-Gordon commanded UK and Nato CBRN Forces. His memoir Chemical Warrior describes how he dealt with chemical and biological threats around the world
summary: Biological warfare is emerging as a critical and inadequately regulated threat, made increasingly accessible by advancements in artificial intelligence. Unlike nuclear weapons, biological agents can be produced with fewer resources and lower expertise, potentially creating engineered pathogens that spread faster than governments can contain them. Strengthening international regulations, such as the Biological Weapons Convention, and improving detection and defense capabilities are urgently required to prevent a biological catastrophe.
key_points: Biological weapons are currently the least regulated category of weapons of mass destruction compared to nuclear and chemical arms.
Artificial intelligence is lowering the technical expertise and resources required to conduct dangerous biological research and design pathogens.
An invisible biological threat, whether real or a false alarm, can quickly cause fear, uncertainty, and operational paralysis.
International frameworks like the Biological Weapons Convention currently lack the verification machinery and political weight needed to meet modern biotechnology risks.

title: ‘It makes you feel helpless’: patients and doctors cast doubt on standard treatment for endometriosis
author: Denis Campbell
content:
“It’s really frustrating to be in this cycle of continuous surgery. It makes you feel helpless,” says Natalie Greenwood, of a condition that affects her so badly she is “non-functioning most of the time because of the constant fatigue”.
Greenwood, 36, needs to have an operation every few years to limit the impact of the endometriosis that gives her chronic pelvic pain, as well as extreme tiredness and brain fog.
She says the trouble with depending on surgery is not just having an invasive procedure and then having to recover afterwards. It’s more that the benefit gained – the relief from persistent pain – is brief.
She is not alone in her lack of belief in surgery and hormonal medication being effective for chronic pelvic pain. A study has found that dual approach, which is the NHS’s usual way of treating the condition, does not improve quality of life for female patients.
Greenwood was diagnosed with endometriosis 13 years ago, after leaving university. It is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus – the endometrium – is found outside the uterus, most commonly in the pelvic cavity, and can cause inflammation and pain.
![Natalie Greenwood in her home in West Yorkshire](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c31204bc36e8331e7c0f99d931afc94613d07e7d/0_0_8640_5760/master/8640.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Greenwood, who is a languages teacher in West Yorkshire, has already had surgery three times: when she was 23, 28 and 32. In the first two operations she underwent ablation, in which the endometriosis is removed using heat or cold. The last procedure involved excision, in which the surgeon cuts out the endometriosis.
“The surgery is effective in that it can keep the pain at bay for a few more years. But I’ve never come out of it feeling better,” she said. “And in between surgeries I’ve still had to have hormone treatments, like a hormonal coil, or been put into chemical menopause. That keeps the endometriosis at bay by shutting down the hormones that cause it. But the endometriosis keeps growing. So you might feel better for a while but it’s always there in the background.”
Even after surgery, Greenwood has still needed what she calls her “pain management toolkit” – Tens machines, peppermint teabags, cooling patches, hot-water bottles and CBD oil.
Endometriosis is one of the main causes of chronic pelvic pain, a condition that affects between 6% and 27% of women worldwide. Others include vulvodynia and bladder pain syndrome.
“The surgery has never been a magic fix for me,” said Greenwood. “I don’t think it’s a magic fix for many people. You don’t just suddenly feel completely better. A life of surgery every five years is just not something you want to do. It’s not sustainable. It’s like a constant rut.”
Greenwood has a boy of five and is keen to have another child. But endometriosis has affected her fertility so much that she will soon start a course of IVF.
Whatever the outcome of that treatment, she is sure of one thing: “I won’t have surgery again. It’s not manageable to keep having surgery every five years. Whatever happens with the IVF, after it I’m going to have a hysterectomy and my ovaries removed because that might give me some relief from endometriosis.”
Dr Jasmine Hearn, a reader in health psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University who co-led the research in the new study, said: “Sadly patients are often left struggling due to current pain management strategies not sufficiently alleviating pain.
“Chronic pelvic pain is often invisible but its impact can be profound. Our findings highlight that women with pelvic pain report poorer quality of life when they’ve had surgery and hormonal medication for pelvic pain and better quality of life when psychological support is part of treatment.”
The 147 women in the study, who were aged 18 to 66, all reported that their pelvic pain had a major impact on both their physical and psychological quality of life and ability to function normally.
Surgery was found to be associated with lower physical quality of life while painkillers were associated with women having poorer physical, psychological and environmental quality of life.
In contrast, women who received psychological help as part of their treatment to help them manage their pain said their quality of life was better. The evidence for its effectiveness was so great that all those who suffer pelvic pain should be offered it, Hearn added.
Dr Lucy Whitaker, a researcher with the charity Wellbeing of Women and a clinical lecturer in obstetrics and gynaecology at the University of Edinburgh, agreed. She said the same suggestion was made in 2020 by Westminster’s all-party parliamentary group on endometriosis and by a confidential national inquiry into the condition in 2024.
Whitaker added: “Chronic pelvic pain conditions like endometriosis carry a well-documented psychological burden and integrating psychological support alongside medical management reflects a more holistic approach to a condition that has long been under-resourced.”
A spokesperson for NHS England said: “Chronic pelvic pain can have a significant impact on women’s lives and mental health. That’s why psychological professionals provide specialist pain-management support as part of wider physical health services – including for chronic pelvic pain – while women can also self-refer to NHS talking therapies for support with long-term physical health conditions.”
summary: Patients and researchers are casting doubt on standard NHS treatments for endometriosis, such as repeated surgeries and hormonal medication, which provide only brief relief. A recent study found that these dual approaches do not improve quality of life, whereas incorporating psychological support leads to better outcomes. Sufferers like Natalie Greenwood describe the cycle of continuous surgeries as unsustainable and plan to seek alternative solutions.
key_points: A study found that the standard NHS approach of surgery and hormonal medication does not improve quality of life for women with chronic pelvic pain.
Patients who received psychological support as part of their treatment reported a better quality of life.
Surgery was specifically found to be associated with a lower physical quality of life.
Endometriosis affects between 6% and 27% of women worldwide and carries a heavy physical and psychological burden.

title: Pennsylvania officials report fourth measles-associated death in 'surge' of cases
author: Madeline Halpert
content:
![Measles vaccine](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/4227/live/424ef8c0-b139-11f1-8e7a-7b6c4dcbe4b5.jpg)
- Published
A fourth person has died from complications related to measles in Pennsylvania, say state officials, in an outbreak that has infected hundreds of people.
An 18-year-old died from acute encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of measles, the Mifflin County Coroner's Office in Pennsylvania said.
The Keystone state has seen over 600 cases of measles this year, primarily in Lancaster County.
The US eliminated measles in 2000 with the help of vaccines, but it has this year experienced the highest number of deaths from the virus since the 1990s.
Last year, three people - including two children - died from a measles outbreak in Texas that spread predominantly among the Mennonite community.
The rising number of cases has come as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates.
In Pennsylvania, state and local officials have said the 18-year-old and a 40-year-old - both unvaccinated - died from measles-related complications over the past month.
Two infants have also died. US children typically do not receive their first MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine until 12 months of age.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented.
The highly contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia.
To achieve herd immunity, around 95% of the population must have the vaccine, say health officials.
Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro posted on X on Tuesday: "This disease was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 - yet decades later, we are seeing it surge due to lower vaccination rates."
