The reporting of the deaths in Pennsylvania has led to tensions between Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about vaccines and has said he would withhold information about the deaths from the top health official in order to protect the families of the deceased.
Kennedy has questioned whether the infant deaths were in fact from measles.
A 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, on Saturday, with the coroner saying the cause of death was respiratory failure due to measles.
Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni said a six-week-old born with a rare genetic condition, Amish lethal microcephaly, died of measles on 18 August.
Diamantoni has said another infant who tested positive for measles died soon after birth on 14 August, with the primary cause of death listed as a spleen laceration.
Measles infections can cause the spleen to enlarge, raising the risk of rupture. State health officials have said the death was from a measles infection that resulted in a spleen rupture.
In a post on X after the first two deaths in the state, Kennedy accused Shapiro of "political grandstanding".
The health secretary said the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would only update its information on deaths once reviews were complete.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it had conducted "rigorous investigations" with the coroner's offices to confirm that the latest two deaths were indeed from measles.
"These investigations included confirming clinical evidence of a measles infection, a positive laboratory test, and that the death was not due to an unrelated cause," the health department said.
In November, a panel is set to decide whether the US will lose its status of having eliminated measles, which Canada lost last year.
Kennedy has been criticised by public health experts who argue his remarks and remaking of US vaccine policy has hindered efforts to stop the outbreaks.
A vaccine sceptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, which has proven safe and effective.
The health secretary has said the worsening measles outbreak is a global problem.
Speaking before a Senate committee last month, he said: "A lot of nations have lost their elimination status. The whole world had their worst measles year."
summary: Pennsylvania officials have reported a fourth measles-associated death during a surge of over 600 cases in the state this year. The latest victim was an 18-year-old who died from acute encephalomyelitis, joining two infants and a 40-year-old woman among the fatalities. The rising case numbers and deaths are linked to lower immunization rates and increased vaccine hesitancy, sparking tensions between Governor Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
key_points: Pennsylvania has recorded over 600 measles cases this year, primarily centered in Lancaster County.
Four measles-associated deaths have been reported in the state, including an 18-year-old, a 40-year-old, and two infants.
Health officials state that the individuals who died from measles-related complications were unvaccinated.
Governor Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. have clashed over vaccine messaging and the verification of the reported deaths.
The US measles surge is attributed to growing vaccine hesitancy and lower immunization rates, threatening the country's measles elimination status.

title: I lived like a 90-year-old Italian for a month and my health was transformed
author: Rosie Taylor
content:
![Rosie Taylor in Liguria, Italy, 2026,](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501652305_17889477274210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq6LhdSp3_3r2qHGh5ZxYWxiXzMUtuA8TWLPeztUfUplI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Rosie Taylor in Liguria, Italy, 2026,](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501652305_17889477274210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq6LhdSp3_3r2qHGh5ZxYWxiXzMUtuA8TWLPeztUfUplI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Amid the woodland-covered mountains of upper Liguria, in northern Italy, you can find small villages with clusters of houses made of terracotta and stone – and some of Europe’s longest-living residents.
When I first stayed in this area for an extended period a few years ago, I noticed my chronic joint pain and fatigue disappeared, only to quickly return once I was back in the UK. Was it the weather, or had the Ligurian lifestyle turned back the clock at a more fundamental level?
Italy is home to the oldest population in Europe, and new research by the University of Salerno shows Liguria is now the region with the greatest proportion of people living into their 90s, beating the country’s Blue Zone region of Sardinia.
So, what’s its secret? Determined to find out, I spent a month living in a mountain village in Liguria this summer with my husband and six-year-old son. I had no intention of skimping on pasta or wine, but I was keen to monitor how this new lifestyle affected my health.
![A village in the mountains of Liguria, northern Italy](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/09/14/TELEMMGLPICT000502999666_17893846605940_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqgsaO8O78rhmZrDxTlQBjdLdu0TL-Cg_AMOUqySXmFgU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Before I left, I recorded my weight, waist circumference, BMI and blood pressure, and checked my cholesterol levels with One Day Tests, which has private clinics around the UK. I also tracked my daily activity levels with a smartwatch.
At 39, my health was deemed normal for my age, but joint issues and a sedentary desk job meant I was quite unfit. The clinic’s Dr David Weinstein, a longevity expert, said this could reduce my “healthspan”.
Taking pride in the ageing process
Within days of arriving in Liguria, we were invited by a neighbour to a street party in a small square that connects the cobbled alleys. Everyone brought a home-cooked dish and ate together under the grapevines. I explained to a group of older women that I was writing about my trip for an article, and they delighted in asking me to guess their ages. “Can you believe I’m 82?” exclaimed Anna*, who could easily pass for 60. The eldest, Silvia*, 87, a self-proclaimed “la campionessa” (female champion) of ageing, said she still walks up hills each day without the use of a stick.
![Rosie enjoyed fresh, locally grown fruit and vegetables during a month in Liguria](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501652296_17889477261715_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The women I spoke to – all aged between 75 and 87 – believe a mix of breathing clean air, eating nutritious food, being actively part of a community and navigating steep hills daily improves both the quality and the length of their lives here. “We don’t live like this back in Milan,” explained Maria*, 75, who stays in the mountains for summer. The rest of the time she looks after her grandchildren while her daughter works long hours in the city.
While older women here are always well turned-out, few have had any “tweakments” to alter their looks, and they all wear bikinis at the beach or river, regardless of their age, shape or size. Ageing bodies are considered a badge of honour, rather than something to hide.
Navigating steep hills and cobbled streets
None of the elderly villagers I met used walking sticks or aids. That could be partly because constantly climbing steep cobbled streets and stone steps improves core strength and balance.
Indeed, it is not difficult to keep physically active in a Ligurian village, most of which were built centuries ago on precipitous slopes to protect against invaders. Apart from one main road, built in the 1960s, every street in our village is steep, cobbled and too narrow for cars. Most villagers have no option but to walk up and down daily to get everything they need.
![Rosie Taylor in Liguria, Italy, 2026](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501652289_17889477276117_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhQelLrTDvVmMF_2MRiRVvbxlL4JJZFr6G2BGlsAngeI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In my first few days in Liguria, I struggled for breath as I walked up the steep paths at more than 1,500ft above sea level, while my neighbours in their 80s waited for me to catch up. However, within two weeks I found myself striding up the uneven cobbles carrying a heavy bag of fresh vegetables from the village shop without pausing.
Unlike in the UK, where I have to push myself to take walks or go for a run, I didn’t do any formal exercise in Italy, except for adopting the local tradition of taking a daily dip in the river to cool off. Yet, on average, I racked up 8,000 steps walking around the house and village each day (2,000 more than I would usually manage at home), and climbed the equivalent of 40 flights of stairs.
“Keeping active by walking, climbing stairs or gardening helps build and maintain strength – it’s much better for you than living a sedentary lifestyle and doing a Pilates class once a week,” notes Dr Weinstein. “We need to keep consistently active and strong in our 60s and 70s to reduce our risk of falls as we go into our 80s and 90s.”
Eating simple, seasonal food
I was also struck by how much simpler and less processed the food is here in comparison to the British diet. Back home I often grab an ultra-processed supermarket meal deal for lunch. In Liguria, you can pick up a slice of home-made torta verde – a delicious pastry filled with rice, seasonal vegetables, egg and parmesan – for just €2 (£1.70). Reducing ultra-processed foods in your diet is key to healthy ageing and weight control, advises Dr Weinstein. “When you eat real, fresh food which contains fibre, you feel much fuller so you eat less.”
![Fresh, seasonal ingredients are at the heart of Liguria's traditional diet](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501652303_17889477263302_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqiMxc5qUdCFqatIlsqmFP00vl8kzSrCvaP9vcmuEVRMQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The traditional Ligurian diet is built around home-grown vegetables, olive oil, pulses and foraged ingredients, with meat like rabbit and wild boar eaten more rarely. It’s a diet that stems from rural poverty in a rugged landscape, where crops and livestock are hard to farm. Even snails (lumache) are a traditional source of protein here.
It was impossible to fully replicate the traditional diet in just a month, though. Many locals grow all the vegetables they need in meticulously maintained allotments, whereas we could only buy what was available in the village shop. Plus, with a six-year-old who is unenthusiastic about cured wild boar, our family meals consisted of far more pasta and pizza than is traditional.
Still, even the pizza is freshly handmade with local ingredients. We swapped butter for olive oil, gathered blackberries and ate sun-warmed figs from the tree. Here, a simple plate of spaghetti with fresh tomatoes, trombette (curved, pale courgettes) and olive oil is delicious and nutritious. In the UK it would taste bland, as our supermarket produce is so often shipped in chilled containers or artificially forced to ripen, reducing its nutritional value.
Enjoying a strong community spirit
There is a strong sense of community among long-lived Ligurian villagers, which came as no surprise to me: research shows “super-agers” (those over 80 with the same brain function and memory skills as a middle-aged adult) tend to have lots of positive social relationships.
In the first few weeks of August alone, our village hosted a history talk, a film screening, a classical music concert, two village parties with food, live music and dancing, and a children’s magic show – all free to attend and funded by the village council. In the UK, similar events are usually ticketed and extortionately priced, often making you feel ripped off instead of welcome.
![Rosie Taylor in Liguria, Italy, 2026, , for health piece on blue zone village ... Ligurians of all ages dance at a community party](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501652304_17889477260401_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqrfzZskasdHxLRTTh7do0m47e1lkwS0JKUaHflh0HnsI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
That the authorities are willing to invest so much in these activities reflects the huge cultural importance that social interaction has here, with research showing that simply feeling included is key to ageing well. “Studies have found loneliness can be as bad at reducing your longevity as smoking, so it’s fundamental to stay socially active as you age,” adds Dr Weinstein.
Living a Ligurian lifestyle in the UK
Back in the UK, I had another health check and was surprised to find that I’d lost 1.6kg (3lb) and more than 2in from my waist, despite eating as much as I liked. My overall BMI score had also dropped.
However, my total cholesterol had slightly increased. Before the holiday my total cholesterol was 3.92, when I returned it had gone up to 4.28 (mmol/L) – a slight rise within normal range. Dr Weinstein suggested this could reflect my increased intake of healthy fats, like olive oil, which boost “good” HDL cholesterol. He warned that the slight rise in my “bad” LDL cholesterol, from LDL 1.85 to 2.27 (mmol/L), could be due to my failing to strictly adhere to the tradition of only having wine with food and increasing my alcohol intake over summer. It’s a reality check that even a month of hill walking can’t undo the damage caused by alcohol.
What I’ve really noticed is the difference in my fitness levels. Now, I can walk up the steep hill on my commute while chatting on the phone without having to pause for breath. Although my blood pressure is unchanged at 102/68, I’m confident that maintaining this level of fitness will help to protect my health as I age.
With high living costs and long working hours, it is not realistic for many Britons to live on home-grown vegetables and freshly caught rabbit, but there are parts of the Ligurian lifestyle I plan to replicate at home: eating simple, local, seasonal food; engaging with community events; and making sure I get outside in the fresh air each day.
I’ve even promised myself I’d keep walking up that steep hill instead of taking the bus. As Silvia – la campionessa of ageing – told me: “Walking the hills every day keeps you young.”
*Names have been changed
summary: A journalist spent a month living in a mountain village in Liguria, Italy—a region known for its exceptionally long-living residents—to observe how the local lifestyle affected her health. Without doing formal exercise or dieting, she naturally increased her daily steps, improved her core strength through steep hill walking, and ate simpler, seasonal foods, resulting in a measurable loss of weight and waist circumference. Her experience highlighted that consistent physical activity, fresh local diets, and a strong community spirit are central to healthy ageing.
key_points: Liguria is a region in northern Italy with one of the greatest proportions of people living into their 90s.
Constant navigation of steep, cobbled village streets naturally improved the author's fitness, step count, and strength without formal workouts.
The local diet relies on fresh, seasonal, and minimally processed ingredients like home-grown vegetables and olive oil rather than ultra-processed foods.
A strong sense of community and frequent social events help combat loneliness, which is closely linked to longevity.
After one month living this lifestyle, the author lost 1.6kg and over two inches from her waist while eating as much as she liked.

title: The 10,000-Steps Myth Is Dead. Here's What Science Says Works Instead
author: David Nield
content:
We know, broadly speaking, that staying active keeps us healthy, and getting in a certain amount of steps each day is a simple way to go about it.
What's not as clear are the combinations of time, distance, and briskness that work best for getting those steps in.
The opportunity to get out for a daily stroll isn't equally available to everyone, whether it's due to schedule pressures, health conditions, or other circumstances.
For some people especially, knowing the most optimum ways to boost health can be really useful.
In a new study in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, researchers led by a team from the University of Sydney analyzed records from more than 64,000 middle-aged individuals in a large health research database, following them for an average of eight years.
![Mortality risk chart](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/09/MortalityChart.jpg)
Step counts and stepping intensity were cross-referenced against deaths and cause of death across the study period, to find relationships between exercise habits and health outcomes over several years.
The biggest takeaway is that people don't have to hit 10,000 steps a day to see benefits from walking.
"That heavily quoted step target actually came from a 1960s Japanese pedometer campaign rather than from evidence," says behavioral scientist Nicholas Koemel from Monash University.
"The important message is that every step counts, and how you take those steps can also matter."
What the researchers found is that a variety of step counts and intensities were associated with lower mortality risk.
"Most prior step-related studies focused on intensity and amount in isolation, resulting in a paucity of evidence understanding the joint relationship between volume and intensity of total daily steps," write the researchers in their published paper.
"Our study, using a large prospective cohort coupled with an advanced accelerometry algorithm to identify steps, examined different step-based strategies associated with all-cause mortality (ACM) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality risk."
For analysis, the participants were sorted into four groups: those taking under 5,000 steps a day, then 5,000–7,500 steps a day, 7,500–10,000 steps a day, and people taking more than 10,000 steps a day.
Some interesting patterns emerged.
For example, there was a similar and substantial reduction in mortality risk for those walking less than 5,000 steps a day but walking briskly (around 80 steps per minute), and those walking between 5,000-7,500 steps a day but doing them more slowly (around 60 steps per minute).
In other words, if you don't have time to cram in 7,500 steps as you would like, try walking with more intensity – it may well have the same health benefits. If you can't walk quickly, see if you can clock up more steps instead.
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
Reaching a peak 30-minute cadence of around 90–100 steps per minute – averaged across the 30 highest-cadence minutes of the day – was something of a sweet spot, the researchers found, and could be a useful health target.
Taking the pace out of the equation, meanwhile, 7,500–10,000 steps per day was linked to the lowest mortality risk.
"Our findings contribute to the evidence base for step-based approaches targeting both daily step counts and stepping intensity to lower risk, and may inform step-based interventions for middle-aged and older adults, particularly individuals with barriers to increasing daily step counts or stepping intensity," write the researchers.
The observational nature of the study means cause and effect can't be proven – the researchers only observed what was happening, rather than testing different scenarios against each other. Step activity was only recorded for part of the study period, and may have changed over time.
Even though multiple factors were accounted for in the data, including diet and age, there may have been other 'hidden' influences affecting both step count and mortality risk (such as illness or social isolation).
Related: One Factor in Walking May Improve Your Heart Health More Than Your Step Count
Despite those limitations though, the extended study period and large number of participants make this a useful reference for future health guidelines – and it seems likely that a simple daily step count isn't all that matters.
"Our study moves beyond single-metric approaches (eg, focusing solely on daily step counts) to examine combinations of different step dimensions in relation to mortality risk, informing future step-related public health and clinical guidelines," write the researchers.
The research has been published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.
summary: A new study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine analyzed data from over 64,000 middle-aged individuals to examine how daily step volume and walking intensity jointly impact mortality risk. The researchers found that people do not need to reach the popular 10,000-steps target to gain health benefits, as lower step counts combined with higher intensity can yield similar reductions in mortality risk. Conversely, walking at a slower pace can be offset by taking more total steps.
key_points: The 10,000-steps target originated from a 1960s Japanese pedometer campaign rather than scientific evidence.
A brisk walk of around 80 steps per minute under 5,000 steps a day showed similar mortality risk reduction to walking 5,000–7,500 steps slowly at around 60 steps per minute.
A peak 30-minute cadence of 90–100 steps per minute served as a beneficial health target.
Taking 7,500 to 10,000 steps per day without factoring in pace was linked to the lowest overall mortality risk.
Limitations of the study include its observational nature, meaning direct cause and effect could not be proven.

title: Reading for pleasure cuts dementia risk by third, Cambridge study finds
author: Laura Donnelly
content:
Prof Barbara Sahakian and Dr Christelle Langley, from the department of psychiatry at Cambridge, published a review of the science in the journal Psychological Medicine.
Overall, the study found that reading at any age improved brain and mental health, leads to better cognitive performance and reduces the risk of mental decline.
“Survey data in adults suggested that reading was associated with reduced stress, greater empathy, enhanced wellbeing, and decreased loneliness,” the study said.
“Studies further indicate that cognitively stimulating activities, particularly reading, are associated with a lower risk of dementia and slower cognitive decline, even among individuals with lower educational attainment.
“Neuroimaging findings suggest that reading is associated with structural and functional differences in brain regions supporting executive control, emotional regulation and social cognition. Importantly, these benefits appear independent of socioeconomic background.”
Children who read lead healthier lifestyles
Another study included in the review, which examined more than 10,000 young people, found that children who began reading for pleasure early in life had a better attention span, memory, and executive functioning, such as when it came to problem solving.
They also fared better at school, had fewer mental-health problems and led healthier lifestyles – including more sleep and less screen time.
Dr Langley said: “Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
“The important thing is to find something they’d really enjoy reading about – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in.
“Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
Book clubs also promote social connection, the study found.
summary: A Cambridge University review published in Psychological Medicine found that reading for pleasure at any age improves mental health, enhances cognitive performance, and reduces the risk of dementia. The study also revealed that children who read early in life exhibit better attention spans, memory, and academic performance, alongside healthier lifestyles involving more sleep and less screen time. Furthermore, neuroimaging indicates that reading is linked to structural and functional brain differences that support executive control, emotional regulation, and social cognition.
key_points: Reading for pleasure is associated with a lower risk of dementia and slower cognitive decline.
Adult surveys indicate that reading reduces stress, increases empathy, and decreases loneliness.
Children who start reading early show better attention spans, memory, and problem-solving skills.
Early reading in youth is linked to fewer mental health problems and healthier lifestyles, such as less screen time.
Reading benefits appear independent of socioeconomic background and educational attainment.

title: St Albans woman learns donated umbilical cord saved child's life
author: Louise Parry
content:
![Jade as a toddler smiling widely at the camera with four baby teeth showing. She is standing and leaning on a baby-walker.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/25f6/live/96230bf0-b01f-11f1-95e6-93ee8a80cb38.jpg)
Jade Reed was born in 1996, the same year the NHS launched its cord blood bank
- Published
A 30-year-old woman said it was "incredible" to learn her donated umbilical cord was used by the NHS to save a child's life in Australia.
Jade Reed from St Albans, Hertfordshire, became the first person whose stem cells were used for emergency treatment via the NHS cord blood bank after it launched in 1996.
The process is anonymous so the NHS was unable to give full details of the beneficiary - but to mark the blood bank's 30th anniversary, Jade and her mum were told their donation helped a child with blood cancer.
"My cord blood went across the world to save the life of another child, when I was a toddler, it's insane - just mad," said Jade on hearing the news.
"My best friend had blood cancer as a child so it seems fitting to have helped someone in similar circumstances, that means a lot.
"It's amazing my cord blood went all that way to Australia," she added.
![A grainy photo showing mum Sharon in a hospital bed holding newborn Jade, wrapped in swaddling blankets. Sharon has curly dark hair and a fringe.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/94ff/live/2822d710-b020-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Jade's mum Sharon says it was "special" to be one of the bank's earliest donors
Run by the NHS Blood and Transplant service (NHSBT), the bank in Bristol has now issued more than 1,000 units.
Umbilical cords are rich in stem cells and the cord blood can be donated after birth without impacting baby or mother.
It is cryogenically frozen until a match is found.
Jade's cord was donated in 1996 and transported to Australia in 1998, becoming the first cord blood issued.
"I've always known we donated, my mum talks about it. It's nice to have been part of the early days," she said.
"It's done what we wanted the donation to do, save a life.
"You're not going to use it, there's nothing you can really do with it, why not donate it to help someone?" Jade added.
![A close up shot of a worker's hands selecting frozen samples of stored blood. They wear blue gloves and a white protective jacket. One vial is open and you can see blood in it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/acef/live/0703fc20-b02b-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
The donated cord blood is stored at -196C until a match is found
Jade's mum Sharon Keough, 52, said: "I thought it was quite amazing you could donate your cord blood and was happy to.
"To hear I was one of the early donors is special. When I was told our unit was the first one issued, I was blown away.
"I am really pleased, especially as we helped a child."
Sharon added: "We've done a good thing, why wouldn't you do that? It was so easy.
"I couldn't ask for more, to have had 30 years of Jade and to know we've saved a life."
![Sharon and Jade smiling for a selfie on the beach with the sea behind them. Jade wears sunglasses and the both wear blue hoodies.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d7d5/live/a35ecfc0-b02e-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Sharon and Jade are thrilled to learn their donation was used to save a child's life
NHSBT said its bank had provided stem cell transplants to 355 patients in the UK and 613 people overseas, including in Australia, the US, Brazil and Hong Kong.
The donations have helped more than 515 adults and more than 450 children, many of whom needed treatment for cancers, immune conditions and genetic disorders.
Alex Ross, the head of NHSBT's cord blood bank, said the 30th anniversary was "a special moment to thank the tens of thousands of mums and babies who have donated cord blood, and continue to do so at the maternity units we work with.
"The generosity of new mums means something that is otherwise thrown away goes on to save lives here and around the world - many of them children."
Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.
summary: A 30-year-old woman from St Albans has learned that her umbilical cord, donated to the NHS cord blood bank in 1996, was used to save the life of a child with blood cancer in Australia. Jade Reed was the first person whose stem cells were used for emergency treatment via the NHS cord blood bank after it launched. Her mother, Sharon, expressed pride in being one of the bank's earliest donors and helping save a life.
key_points: Jade Reed's umbilical cord was donated in 1996 and transported to Australia in 1998, becoming the first cord blood issued by the NHS cord blood bank.
The donation was used to save the life of a child suffering from blood cancer.
The NHS cord blood bank, run by NHS Blood and Transplant in Bristol, has now issued more than 1,000 units for patients in the UK and overseas.
Umbilical cord blood is rich in stem cells, can be donated safely after birth, and is cryogenically frozen until a match is found.

title: Drug firms’ secret data supercharge AI protein models
author: Callaway; Ewen
content:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
Artificial-intelligence-based models of protein structure could be improved by incorporating data from pharmaceutical companies.Credit: Miyako Nakamura/Getty
For drug discovery, protein-folding models such as AlphaFold have a data problem: there isn’t enough of it in public databases. Improving the performance of these artificial-intelligence-based tools will require extra data that provide examples of how proteins and drugs interact, some scientists argue.
Protein structures— locked away by the thousands in drug company vaults— offer one promising source. Today, a consortium of pharmaceutical companies reports that using such data to train AI models of protein folding improves model performance markedly.
The group used OpenFold3 — an open-source replication of AlphaFold 3 — to develop a new model trained on more than 20,000 proprietary protein structures. The system outperformed both comparable ones trained on public data alone and those trained on the siloed datasets of individual firms. The study, described in a blog post, has not been peer-reviewed, and the model is not publicly available.
“You add all this data, and you get a pretty big bump in performance,” says Mohammed AlQuraishi, a computational biologist at Columbia University in New York City, who was part of the effort.
The findings, he says, strengthen the case for generating similar publicly available datasets to supercharge protein-folding AIs. One such project, called OpenBind and supported by up to £8 million (US$10.8 million) in UK government funding, released hundreds of new protein structures last month, with thousands more in the works.
The model’s successors, including AlphaFold 3, added the ability to predict how proteins will interact with other molecules, including potential drugs. But the PDB has relatively few examples of experimentally determined structures interacting with drug-like molecules — maybe just 10,000, says Paul Mortenson, vice-president for computational chemistry and informatics at Astex Pharmaceuticals in Cambridge, UK.
That lack of data is a problem for drug-discovery efforts. Research has suggested that the accuracy of AlphaFold 3 and other ‘co-folding’ models — which predict the structure of proteins interacting with each other — drops off a cliff when the models are challenged to predict interactions between molecules highly dissimilar to those on which they were trained1.
To make such tools more useful in drug discovery, researchers say, they need access to more data — which is why they have turned to vaults of molecular structures from pharmaceutical companies.
These data are generated during drug-discovery programmes, using techniques such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy. Many of the protein structures have never been deposited in public databases because they relate to proprietary drug-development efforts. The total size of these vaults is unknown, but some have estimated that they could contain more data than the PDB does.
“The data that’s missing from the PDB is exactly the data that’s present in our internal data,” John Karanicolas, head of computational drug discovery at the pharma company AbbVie in Chicago, Illinois, told Nature last year.
Better predictions
To test whether their data could be useful for protein-folding models, AbbVie, Astex and several other drug companies last year formed a collaboration called the AI Structural Biology (AISB) Network.
It involved ‘fine-tuning’ OpenFold3 – previously trained only with PDB data – on an additional 20,167 structures capturing proteins bound to potential drugs, or ligands. The structures came from five companies and were provided to the model in such a way that proprietary data remained private.
The AISB study found that the extra data enhanced predictions. When tested on 1,056 protein–ligand structures that were set aside from the training data, the AISB model predicted more than half of them to a high level of accuracy. By contrast, the publicly available version of OpenFold3 achieved the same performance on just one-third of the structures, and a competing open-source model called Boltz-2 achieved around 40%. The team plans to submit a paper describing the work to a peer-reviewed journal.
The fact that the AISB model also outperformed co-folding tools that were trained only on each company’s individual data highlights the benefits of pooling information, says Karanicolas.

summary: AI protein-folding models currently face a data shortage regarding how proteins and drugs interact, limiting their effectiveness in drug discovery. To address this, a consortium of pharmaceutical companies trained an open-source model using more than 20,000 proprietary protein structures from industry vaults. The resulting model significantly outperformed versions trained solely on public data or isolated company datasets.
key_points: Public databases lack sufficient examples of protein-drug interactions needed to improve AI drug-discovery tools.
A pharmaceutical consortium formed the AI Structural Biology Network to test proprietary data on OpenFold3.
Training the model on over 20,000 proprietary protein structures markedly improved its predictive accuracy compared to public models.
The findings highlight the benefits of pooling siloed industry data to enhance artificial intelligence models.

title: Men and women are turning to genital fillers for pleasure and size – here’s what can go wrong
author: Adam Taylor
content:
Fillers are everywhere now – smoothing lines, plumping cheeks, adding volume around the eyes, nose and lips in clinics up and down the country. But some men are now having fillers injected into their penises to increase their size.
These fillers often contain hyaluronic acid, a substance naturally found in the body that draws water into the tissues – which is why it can smooth wrinkles and fine lines.
When injected into the penis, it can increase girth. One Korean study found an average girth increase (flaccid) of 2.3cm, or almost 30%. However, more than half of men who had hyaluronic acid filler needed an average of 1.5 further retouch injections to “correct contour irregularities”.
One issue is that the results don’t last forever. The body naturally produces an enzyme called hyaluronidase, which gradually breaks the filler down. By 18 months, about 44% of the increase from the injection has been lost. Repeat injections are needed to maintain the effect.
In situations where filler injections have gone wrong, this does also mean that the effects can be reversed with hyaluronidase injections, although this takes a few hours to work.
![A tape measure against an orange background.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/755739/original/file-20260824-50-41h8ib.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
Not without harms
Research is limited when it comes to the risks, but a recent study estimated that complications occur in about 9% of men receiving hyaluronic acid fillers.
These complications can include bruising and swelling, as well as lumps and nodules. More serious problems include skin irritation, tissue breakdown and infections.
The timing of these problems can vary. Bleeding and bruising tend to occur during the first week or two. Nodules may appear around the third week. Infections often appear around six or seven weeks after treatment, although they can occur years later.
In severe cases, infection can progress rapidly to multiple organ failure. There have also been cases of tissue death requiring part of the penis to be removed. And in March, social media influencer Igho Ubiribo, known as “Ego”, died from a pulmonary embolism following a penis filler procedure in Thailand.
Hyaluronic acid is not the only way men are trying to increase penis size. Another option involves taking fat from elsewhere in the body and injecting it into the penis. This carries its own risks.
These include injecting fat into the wrong area, as well as swelling and bruising. Men can also develop lumps or deformities caused by uneven fat distribution or the death of the injected fat.
There is also the risk of infection with bacteria such as S aureus or E coli. In the most serious cases, tissue can die or the patient can die from a fat embolism.
A procedure marketed to men and women
Another treatment being offered for sexual enhancement is PRP, or platelet-rich plasma.
These injections are not just marketed to men. The so-called “P-shot”, or priapus shot, is promoted for men, while the “O-shot”, or orgasm shot, is marketed to women.
The treatment involves taking blood from the patient’s arm and spinning it at high speed to separate the different components. The platelet-rich part is then injected into the target area.
The claims surrounding PRP can be broad, and “enhancement” can mean very different things.
PRP is not intended to increase penis size. Instead, it has been promoted as a way to improve appearance, blood flow and nerve function.
For women, the O-shot involves injections into the labia or clitoris. It is claimed to increase vaginal sensation, improve sexual satisfaction and make it easier to achieve orgasm. However, the evidence for these claims is weak.
PRP has been studied in men with erectile dysfunction, and one review found evidence of moderate improvements. However, a more recent study suggests the benefit may be smaller than previously thought.
In women, PRP has also been studied as a treatment for stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse. A systematic review found some improvement in symptoms.
Even so, the European Association of Urology says there isn’t enough evidence to recommend PRP for erectile dysfunction.
This is an important point when considering cosmetic and sexual enhancement treatments.
Many of these procedures began as treatments for medical conditions affecting the same parts of the body. But treating a medical problem is not the same as changing someone’s appearance.
When it comes to the penis and reproductive organs, appearance also has little bearing on fertility or the ability to produce children.
Many of these treatments promise a quick improvement in appearance or sexual function. But until we have larger, better-quality studies, it is difficult to know whether those benefits are worth the potential risks.
summary: Men and women are increasingly turning to genital procedures, such as hyaluronic acid fillers, fat injections, and platelet-rich plasma (PRP), to enhance size, appearance, and sexual function. However, these treatments carry various risks, ranging from minor issues like bruising and lumps to severe complications such as infections, tissue death, and even death. Many procedures lack robust supporting evidence, and medical organizations note that more research is needed to determine if the potential benefits outweigh the risks.
key_points: Hyaluronic acid fillers can increase flaccid penis girth by an average of about 30%, but results are temporary and degrade over time.
Complications from genital fillers include bruising, swelling, lumps, infections, tissue breakdown, and in severe cases, tissue death or death.
Fat transfer is another method used for penile enlargement, carrying risks such as uneven fat distribution, lumps, infections, and fat embolisms.
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatments, such as the 'P-shot' and 'O-shot,' are marketed for sexual enhancement in both men and women, though evidence supporting their claims is often weak.
Major medical bodies, such as the European Association of Urology, state there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend PRP for conditions like erectile dysfunction.

title: Not just tea: As a study finds hot beverages raise cancer risk, we look at 5 foods Indians love eating piping hot
author: Aadya Jha
content:
A steaming cup of chai is a familiar comfort across Indian homes. But tea is not the only thing people enjoy straight from the stove. From hot rotis to fresh pakoras, many everyday favourites reach the plate while they are still almost too hot to touch.
The concern is not the food itself. Repeatedly consuming food or drinks at extremely high temperatures may damage the lining of the oesophagus, or food pipe, and increase the risk of certain cancers. A large study of nearly 10 lakh adults in the UK has added important evidence to this connection.
2/6
What the study found about very hot drinks
Researchers analysed data from 977,282 adults in two large UK studies. During follow-up, 2,348 people developed oesophageal cancer. Those who preferred very hot drinks had more than three times the risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma compared with those who preferred warm drinks. The study also found a higher risk among people who drank six or more hot drinks daily.
The findings do not mean that every hot cup of tea causes cancer. They point to a possible risk from repeated exposure to very high temperatures.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization, classifies beverages consumed above 65°C as probably carcinogenic to humans, specifically in relation to oesophageal cancer. Its assessment concerns the temperature, not tea or coffee as a whole.
3/6
Here are 5 other foods Indians enjoy piping hot but could be dangerous.
Roti and paratha  Fresh rotis and parathas often go straight from the tawa to the plate. A few minutes of cooling can make them easier to eat and reduce the chance of burning the mouth.
Samosa and kachori  The crisp outside can hide an intensely hot potato, pea or lentil filling. Breaking one open and allowing the steam to escape is a small but useful habit.
Dal and sambar  Hot dal, sambar and rasam are staples in many Indian kitchens. They are best enjoyed warm enough to eat comfortably, rather than immediately after boiling.
Soup and rasam  A steaming bowl can feel soothing, especially during cold weather. But the heat can linger beneath the surface, so tasting a small spoonful first is sensible.
Idli and other steamed foods  Fresh idlis, dhoklas and steamed snacks can retain considerable heat inside. Allowing them to cool slightly before eating helps avoid repeated thermal irritation.
These foods are not established causes of cancer simply because they are served hot. The concern is the temperature at which they are consumed. Research on very hot food and beverages, including a study from Malawi and Tanzania, has also examined the relationship between thermal exposure and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
4/6
Doctor explains why temperature matters
Dr Shubham Vatsya, Director and Head of Department, Gastro Sciences, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, explained that repeated exposure to extreme heat can affect the food pipe.
“When they are very hot, tea, coffee or other drink can be harmless, but if they are exposed to very high temperature repeatedly, it may cause damage to the lining of the oesophagus or food pipe. The oesophagus is sensitive and repeated thermal damage can lead to years of inflammation and damage to the inside lining of the oesophagus.”
He added that the temperature matters more than whether the drink is tea, coffee or another beverage. Repeated injury and healing may damage the cells lining the food pipe over time. Smoking and alcohol use remain important risk factors for oesophageal cancer as well.
5/6
A simple habit that can help
There is no need to give up tea, coffee, dal or favourite snacks. Letting them cool before eating or drinking is a practical way to avoid unnecessary heat exposure.
Dr Vatsya offered a simple guideline, “If the beverage is hot enough to burn your lips, mouth or throat, then it is too hot for you.”
Persistent difficulty or pain while swallowing, unexplained weight loss, food getting stuck, ongoing chest discomfort or persistent heartburn should not be ignored. These symptoms can have several causes, but a doctor should evaluate them if they continue.
6/6
Medical experts consulted
This article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:
Dr Shubham Vatsya, Director and Head of Department, Gastro Sciences, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital.
Inputs were used to explain how consuming food and drinks at extremely high temperatures may increase oesophageal cancer risk and why allowing them to cool before consumption is a simple precaution.
summary: Recent research and health organizations indicate that repeatedly consuming foods and beverages at extremely high temperatures can damage the oesophageal lining and increase the risk of certain cancers. A large UK study found that individuals preferring very hot drinks faced a significantly higher risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Medical experts advise letting hot foods like tea, rotis, soups, and snacks cool slightly before eating to prevent thermal injury.
key_points: Consuming very hot food and drinks repeatedly can damage the lining of the oesophagus and increase oesophageal cancer risk.
A study of nearly 10 lakh adults in the UK showed that those who preferred very hot drinks had more than three times the risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies beverages consumed above 65°C as probably carcinogenic to humans.
Popular Indian foods served piping hot, such as rotis, samosas, dal, and idlis, can cause thermal irritation if not allowed to cool.
Allowing hot items to cool before consumption is a simple, practical habit to avoid unnecessary heat exposure.

title: Dentists offered training to spot motor neurone disease
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Jessica Lee, director of research at the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation,](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/13/TELEMMGLPICT000502823650_17893059585560_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Jessica Lee, director of research at the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation,](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/13/TELEMMGLPICT000502823650_17893059585560_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dentists, general practitioners and other healthcare professionals are being offered training to recognise potential early signs of motor neurone disease (MND).
The charity foundation set up by Doddie Weir, the former Scotland rugby international who died after being diagnosed with the disease, is launching the first programme of its kind in the UK.
Called Race to Diagnose, it will offer guidance to healthcare professionals who may encounter patients with early signs of the disease.
MND can be difficult to diagnose in its early stages and it is hoped that treating the disease earlier will improve outcomes.
![Doddie Weir, the former Scotland rugby international](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/13/TELEMMGLPICT000320161395_17893059171210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqnxsVzbFt55yT5iapkHrLYYX55UGE1-QmdhXTcMmlCx4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The training programme also shows professionals how to explain an urgent referral without causing unnecessary alarm, and what clinical details to include so that specialist teams can assess and prioritise the patient.
Early indicators of the life-shortening condition can include progressive or unexplained muscle weakness and wasting, or changes affecting speech, the tongue or swallowing.
Jessica Lee, director of research at the My Name’5 Doddie Foundation, said: “MND is not common, its early signs can vary considerably and there is no single test that tells you conclusively that someone has it. That means people can move between different parts of the healthcare system before they reach the right specialist.
“Race to Diagnose gives professionals practical guidance on what to look for, how to assess what they are seeing and when to make an urgent referral.
“As treatments begin to emerge, reaching people earlier in the course of the disease may be critical to giving those treatments the best possible chance of having an effect.
“But earlier diagnosis is about much more than treatment.
“It can give people with MND and their families more time to understand what is happening, access the right support, adapt their homes and decide how they want to approach the future.”
Andy Vaughton, a former NHS consultant anaesthetist, experienced symptoms for several years before being diagnosed with MND in 2021.
![Andy Vaughton, a former consultant anaesthetist who has MND, Sept 14, 2026](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/13/TELEMMGLPICT000502823647_17893059881310_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqrpfQw2hJyG_yckwxPAr0gmyy-GsNrhPQbLesooHneHs.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
He said delays to diagnoses can deprive people of access to care and postpone important decisions about their lives.
![Andy Vaughton with his family after completing a continuous 100km challenge along the Jurassic Coast, UK, Aug 10, 2026.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/13/TELEMMGLPICT000497827642_17893077861080_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Vaughton, from Poole in Dorset, said: “For most people, MND doesn’t progress as slowly as it has for me.
“You need time to process what is happening, access the care you are going to require and bring together all the hospital specialists who will be involved.
“You also need to deal with everything at home and with your family. I knew I had a limited window of able-bodied life left, when I could still do the things I wanted to do.
“Having time to decide how to make the most of that window was incredibly important.
“I travelled, did the sports I loved and spent precious time with my wife and boys.”
The father of three recently completed a continuous 62-mile challenge along the Jurassic Coast to raise money for MND causes.
Mr Vaughton continued: “I look back on that as a period well spent and know I made the right decision.
“I have been fortunate because my MND has progressed slowly, but for some people that window can be very short.”
summary: Dentists, general practitioners, and other healthcare professionals in the UK are being offered a new training programme to help them recognise the early signs of motor neurone disease (MND). Launched by the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, the "Race to Diagnose" initiative aims to improve patient outcomes by facilitating earlier diagnoses and urgent referrals. Experts and patients note that earlier detection gives families more time to access support, adapt their homes, and make important future decisions.
key_points: A new UK training programme called Race to Diagnose is being offered to dentists and other healthcare professionals to spot early signs of motor neurone disease.
The initiative was created by the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, a charity set up by the late Scottish rugby international Doddie Weir.
Early indicators of MND include unexplained muscle weakness, muscle wasting, and changes affecting speech, the tongue, or swallowing.
The training provides guidance on how to make urgent referrals and how to explain them to patients without causing unnecessary alarm.
Earlier diagnosis can provide patients and their families with crucial time to access care, secure support, and plan for the future.

title: Researchers hope powerful new microscope will reveal ‘root cause’ of incurable bowel disease
author: Nicola Davis
content:
The number of young people living with debilitating and incurable bowel conditions worldwide is growing, but researchers now hope a one-of-a-kind microscope will help them understand such diseases and find new treatments.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology, more than half a million people in the UK are living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis the two main forms.
While such conditions can develop at any age, experts say they are most often diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 40, blighting lives at a crucial time for education, work and relationships.
Now a new piece of kit could bring fresh hope to those affected by IBD.
“What this microscope technology and what the science we do in the lab can bring is really to understand the mechanism [of IBD] better,” said Dr Karina Pombo-Garcia, a group leader at the Rosalind Franklin Institute at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Oxfordshire, where the microscope is housed.
“With IBD, and with other many diseases that we collaborate with other groups to study, there [are] some treatments, but maybe those treatments still are not maybe the best or the most targeted that we can do because we … fundamentally don’t understand the disease fully.”
![A woman in glasses and a man, both in white lab coats, examine a black medical microscope.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e3a31840f0b6e7d671e1a79009fb1263664423c1/0_0_7952_5304/master/7952.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
With its black casing, grey hoses and a plethora of wires, the microscope is remarkably unobtrusive.
Yet this is no run-of-the-mill bit of tech: the microscope operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional light microscopy, allowing researchers to see the details down to just 20nm in size.
To do so, the microscope, which researchers have nicknamed “Curie”, uses a two-laser technique known as stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy that scooped its inventors the Nobel prize in physics in 2014.
In this setup, features of interest within cells are labelled with fluorescent tags – these absorb energy from the first laser beam and then emit light, or fluorescence.
A second, doughnut-shaped laser beam overlaps with the area illuminated by the first. Crucially, this second beam “switches off” fluorescence within its outer ring, meaning fluorescence is only detected from the centre of the doughnut – a very small region.
“This allows the microscope to distinguish structures that are much closer together than would be possible using a conventional fluorescence microscope, producing images with exceptionally high resolution,” said Pombo-Garcia.
The microscope also has additional features, making it the only one of its kind in the UK. These, Pombo-Garcia notes, include deformable mirrors that can correct for optical distortions caused by the sample.
“This allows researchers to obtain clear images from deeper within relatively thick tissues and mini-organs,” she said. “It also has a temperature-controlled stage, enabling living cells and mini-organs to be studied under conditions close to normal body temperature.”
![Seated man in white lab coat works at a monitor, as standing woman in white coat looks on.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7185ad3ff6bed4abe09fce54620a2ea28e740656/1066_0_6630_5304/master/6630.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Dimitrios Ioannidis, a PhD student, is using the microscope to understand how cells that line our internal organs, including the intestines, come together and create protective barriers.
“For this to happen, we have specific protein complexes, which we hypothesise might change over time. So using this piece of equipment, we are able to visualise these complexes beyond what [we can see with a] conventional microscope,” he said, adding that he was looking at how the structure of these protein complexes changes from foetal development to adulthood. “If the structure changes, so does the function,” he said.
Ioannidis noted that by understanding what healthy tissue should look like, and then comparing and understanding the differences seen in people with disease, there was the potential to shed light on what had gone wrong.
“And then if you work and dig a little bit deeper, you can potentially find the root cause of some of the diseases that are affecting individuals,” he said, noting that this included IBD.
The microscope was unveiled by science minister Chris McDonald, alongside the announcement of £67m of funding for the Rosalind Franklin Institute over the next five years from April 2027, and a further £90m over the same period for the Henry Royce Institute, which focuses on materials research. In both cases, the funding has come from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council via the core budget of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) set in the 2025 spending review.
The announcement comes at a difficult time for UK science facilities. Earlier this year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), also part of UKRI, revealed it needs to make £162m in savings by 2030 as a result of factors such as soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates.
The situation has put some national facilities at risk of closure, with the Diamond Light Source, Central Laser Facility and ISIS Neutron and Muon Source – all of which sit on the same campus as the Rosalind Franklin Institute – jointly facing a 15% drop in funding, leading to concerns from the scientific community.
However, McDonald maintained such facilities still receive a very high level of funding, and stressed not every project or initiative backed by the STFC will be funded in perpetuity.
“I’m not particularly happy about the characterisation of cuts because that’s not the case at the high-level budget,” he said. “But it is right that STFC live within their means and prioritise their own budget,” he said.
summary: Researchers at the Rosalind Franklin Institute are utilizing a one-of-a-kind, high-resolution microscope nicknamed "Curie" to study inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and find its root cause. Operating at ten times the resolution of conventional light microscopy, the advanced STED microscope allows scientists to view living cells and thick tissues in detail. This technology aims to help researchers understand cellular mechanisms and develop more targeted treatments for incurable bowel conditions.
key_points: Over half a million people in the UK live with inflammatory bowel disease, which is most often diagnosed in individuals aged 15 to 40.
The new microscope operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional light microscopy, allowing researchers to see details down to 20nm in size.
The device uses a two-laser STED technique and features deformable mirrors and a temperature-controlled stage to image living cells and thick tissues.
Researchers are using the microscope to study how protein complexes form protective barriers in organs like the intestines, aiming to identify what goes wrong in diseases like IBD.
The microscope was unveiled alongside announcements of multi-million-pound funding for research institutes, amid broader financial pressures and funding debates within UK science facilities.
