title: Successful free fitness event in Swindon seeks funding to expand
author: Rachel Candlin
content:
![Tim is on an athletics track with a few other people, all in sports gear. He is wearing a bright pink t-shirt and black shorts. There is a patch of grass behind, and a concreted area in the background with several picnic tables in front of a sports building](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/2c21/live/c8243090-adca-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Tim Howe (Centre) founded The Longevity Games in 2024
- Published
A man who founded a community-based fitness event said it had been so successful that he is bidding for funds to extend it.
Tim Howe, from Swindon in Wiltshire, started The Longevity Games (TLG) in 2024. It runs four times a year and includes functional exercises for improving everyday mobility.
The latest games take place on Sunday at Swindon Harriers, with hundreds of participants expected to take part in the free event.
"We've applied for our first bit of funding, and we're looking to go into socially deprived areas and put on community training groups run by PTs, which are free of charge," Howe said.
The 52-year-old has started promoting the benefits of the games amongst healthcare providers.
"I'm working with GPs, health professionals, social prescribers and pillars of the community, explaining what we're doing and the impact it's having in the long-term," he said.
"So the next stage is to put training groups throughout Swindon that are fully funded and gradually roll them out throughout the town."
![Junab is standing with about six other people, all in red t-shirts with the Longevity Games logo on, in a large gym. They are smiling to camera, and Junab is holding up a banner saying 'The Longevity Games'](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/918/cpsprodpb/05a1/live/71d4bdd0-adcb-11f1-82c1-5ff19bf7a2f2.png)
Junab Ali has taken part in six games and said he has reversed his type 2 diabetes
Junab Ali, 52, from Swindon, has done six of the games and said it had helped reverse his type 2 diabetes.
"I said to Tim, 'can you guarantee me that I'll get healthier and fitter doing these exercises?' and he said, '100 per cent', so I said, 'all right then, I'll sign up'," he said.
"I didn't know that just those simple exercises make a hell of a difference on your bones and muscles to keep you stronger."
![Becky is standing in a large gym holding up a huge cardboard frame, which says The Longevity Games and looking through it. She is wearing a neon lime t-shirt and black shorts.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/cfd2/live/0848fa10-adcc-11f1-82c1-5ff19bf7a2f2.jpg)
Becky Dean said she felt healthier and happier after joining the games last year
Becky Dean, 35, also from Swindon, had two slipped discs about four years ago and relied on her young son, Dylan, to help her with everyday tasks.
After joining TLG last year, she now finds activities such as getting out of the car and climbing stairs much easier.
"It's been very beneficial for myself; I am a lot healthier, a lot happier mentally as well," she said.
"I've met about 20 people through the games because I can get out and do something and talk to them."
![A close-up of Anna outside with a trellis on a wall behind her and a little greenery. She is smiling to camera and wearing a blue dress with a pale leaf pattern on it. She has brown shoulder-length hair](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/cd63/live/1b8ed4c0-af3c-11f1-870f-d3ec92d75257.jpg)
Anna Woodman, a Wiltshire GP, will be taking part in her fifth games with other healthcare professionals
Anna Woodman, a Wiltshire GP and chair of Swindon Educational Trust, will be taking part in her fifth games later, alongside other healthcare professionals.
"We hope to inspire and motivate our patients to join us," she said.
"We believe that rather than firefighting in the NHS, which is often our day job, we can take a positive, preventative, proactive approach to get our local community moving.
"I think this is something that could be rolled out nationally or even internationally for people to recognise the power that [the games] have in terms of reversing chronic disease, and also in enabling us to live longer."
summary: Tim Howe founded The Longevity Games in Swindon in 2024 as a free, quarterly fitness event focused on everyday mobility. Following its success, Howe is bidding for funding to expand free community training groups into socially deprived areas. Participants and healthcare professionals have praised the event for improving mobility, supporting chronic disease prevention, and enhancing mental well-being.
key_points: The Longevity Games is a free fitness event in Swindon that runs four times a year.
Founder Tim Howe is seeking funding to launch free community training groups in socially deprived areas.
Participants reported significant health benefits, including reversed type 2 diabetes and improved mobility after spinal injuries.
Local GPs and healthcare professionals are participating to promote a preventative approach to health.

title: Not glamorous, but common: how to manage dandruff at home and when to get help
author: Keren Landman
content:
You spy a scatter of white flakes on your collar. Or you’ve got an itch that won’t quit, no matter how much you wash your hair. Dandruff isn’t glamorous, but it’s common: about half the world’s population has it.
An itchy, flaking scalp is rarely dangerous, but it can be annoying. Here’s what you need to know about what might be causing your flakes, what you can do about it, and when it’s time to get help.
What causes dandruff?
Dandruff is the mildest form of a condition called seborrheic dermatitis, a type of skin inflammation that usually affects the head, face or trunk. At its worst, this condition leads to patches of red skin covered in tiny, greasy scales. However, most people with dandruff have just minor scaliness and no redness, affecting only the scalp.
Experts still don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, and it’s likely there are various contributing factors. A yeast called Malassezia is a leading suspect, says James Pathoulas, an assistant professor of dermatology at the University of Minnesota medical school who specializes in hair and scalp disorders. Malassezia usually lives harmlessly on the scalp, but overgrowth has been linked with scalp inflammation.
It’s better to think about seborrheic dermatitis as a system in dysfunction rather than one organism causing trouble, according to Natasha Mesinkovska, an associate professor of dermatology at the University of California, Irvine. Scalp health comes down to a “trifecta” of factors, she says: the scalp’s microorganisms, its ability to keep those organisms out of deeper skin layers, and the skin’s immune response to them.
Who gets dandruff?
It’s not clear why some people get dandruff and others don’t. Genetics may play a role – at least 11 gene variants have been linked to the condition – as can hot, humid weather or a supercharged workout routine.
Hormones that drive oil production can also ramp symptoms up or down, beginning around puberty and changing during pregnancy or menopause.
What should I do about it?
If you’re seeing occasional light scale on your scalp with no significant redness or itch, over-the-counter dandruff shampoo can help. Zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide and ketoconazole are the three most common active ingredients. They’re all equally good at lowering Malassezia populations, tamping down inflammation, and stopping the flakes.
Pathoulas recommends massaging the shampoo into your scalp, not just your hair, and leaving it on for a few minutes before rinsing. Use it three times a week; either your regular conditioner or a dandruff-specific product is fine. If you want to wash your hair on in-between days, your regular shampoo and conditioner are fine.
Ketoconazole and selenium sulfide can dry out hair and cause breakage, especially for dry, highly textured or coily hair, Pathoulas says. If that occurs, or you already rely on hair oils or leave-in conditioner, look for a gentler, sulfate-free zinc pyrithione formulation made for textured hair.
Go fragrance-free where you can, says Pathoulas. Fragrance is a common cause of scalp contact allergy, and it doesn’t have to be synthetic to cause a reaction: natural botanical fragrances can also wreak havoc.
after newsletter promotion
Once symptoms clear, most people can taper dandruff shampoo use to once a week. If a shampoo that’s worked for months suddenly stops being effective, the yeast may have grown resistant to it, Pathoulas says. Switching to a different active ingredient for a while, then back again, can restore control.
When do I need to see a doctor?
If your scalp clears up with a medicated shampoo but flaking resumes within days of stopping, that’s a signal the underlying problem needs more attention, says Mesinkovska.
Thick, red, sharply defined plaques with silvery-white scale point toward psoriasis rather than dandruff, especially if you also have them on the elbows and knees. If the redness or scaly skin shows up elsewhere on your body, it could indicate an allergic reaction, depending on its location and your exposures, says Mesinkovska. Dandruff shampoo won’t have any effect on scalp flakes resulting from either of these conditions.
Hair loss or a burning or stinging sensation accompanying flakes is never normal, says Pathoulas. If you have these symptoms, a clinician should evaluate you for scarring alopecia.
If an evaluation shows that you just have ordinary dandruff but it isn’t responding to the basics, there are prescription options. The experts suggest ciclopirox shampoo, an antifungal with some antibacterial activity built in, and prescription-strength ketoconazole. Roflumilast is a newer option that you apply to your dry scalp as a foam.
Some researchers are trying to understand if manipulating the scalp’s bacterial populations might help – that is, adding good germs to outcompete any bad ones that might be causing problems. But that research is still in its early stages, so for now, experts aren’t recommending approaches like applying yoghurt or kombucha.
summary: Dandruff is a common, mild form of seborrheic dermatitis affecting about half the world's population. It is often managed effectively at home using over-the-counter medicated shampoos containing ingredients like zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, or ketoconazole. However, individuals should consult a doctor if they experience symptoms like hair loss, a burning sensation, severe redness, or if over-the-counter treatments fail.
key_points: Dandruff is the mildest form of seborrheic dermatitis, linked to factors such as yeast overgrowth, genetics, hormones, and scalp immune response.
Over-the-counter shampoos with active ingredients like zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, or ketoconazole can reduce Malassezia populations and stop flakes.
Experts recommend massaging medicated shampoo into the scalp and leaving it on for a few minutes before rinsing, typically three times a week.
A doctor should be consulted if flakes are accompanied by hair loss, burning, stinging, severe redness, or if home treatments are ineffective.

title: Older drivers diagnosed with one common illness at risk of ‘£1,000 DVLA fine' - AOL
author: Luke Chillingsworth
content:
![Express UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/express-uk.png?v=1784568534)
![Mature female driver looking round to reverse a car](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/09/13/302ffd09-f1f3-33ed-8496-86a91af78b2f/7bec6968-6242-43a1-a3b8-b68be27b6a12.jpg)
Older drivers are at risk of being slapped with a £1,000 fine if they are diagnosed with a common illness, according to experts. Specialists at the Older Drivers Forum have explained road users diagnosed with dementia must inform the DVLA or risk facing the bill.
Dementia is a serious condition, with damage to nerve cells in the brain leading to consequences such as memory loss. Age is the biggest risk factor for dementia, with elderly individuals more at risk of developing the condition. It is believed that an estimated 982,000 people are currently living with dementia in the UK, meaning many may be breaking the rules when it comes to driving.
![Focused senior woman driving car alone, holding steering wheel firmly. Safe driving for elderly adults, older driver safety.](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/09/13/302ffd09-f1f3-33ed-8496-86a91af78b2f/1d163d8d-9b46-4ad6-a087-30e9f85bd17c.jpg)
The Older Drivers Forum explained: "If you are diagnosed with any form of dementia, you must inform the DVLA straight away, failure to do so may incur a fine up to £1,000."
Informing the DVLA doesn't signal the end for motorists freedoms, with many able to keep their licence and stay on the road. If a person with dementia wants to keep driving, the DVLA will usually ask about the person's medical information and decide if they are safe to stay behind the wheel. The DVLA may also ask the person to undergo a driving assessment to test their abilities..
The Older Drivers Forum added: "A diagnosis of dementia is not in itself a reason to stop driving. One in every three people with dementia still drives. What matters, from both a legal and a practical point of view, is whether the person is still able to drive safely."
However, some people diagnosed with the condition decide to stop driving and send their licence back to DVLA in what is known as a voluntary surrender.
The Alzheimer's Society stressed that it was motorists duty to inform the DVLA of a condition as soon as possible. They stressed road users weren't just risking a fine, with car insurance agreements also at risk.
They said: "Some people who are diagnosed with dementia do not tell the driver licensing authorities and keep driving. This may be because they do not accept or recognise their diagnosis, or they aren't aware of how much their dementia is affecting their driving.
"Not telling DVLA/DVA puts the person at risk of a fine and arrest as well as a possible accident. It also puts them in danger of driving without insurance as their policy may now be invalid."
summary: Older drivers diagnosed with dementia are required by experts to inform the DVLA immediately to avoid a fine of up to £1,000. A dementia diagnosis does not automatically mean a person must stop driving, as the DVLA will assess their medical information and driving abilities. However, failing to notify the authority can also invalidate car insurance policies and lead to arrest.
key_points: Drivers diagnosed with any form of dementia must inform the DVLA straight away.
Failure to report a dementia diagnosis can result in a fine of up to £1,000 and potential arrest.
A diagnosis does not automatically revoke driving privileges, and many individuals are still permitted to drive safely after an assessment.
Failing to notify the DVLA can invalidate car insurance agreements.
Drivers may also choose a voluntary surrender by sending their licence back to the DVLA.

title: A common stomach infection may be linked to bowel cancer – here’s what we know
author: Justin Stebbing
content:
A bacterium that can live quietly in the stomach for decades may have an unexpected connection with bowel cancer.
A new study estimates that exposure to Helicobacter pylori (H pylori) could be associated with more than one in five cases of bowel cancer worldwide.
That is a striking figure, particularly because H pylori is extremely common. But it comes with an important qualification: the study doesn’t prove H pylori causes bowel cancer. Instead, it estimates how much bowel cancer might be linked to the infection.
Bowel cancer, also called colorectal cancer, develops in the colon or rectum. It’s one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers worldwide, affecting around 1.9 million people each year.
We already know several factors that can increase the risk of developing bowel cancer. This includes older age, family history, smoking, obesity, alcohol and diets high in processed meat. But researchers are increasingly interested in another possible contributor: the trillions of microorganisms that live in our digestive system (our microbiome), and the infections that can alter this environment.
H pylori is an especially interesting candidate. Not only is the bacterium adapted to survive in the stomach’s acidic environment, it is also known to cause gastric cancer.
It’s thought around half of the world’s population are infected with H pylori– although rates vary greatly between countries. Infection often occurs during childhood.
Most infected people never develop symptoms. But in some, H pylori causes long-term inflammation of the stomach lining. This can lead to ulcers and, in a small proportion, stomach cancer. The evidence that H pylori causes cancer is strong enough that it’s classified as a carcinogen.
But the bacterium’s relationship with bowel cancer is less clear.
Previous studies have found that people infected with H pylori have a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.
This latest study attempted to contextualise these findings. It gathered data from 43 studies involving almost 49 million people and combined it with information about the prevalence of both H pylori and bowel cancer globally.
Overall, people exposed to H pylori had about a 1.6 times greater risk of being diagnosed with bowel cancer compared to those without evidence of infection. Using these figures, the researchers calculated that approximately 22% of bowel cancers worldwide could be associated with H pylori.
This doesn’t mean H pylori has been shown to cause one in five bowel cancers. The calculation depended heavily on the studies included – and, crucially, assumes that at least some of the observed association is causal.
![A doctor writes on a notepad, while a patient in the background points to their pelvic area to indicate pain. There is a medical model of the large intestine on display.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759323/original/file-20260911-50-ya6mo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
When the researchers restricted their analysis to 14 population-based and cohort studies – designs generally better suited to studying how risk develops over time – the estimated proportion of bowel cancers associated with H pylori fell to about 12%.
It’s also possible that some of the apparent link reflects other differences between people who acquire H pylori and those who don’t – including diet, smoking, physical activity levels, socioeconomic conditions conditions and healthcare access.
H pylori and cancer
Nevertheless, there are several plausible ways H pylori might influence bowel cancer.
One is through chronic inflammation. H pylori can provoke an immune response that lasts for decades. Long-lasting inflammation can affect chemical signals involved in cell growth and repair. In some circumstances, this inflammation also creates an environment in which damaged or abnormal cells are able to survive.
Chronic inflammation is already known to contribute to the development of several cancers, so this provides a biologically plausible connection.
Another possibility involves the gut microbiome. By changing inflammation and stomach acid production, H pylori may affect which microorganisms survive in the digestive system. These changes could influence the chemicals produced in the bowel and how its lining responds to damage.
H pylori may also affect hormones and other molecules involved in digestion and cell growth. Although an intriguing possibility, there’s no evidence yet of the chain of events that leads from infection in the stomach to cancer in the colon or rectum.
Perhaps the most interesting finding from the study concerns what happens when the infection is treated.
H pylori can usually be eradicated using a combination of antibiotics and medicines that suppress stomach acid. Across four observational studies included in the analysis, people who received treatment for H pylori appeared to have a lower subsequent risk of bowel cancer – with the difference becoming apparent after ten years.
But as these were observational studies, not trials in which people were randomly assigned to treatment or no treatment, so we cannot yet conclude that eliminating H pylori prevents bowel cancer.
So should people now ask to be tested for H pylori to reduce their bowel cancer risk? On the evidence available today, no. We need stronger evidence showing that detecting and treating H pylori actually reduces colorectal cancer incidence.
At present, the most useful ways of reducing your risk of bowel cancer remain the ones supported by strong evidence.
This includes bowel cancer screening, which can find cancers at an earlier, more treatable stage and can sometimes prevent cancer by detecting and removing precancerous growths called polyps. Maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, not smoking, limiting alcohol intake and eating less processed meat can also reduce risk.
Symptoms such as blood in the stool, a persistent change in bowel habits, unexplained weight loss or ongoing abdominal discomfort should not be ignored, although they are often caused by conditions other than cancer.
Read more: Five ways to cut your risk of cancer – by an oncology consultant
The wider significance of this research may be what it tells us about the causes of cancer. We tend to think of bowel cancer mainly in terms of genes, ageing and lifestyle. But some cancers also have an infectious component.
The possibility that an infection acquired in childhood could influence the risk of bowel cancer decades later therefore deserves serious investigation.
summary: A new global study suggests that exposure to the bacterium Helicobacter pylori (H pylori) may be associated with more than one in five cases of bowel cancer, though the research does not prove a direct causal link. H pylori is extremely common and already known to cause stomach ulcers and gastric cancer through long-term inflammation. While observational studies indicate that treating the infection with antibiotics might lower subsequent bowel cancer risk, experts emphasize that stronger evidence is needed before recommending screening and treatment specifically for bowel cancer prevention.
key_points: A study combining data from 43 studies estimates that H pylori exposure is associated with approximately 22% of bowel cancer cases globally.
People with H pylori showed about a 1.6 times greater risk of being diagnosed with bowel cancer compared to uninfected individuals.
Plausible links between H pylori and bowel cancer include chronic inflammation, alterations to the gut microbiome, and effects on digestion-related hormones.
Observational data suggests treating H pylori with antibiotics may lower subsequent bowel cancer risk, but definitive proof from randomized trials is currently lacking.
Established risk reduction methods remain vital, including bowel cancer screening, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and reducing processed meat intake.

title: Dad nearly died after pub roast dinner gave him sepsis
author: Sam Corbishley
content:
![Udhyam Amin with his wife holding glasses.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/comp-1789198403.png?w=646) 
A man was given just hours to live after a roast chicken dinner led to him developing sepsis.
Udhyam Amin, 64, from Kingswood in Surrey, went to A&E with suspected food poisoning in February after having the meal in a pub.
Doctors at St Helier Hospital in south London told him he was infected with the bacteria campylobacter.
He was soon rushed to the resuscitation room where his blood pH fell dangerously low and he suffered a cardiac arrest.
Mr Amin was placed on a ventilator in intensive care, with medics warning his family he had developed sepsis and may only have hours to live.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
His daughter Parisha Bains, said: ‘We were told he had gone into sepsis and multi-organ failure. Most of his critical organs had shut down. But he made it through the night and that wasn’t expected.
‘It felt like our world had fallen apart. Nothing prepares you for hearing that the person you love may not make it through the day.’
![Undated handout photo of Udhyam Amin, 64, from Surrey, who was left with life-threatening sepsis after getting food poisoning from a roast chicken dinner. His family were told he only had hours to live but he has since recovered. His daughter, Parisha Bains, a surgical registrar at Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust, described her father as a 'cat with nine lives' and hailed the care provided by doctors at St Helier Hospital in London. Issue date: Friday September 11, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Family Handout/PA Wire NOTE TO EDITORS: This handout photo may only be used for editorial reporting purposes for the contemporaneous illustration of events, things or the people in the image or facts mentioned in the caption. Reuse of the picture may require further permission from the copyright holder.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_311842587-3676.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Campylobacter can cause sickness, diarrhoea, tummy pain and fever, and symptoms begin within a few hours or days of eating food that is infected.
It usually gets better when patients rest and replace fluids but can lead to sepsis in rare cases.
After spending a little over two weeks in an induced coma, Mr Amin is now well and back working.
The former subpostmaster turned businessman has learned to walk and speak clearly again.
Ms Bains, a surgical registrar at Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust, said: ‘His kidneys started to work again and he was gradually weaned off his blood pressure support medication, and from then things improved.
![Undated handout photo of Udhyam Amin, 64, from Surrey with his wife Bhavini. Mr Amin was left with life-threatening sepsis after getting food poisoning from a roast chicken dinner. His family were told he only had hours to live but he has since recovered. His daughter, Parisha Bains, a surgical registrar at Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust, described her father as a 'cat with nine lives' and hailed the care provided by doctors at St Helier Hospital in London. Issue date: Friday September 11, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Family Handout/PA Wire NOTE TO EDITORS: This handout photo may only be used for editorial reporting purposes for the contemporaneous illustration of events, things or the people in the image or facts mentioned in the caption. Reuse of the picture may require further permission from the copyright holder.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_311842669-0283.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘It’s nothing short of a miracle that he is still with us. We laugh and joke that he’s like a cat with nine lives.
‘One of the first things he asked us when he woke up was what date it was because he had to submit his tax returns.
‘Now he is back to work seven days a week and enjoying his life again.’
The family have now launched a fundraiser for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity to support the intensive care unit, with £37,000 raised so far.
Mr Amin is also sharing his story to raise awareness ahead of World Sepsis Day on September 13.
He said: ‘Words cannot express my gratitude for the exceptional care, compassion and dedication the medical teams showed me during the most difficult time of my life.
![Undated handout photo of Udhyam Amin, 64, from Surrey with his wife Bhavini. Mr Amin was left with life-threatening sepsis after getting food poisoning from a roast chicken dinner. His family were told he only had hours to live but he has since recovered. His daughter, Parisha Bains, a surgical registrar at Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust, described her father as a 'cat with nine lives' and hailed the care provided by doctors at St Helier Hospital in London. Issue date: Friday September 11, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Family Handout/PA Wire NOTE TO EDITORS: This handout photo may only be used for editorial reporting purposes for the contemporaneous illustration of events, things or the people in the image or facts mentioned in the caption. Reuse of the picture may require further permission from the copyright holder.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_311842671-dece.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘Their skill and commitment saved my life, and I will be forever grateful. I cannot thank them enough for giving me a second chance.’
- 
	![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/comp-1789232038.png?crop=0px%2C0px%2C1193px%2C670px&resize=646%2C363)

- The haunting story of the 'waving woman' seen at North Tower impact site
Molly Simpson, head of charity and fundraising at Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity, said: ‘Udhyam’s story is both remarkable and inspiring. We are enormously thankful to Udhyam’s family for turning their gratitude into action by raising funds to support St Helier.
‘Their generosity will help us enhance the environment, equipment and support available to patients and their loved ones when they need it most.’
Mr Amin is fundraising for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity. Donations can be made at justgiving.com/page/aminfamily.
Get in touch with our news team by emailing us at webnews@metro.co.uk.
For more stories like this, check our news page.
summary: Udhyam Amin, a 64-year-old man from Surrey, developed life-threatening sepsis and multi-organ failure after contracting campylobacter food poisoning from a pub roast chicken dinner in February. His family was told he had only hours to live after he suffered a cardiac arrest and was placed on a ventilator in an induced coma. Mr Amin has since fully recovered, returned to work, and is sharing his story while raising funds for the hospital's intensive care unit ahead of World Sepsis Day.
key_points: Udhyam Amin contracted campylobacter from a pub roast chicken dinner, leading to severe food poisoning and sepsis.
He suffered a cardiac arrest, multi-organ failure, and spent over two weeks in an induced coma at St Helier Hospital.
Despite doctors warning his family he had only hours to live, Mr Amin made a full recovery and has learned to walk and speak clearly again.
His family has launched a fundraiser for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity, raising £37,000 so far to support the intensive care unit.

title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
author: Ruth Clegg
content:
![Jaw pain after waking up or sleeping - Bruxisum, teeth grinding - stock photo](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7bfa/live/afda27d0-ad1e-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teeth
- Published
Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing.
"I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."
The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.
Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.
According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing.
"It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."
![A composite image showing Ella's jaw wider from grinding and after treatment](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/71cb/live/872fd160-ad21-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Ella says constant teeth grinding enlarged her masseter muscles and widened her jaw (pictured, left, before treatment and, right, afterwards)
Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases?
Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting.
Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners.
So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for:
- Worn, chipped or flattened teeth
- Headaches or facial pain in the morning
- Jaw stiffness
- Disrupted sleep and daytime tiredness
- Increased tooth sensitivity
- Earache or pain near the temples without infection
Teeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body.
Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started".
'A way of releasing some of the stress'
Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth.
"If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains.
For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake.
"I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me.
"I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it."
In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment.
![Ella smiling at the camera. She has long blonde hair, she is wearing a white flowery top and she's sat outside on a night out](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/e403/live/14629a20-addd-11f1-81d6-3b7ea3697b2b.jpg)
After her dentist injected her jaw muscles with Botox, Ella says her sleep and mental health improved
Even though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months.
"Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square."
Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge.
He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time.
"Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds."
But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop.
![Scan of teeth showing areas worn down from grinding.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/6c12/live/80cfe910-add3-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
A 3D scan can reveal the damage that teeth grinders are doing to their teeth
While you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai.
"Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening."
It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again.
"That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition.
And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains.
"Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. It cleans the mouth, it protects the teeth and it's vital for digestion."
Some studies also suggest that chewing can help with cognition.
"We know this in animals, and our preliminary research is showing it in humans," he says. "By working our jaw muscles we are stimulating blood flow to the brain."
But teeth grinding can also cause chronic pain, which can have a huge impact on your daily life.
What is the treatment for bruxism?
Dentist Riaz Yar, a specialist in prosthodontics, treats patients struggling with the effects of severe bruxism - worn, cracked and fractured teeth, and dental work that keeps failing. Many also arrive with chronic jaw or facial pain and report poor sleep, all of which need assessing in their own right, he says, rather than simply being blamed on the grinding.
In the past, Yar says, teeth grinding was considered simply a mechanical problem of the jaw, but now there is strong evidence that it is much more complex. It's a "biopsychosocial issue", he says, driven by the brain and nervous system and shaped by the whole person.
"We take into account their sleep patterns, their diet, their weight, the amount they exercise, what medication they might be taking and we assess for signs of sleep disorders," he says. "Many factors can contribute to a patient grinding their teeth, so addressing the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach."
How best to tackle it? These things might help:
- Mouthguard to wear at night to protect your teeth
- If linked to sleep apnoea, devices such as a CPAP machine or a mandibular advancement device (MAD) to help keep the airway open
- Physiotherapy
- Talking therapies such as CBT
- Lifestyle changes to help reduce stress and improve sleep such as exercise, cutting down on alcohol, stopping smoking and eating healthier
Along with muscle-relaxing injections, Ella says she is also meditating to try to reduce her anxiety and free herself from the tension she regularly carries.
"Having treatment has transformed my life," Ella says, "now I want to try and figure out the root cause."
summary: Bruxism, or teeth grinding, affects nearly one in four people and is often linked to stress, anxiety, and the nervous system. While many individuals are unaware they do it until physical symptoms like worn teeth or jaw pain appear, dentists are noting an increase in younger people experiencing the condition. Treatments range from mouthguards and lifestyle changes to jaw muscle injections, physiotherapy, and addressing underlying sleep disorders.
key_points: Bruxism encompasses clenching, grinding, bracing, and thrusting, which can occur during the day or at night.
Common signs of teeth grinding include worn or chipped teeth, morning headaches, jaw stiffness, and tooth sensitivity.
Experts note that bruxism is closely linked to stress and trauma, acting as the body's way of releasing tension.
In some cases, bruxism can serve a biological purpose, such as clearing the airway during sleep apnoea or stimulating saliva production.

title: Stourbridge gran says she remains positive despite her third cancer diagnosis in 15 years
author: Caroline Gall
content:
![Kirsty and her best friend are sat outside in a bar on a holiday. Kirsty has short blonde hair and is wearing a white waistcoat-looking top. Her friend has longer blonde hair and a denim shirt on. Both women are smiling at the camera. here are people sat on higher stools behind them. It is night time.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/849/cpsprodpb/e9bb/live/b3e61860-ac48-11f1-96a2-2f464854ded4.png)
Kirsty Priest (right) said if she did not remain strong, she would feel sorry for herself
- Published
When Kirsty Priest was told she had cancer for a third time in 15 years, she thought: "What have I done to deserve this? I must be a really bad person."
She was treated twice for separate cases of breast cancer, 10 years apart, but earlier this year was told she had a brain tumour.
On top of that, she found out during her earlier treatment that she had a mutated gene which could double her risk of further breast cancer, meaning regular treatments for the rest of her life.
"Touch wood, I could live for years," the 53-year-old said. "We haven't got a crystal ball, they don't know how long I've got, but if I'm having all of this treatment, I'm heading it straight on," she said.
"It's incurable but it's about controlling it from spreading."
After the successful removal of the brain tumour, Kirsty, a grandmother, said she was "putting my big positive girlie pants on".
She says she plans to enjoy every moment of her life while fundraising and supporting others in similar situations.
![Kirsty stands to the right of a breast cancer poster with two nurses, both either side of it and in their uniforms. They are in the reception area of the hospital with jigsaws stacked on a table on one side.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/547/cpsprodpb/1cd1/live/728e57b0-ac48-11f1-96a2-2f464854ded4.png)
Kirsty has fundraised for the breast cancer unit at Russells Hall Hospital, in Dudley
Her first diagnosis came when she was 38, then a single parent of a daughter and an autistic son.
Told she had stage three breast cancer, she had a mastectomy along with further surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and took the drug Herceptin for 18 months.
"I just thought it was a death sentence, 'I'm not going to survive this, but I've got to survive this because I have two children' - and I did," Kirsty, from Stourbridge in the West Midlands, said.
About 10 years later, she had been given the all clear after a mammogram - when she found a lump.
Doctors confirmed it was cancerous, but different to her first diagnosis.
Kirsty said she chose a second mastectomy and further treatment
Having had two bouts of cancer, the 53-year-old was also offered a genetic test and that was when medics found she had a CHEK2 gene mutation., external
Kirsty said the discovery was fairly new to the doctors she saw at the time as "the nurses were reading it off a piece of paper to me because they hadn't heard about it or been trained about it".
![A woman with short grey hair smiles to the camera while stood before darkened windows. She has a magenta, sparkly jacket over a black top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/547/cpsprodpb/1536/live/f702b000-ac47-11f1-96a2-2f464854ded4.png)
After her diagnoses, Kirsty will need injections and scans for the rest of her life
When more cases of breast cancer are detected in families than expected, it can be due to inheriting such mutated genes, according to the NHS., external
An abnormal CHEK2 gene can, at the very least, double a person's risk of breast cancer in their life, Breast Cancer Trials say.
"It was, 'OK I've gone through it again. I've just got to tackle it head on, what will happen will happen'," Kirsty said.
Later she was told she was in remission from that cancer, prompting her first fundraising efforts for the breast cancer ward at Russells Hall Hospital in Dudley, where she was treated.
The 53-year-old has raised Â£11,500 for the unit since then.
But towards the end of last year, Kirsty said she began having pain in her shoulder.
By February she was feeling dizzy and bumping into things and saw a doctor who told her it was vertigo and prescribed painkillers.
"Luckily, I had a second opinion with nurses at my yearly health check-up later the same day who said 'go straight to A&E, your blood pressure is through the roof'," she remembered.
"I went and within 24 hours I was in a hospital bed being told I've got a brain tumour."
![Kirsty is stood by DJ decks with three friends, dancing and raising an arm in the air with headphones on. Everyone is smiling with the equipment in front of them and a pint of beer on one side.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/345/cpsprodpb/9886/live/49fac4f0-ac48-11f1-96a2-2f464854ded4.png)
Kirsty said she wanted to continue to enjoy life and be surrounded by positive people
She was treated successfully but said she will now need to have Herceptin injections every three weeks, along with MRI scans every three months, for the rest of her life.
"They are treating me for breast cancer again now... and it is stage four," she said.
"Even though I've got no tumours in my body, they're suspecting that I've got lots of cancer cells floating around my body so they're targeting killing that with chemo."
The aim of the injections was to stop cancer cells from "splitting and attaching" in her body, she added.
Telling her family each time that cancer had returned was very traumatic, she said, especially for her parents, particularly her father who she inherited the mutated gene from and who felt a sense of guilt.
Another member of her family also has the gene but her daughter does not.
"You just think, 'What have I done to deserve this? I must be a really bad person', but I know I'm not a bad person. I do a lot for others," Kirsty said.
"I think it's just bad luck. I've got the gene and it's come back."
![Dee is stood behind some DJ decks outside a pub. He is looking up to the camera, smiling as the sun shines and he has some sunglasses on and a light-coloured top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/5310/live/e80fac00-ac48-11f1-96a2-2f464854ded4.jpg)
DJ friends, including Dee Wood, have organised an event to raise money for the two hospitals that have helped Kirsty
Friends have come together to organise a charity fundraising night for the two hospitals who helped her, with DJs playing at The Fox Inn at Stourton, in Staffordshire, next month.
DJ Dee Wood said he was honoured to jointly organise the event.
"Whilst in Tenerife alongside the other DJ's in February, I asked if they would play for this cause to help raise awareness and funds," he said.
"There wasn't really much of a difference in the response I received from each DJ asked - it was unequivocally a 'yes' throughout.
"We are buzzing to do this for Kirsty."
summary: Stourbridge grandmother Kirsty Priest is facing her third cancer diagnosis in 15 years after previously beating two separate cases of breast cancer. Following the successful removal of a brain tumour, she now requires ongoing treatment for stage four breast cancer, alongside lifelong monitoring and injections due to a CHEK2 gene mutation. Despite the incurable diagnosis, the 53-year-old remains positive, focuses on enjoying her life, and actively fundraises for the hospitals that treated her.
key_points: Kirsty Priest, 53, has been diagnosed with cancer three times over a 15-year period, including two bouts of breast cancer and a recent brain tumour.
Medical tests revealed she carries a CHEK2 gene mutation, which can double a person's risk of developing breast cancer.
Although her brain tumour was removed, she is currently receiving treatment for stage four breast cancer and will need lifelong scans and injections.
Kirsty has raised £11,500 for the breast cancer unit at Russells Hall Hospital, and friends are organizing another charity event to support her hospitals.
She maintains a positive outlook, emphasizing that she wants to enjoy every moment and support others in similar situations.

title: 'This doesn't happen to us' - Peterborough mum on child's cancer
author: Shariqua Ahmed
content:
![Nina is wearing a pink headscarf with a bow and a colourful jumper and is posing for the camera, inside a house and by a front door, with a victory sign.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/6406/live/4f02d690-ad24-11f1-9bf8-27bb5a420b3e.jpg)
Five-year-old Nina began treatment on her birthday last year after she was diagnosed with leukaemia just as she was starting school
- Published
The mother of a five-year-old girl has spoken of the shock she felt when her daughter was diagnosed with leukaemia.
"I thought, this doesn't happen to us, this is what happens to other people," said Sam about the moment she found out daughter Nina, from Peterborough, was suffering from cancer days, just days after she had started school.
Sam had become concerned about Nina's persistent bruising and lack of energy, and now hoped to raise awareness about the disease during September's Childhood Cancer Awareness Month.
"She just didn't seem as full of life as she usually was... I couldn't work out what was wrong," Sam said. "I was searching her symptoms and leukaemia kept coming up."
Sam first noticed large bruises on Nina's arms, legs and forehead shortly after she started school last September, but initially thought they were from everyday knocks and bumps.
After Nina's teacher raised concerns that she had fallen asleep in class and was not herself, the then four-year-old underwent blood tests and was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, external (ALL), a cancer of the white blood cells.
![Sam, a woman with golden hair, is wearing a black and white striped top and a black hat. Nina and her sister are sitting next to her, smiling for the camera. Dad Daniel is wearing a white top and black glasses and has black tattoos on his neck and left forearm.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/0f62/live/a52354a0-ad24-11f1-9865-cdb2b8b30437.jpg)
Mum Sam has shared a picture of the family on their last holiday before Nina's treatment began
"I thought maybe I was being an overprotective parent and a bit dramatic about it all," said Sam of her initial concerns.
"You'd think when you get told your child has cancer you would just burst into tears.
"But it was such a shock I didn't cry at all. [Nina's father] Daniel was the opposite. He fell to the floor."
Hospital trial
She began treatment on her fifth birthday in October and underwent eight months of intensive chemotherapy.
She has also taken part in a clinical trial at Addenbrooke's Hospital, in Cambridge, which is investigating ways to improve survival rates and reduce long-term side effects for young people with ALL.
Sam said: "We felt if we were able to help children in the future by doing these trials, it was very important, because if other children in the past hadn't taken part in trials, then Nina wouldn't be on such a good treatment plan."
Her family saw "a turning point" when Nina began a newer treatment designed to help the immune system target leukaemia cells.
"By Christmas Day she was dancing in the front room - that treatment really changed things," said Sam.
"She's a really confident little girl and she's just got on with it. She's made friends at school and in hospital and will happily talk to people about her leukaemia.
"Now we just want Nina to complete her treatment with as few complications as possible and go on to live her life like any other child."
Nina is now in the maintenance phase of her treatment, which is due to continue until December 2027, and is fronting a campaign led by Cancer Research UK to share her story.
![Nina is wearing a hat and glasses. She is sitting on a counter top inside a charity shop, holding a giant fluffy, orange pumpkin.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/1281/live/45ab1070-ad25-11f1-9bf8-27bb5a420b3e.jpg)
Nina will feature in posters displayed in hundreds of Cancer Research UK shops during Childhood Cancer Awareness Month
More stories from Peterborough:
There are about 2,400 new cancer cases in young people in the UK every year, external, which is more than six each day, according to Cancer Research UK.
Jose Ramos, Cancer Research UK's spokesperson for the East of England, said: "We're grateful to Nina's family for sharing their experience.
"Cancer is different in children and young people, from the types of cancer that affect this age group to the long-term effects of treatment.
"That's why it needs a dedicated approach."
Do you have a story suggestion for Peterborough? Contact us below.
summary: The mother of a five-year-old girl named Nina from Peterborough has shared the family's shock after her daughter was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia shortly after starting school. Nina began intensive chemotherapy and a clinical trial on her fifth birthday, experiencing a turning point when a newer treatment helped her immune system. She is now in the maintenance phase of her treatment until December 2027 and is sharing her story to support Cancer Research UK's Childhood Cancer Awareness Month.
key_points: Nina was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia shortly after starting school when she was four years old.
Her mother, Sam, initially noticed persistent bruising and a lack of energy before teachers raised concerns about Nina falling asleep in class.
Nina began treatment and a clinical trial at Addenbrooke's Hospital on her fifth birthday in October.
She is currently in the maintenance phase of her treatment, which is scheduled to continue until December 2027.
Nina and her family are sharing their story to raise awareness for Cancer Research UK during Childhood Cancer Awareness Month.

title: An operational perturbation proteomics-based virtual cell model - Nature
author: Sun; Rui; Liujia; Yongge; Tong; Cheng; Honghan; Xuedong; Zhou; Xueya; Yuecheng; Guangmei; Luo; Zhengchao; Ma; Kunpeng; Wu; Chunlong; Ji; Dongchen; Zhangzhi; Meng; Hongxue; Xiang; Yuhang; Lei; Dingwei; Qianhe; Hu; Wenbin; Deng; Tan; Lingling; Xiao; Zhiwei; Zeng; Liqin; Xuan; Qiong; Nianzi; E; Weinan; Peijie; Han; Zhu; Yi; Guo; Tiannan
content:
Abstract
Artificial intelligence-empowered virtual cell models represent an emerging approach for in silico drug discovery1,2,3, yet most existing approaches lack large-scale, time-resolved perturbation proteomics data and interpretable frameworks for predicting therapeutic responses. Here we generated more than 38 million temporal protein-abundance measurements from systematically perturbed breast cancer cell lines, and developed ProteinTalks, a virtual cell model. Central to ProteinTalks is the synergy of this large-scale dynamic proteomic resource and the model architecture, enabling a new pretraining framework that learns transferable dynamical latent representations from temporal proteome trajectories. By modelling how proteins respond conditionally to different perturbations, this approach enables the model to function as an operational tool for diverse drug discovery tasks: predicting drug efficacy and synergy, discovering new drug combinations, probing proteins associated with drug resistance, stratifying patient responses and prioritizing drug candidates for patient organoids. It also shows robust transferability, extending beyond cell lines to patient-derived organoids and clinical biopsies, generally achieving higher performance than the selected benchmark implementations under the evaluated protocols. Together, ProteinTalks shows how scalable pretraining of transferable dynamic representations enables operational, dynamics-aware, proteomics-based virtual cell models to advance in silico drug discovery.

The PTDS protein matrix and associated resources are available for academic and non-commercial use through the open-access platform db.prottalks.com. Other data used are available from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway at https://www.genome.jp/kegg/pathway.html (ref. 57), from Metascape at https://metascape.org/gp/ (ref. 58), from STRING at https://cn.string-db.org/ (ref. 59) and from Ingenuity Pathway Analysis at http://www.ingenuity.com (ref. 60).

summary: Researchers generated over 38 million temporal protein-abundance measurements from systematically perturbed breast cancer cell lines to develop ProteinTalks, an operational virtual cell model. By leveraging this large-scale dynamic proteomic resource, the model learns transferable latent representations from temporal proteome trajectories to predict therapeutic responses. ProteinTalks successfully facilitates drug discovery tasks such as evaluating drug efficacy, discovering combinations, probing resistance, and stratifying patient responses, while outperforming selected benchmarks across cell lines, organoids, and clinical biopsies.
key_points: Over 38 million temporal protein-abundance measurements were generated from perturbed breast cancer cell lines.
ProteinTalks is a virtual cell model built on a synergy of large-scale dynamic proteomic resources and a novel pretraining framework.
The model performs diverse drug discovery tasks, including predicting drug efficacy and synergy, identifying new combinations, and probing drug resistance proteins.
ProteinTalks demonstrates robust transferability to patient-derived organoids and clinical biopsies, often outperforming benchmark implementations.

title: The four-week reset to boost energy, fight belly fat and lower inflammation
author: Mary Comber
content:
![Rose Ferguson at home in her kitchen](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000501853258_17891244136620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWZ6MmqeGoerdFC8Gneb4g9f11FLKtqwYaxK652uKeQE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Rose Ferguson at home in her kitchen](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000501853258_17891244136620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWZ6MmqeGoerdFC8Gneb4g9f11FLKtqwYaxK652uKeQE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
By our 40s and 50s, we imagine that we’ll be enjoying life to the full. Instead, many of us find ourselves struggling with an expanding waistline, flagging energy, poor sleep, brain fog and that nagging sense that we’re not quite ourselves.
These are complaints that Rose Ferguson, a nutritionist and functional medicine practitioner and author of the new book The Reset: The 4 Week Plan to Feel Better Than Ever, hears repeatedly in her clinic. “A lot of people think, ‘Oh, I’m just getting older.’ But frankly that’s b-------,” says the former Nineties supermodel, who retrained as a nutritionist two decades ago and counts David Beckham and Kate Moss among her clients.
Ferguson regards typical midlife symptoms as “text messages” from the body, nudging us to change the way we live. In midlife, hormonal shifts can combine with chronic stress, poor gut health and low-grade inflammation, meaning that habits our bodies once shrugged off may begin to take a greater toll.
At 51, Ferguson says the secret to feeling well is decidedly unglamorous. “None of it is sexy. Consistency is the thing,” she says. “Simple daily habits can really make a huge difference.”
Now she has distilled her approach into The Reset, a four-week programme designed to improve energy, sleep and metabolic health, and help you feel like yourself again.
The reset
“The reset is a four-week programme that helps your body recalibrate and thrive,” says Ferguson. “It targets the damage from years of poor nutrition and modern life and gives your body a chance to work as it should.”
It’s not a calorie-controlled diet or punishing detox, she stresses, and you don’t need scales or expensive supplements. The plan builds healthy habits around five pillars – food, sleep, movement, morning light and stress management – which Ferguson says work together to change the signals the body receives each day. “Those signals influence inflammation, hormones, appetite and metabolism,” she explains. “The plan will stabilise your blood sugar, support digestion and reset your body clock while easing mental overload.”
Although weight loss is not the primary goal, Ferguson says many of her clients find their waistlines shrink as their bodies begin to work more efficiently. “Your energy will improve, cravings will settle and your body will start to feel like yours again.”
![Rose Ferguson says she has learned to prioritise consistency over perfection in her own daily routine](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000501853261_17891251754980_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq0OgkAgNmFvTaHQeui7hX9eB-6IjKI-EBgEgmvZXgLqY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Week one: Preparation
This week prepares your body for the dietary changes to come. “People tend to go all out with new regimes, then only last for three days,” says Ferguson. “[In this stage], I just want you to take the first steps.”
Eat only whole foods
Aim to eat three balanced meals a day, including protein and healthy fats, such as avocado or olive oil, at each one, and avoid snacking. Gradually increase your intake of vegetables, fruit, nuts, seeds, beans and lentils, and gluten-free wholegrains such as brown rice. At the same time, remove refined carbohydrates (white bread, pasta and cakes), alcohol, added sugar, artificial sweeteners, gluten, dairy products apart from kefir, highly processed oils (sunflower, canola and rapeseed) and ultra-processed foods (UPFs) such as biscuits and crisps. You can usually spot UPFs by their extensive ingredients lists. Drink at least two litres of water or herbal tea daily and limit caffeine to one or two cups, ideally before midday.
Stick to a 12-hour eating window
Confine your meals to a 12-hour window. For example, if you eat breakfast at 7am, finish dinner by 7pm to give your body a 12-hour overnight break from eating. “Extending the gap between your meals gives the digestive system time to reset and allows your body to repair,” says Ferguson. “Your hunger hormones will become more balanced, so you naturally snack less.”
Get outside
The reset extends beyond food. Spend 10 minutes outside within an hour of waking. “Morning light helps to set your circadian clock, regulating your hormones, sleep, digestion and energy,” says Ferguson. Aim for 7,000 brisk steps a day – this should be achievable with a walk mid-morning, mid-afternoon and after dinner.
Incorporate more calm into your day
Each morning, practise Ferguson’s MJMB routine: a few minutes of movement, journalling, meditation and breathwork. “It helps calm the morning stress response so your system doesn’t crash later,” she says.
As for sleep, Ferguson recommends going to bed by 10pm, though it’s more important that your bedtime is consistent. These habits should be continued daily throughout the reset.
By the end of the week, you should feel calmer and less caught in a cycle of snacking and energy crashes, says Ferguson. “Some people are so used to feeling wired, this calmness feels unfamiliar – as though the noise has gone.”
Week two: Reset
Now you’ve laid the groundwork, it’s time to step up the plan. “This week we shift up a gear, focusing on reducing chronic inflammation and giving your body space for a clear-out,” says Ferguson.
Eat eight plants per day
Continue avoiding the foods excluded during week one and eating three meals a day, including protein at each one. Aim for eight portions of plants per day, with as much variety and colour as possible. A portion is equivalent to a banana or apple, a fist-sized serving of broccoli or carrots, three heaped tablespoons of beans or lentils, half an avocado or a tablespoon of nuts and seeds.
![Carrots, courgettes and corn are among the vegetables that can help you reach your daily plant target](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000502223869_17891260868252_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Consume only liquids for a day
Introduce a liquid-only day on day five, choosing from soups, broths, green juices and vegetable-based smoothies. “It’s a simple way to lighten the load on your digestive system,” says Ferguson. “If you feel hungry, have an extra soup or smoothie.”
Add fermented food to each meal
To support your gut microbes, add a tablespoon of fermented food to each meal – for instance, kimchi at lunchtime and sauerkraut with your evening meal. This week, also exclude eggs and vegetables from the nightshade family, which includes potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and aubergine, which may trigger inflammation in some people.
Shorten your eating window to eight hours
Move from a 12:12 to a 16:8 eating pattern, fasting for 16 hours overnight and consuming meals within an eight-hour window. For example, you might have your first meal at 10am and finish your evening meal by 6pm. “A longer gap between meals helps lower insulin so your body can switch from burning glucose to burning stored fat,” says Ferguson.
Raise your steps target to 8,500 and start strength training
Raise your daily walking target to 8,500 steps and add two resistance-training sessions of up to 20 minutes to support your metabolism. Simple bodyweight exercises such as squats, press-ups and planks are ideal. Eat within an hour afterwards to help support muscle recovery.
Week three: Reintroduction
“By now, you should be feeling much more energetic,” says Ferguson. “Perhaps you’ve noticed your jeans are a little less snug and you’re not thinking about food every five minutes now your hormones have had a chance to settle.” Ferguson says your gut should now be stronger and more resilient, so you’ll also begin reintroducing the foods you eliminated, observing how your body responds.
Start to reintroduce eliminated foods
Continue eating three times a day without snacks, including protein at each meal and eight daily portions of plants.
Reintroduce the eliminated foods one at a time, beginning with nightshade vegetables, followed by eggs, gluten-containing foods and dairy. Leave 48 hours between each reintroduction to allow your gut to adapt. “Track how you feel,” says Ferguson. “Notice if it affects your digestion, energy, mood, joints and sleep.” UPFs, added sugar and alcohol are still firmly off the list.
Alternate fasting patterns
Alternate between 16:8 and 12:12 eating patterns. “Think of it as cross-training for your metabolism,” says Ferguson. “It encourages your body to switch between burning carbs and fat, helping stabilise your energy, digestion, mood and sleep.”
On day four, take all your meals in liquid form. “This is your reset button in the middle of the week,” says Ferguson. “If you feel ready, you can try an extra liquid-only day on day two – it can deepen that sense of lightness and clarity.”
Up the step count to 9,000 and include three weight sessions
Raise your daily walking target to 9,000 steps spread across the day, and complete three 20-minute weight-training sessions throughout the week, for upper body, lower body and full body. “Bodyweight exercises or light weights are both fine,” says Ferguson. “Just keep progressing.” Avoid resistance training on liquid-only days.
![Strength training can help build muscle and support a healthy metabolism as you age](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000502223840_17891260846898_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Week four: Integration
This week is about turning the changes you’ve made into benefits that last. “Now you have your healthy foundations in place, it’s time to build a ‘home’ you can live in,” says Ferguson. “Week four returns you to a sustainable rhythm. It’s a springboard into the rest of your year – you could continue week four for the rest of your life.”
Return to a 12-hour eating window
Continue eating three protein-rich meals a day without snacking, but return to a 12:12 eating pattern, consuming all your food within a 12-hour window. “This is sustainable in the long term and keeps your metabolism steady without over-stressing the body,” says Ferguson.
Eat 10 plants per day
Increase your intake of plant foods to 10 portions a day, aiming for as much variety and colour as possible. “A diverse, plant-rich diet is associated with lower levels of inflammation,” says Ferguson. If you tolerated the foods reintroduced last week, you can continue eating them. Leave out anything that left you feeling bloated, sluggish or moody, and continue to avoid UPFs and refined foods.
Allow yourself two alcoholic drinks per week
If you wish, you can have one glass of wine, one bottle of beer or a measure of a spirit with soda (or a non-sugary mixer) twice this week. Pay attention to any effect on your sleep, mood or digestion.
Walk 10,000 steps per day
Raise your daily walking count to 10,000 steps and continue with your three weekly resistance sessions, gradually increasing the intensity. “Muscle helps keep the hormones oestrogen, testosterone and growth hormone steadier as we age,” says Ferguson.
The life stage
By now, says Ferguson, your new healthy habits should feel more natural and you should be recognising what does and doesn’t work for your body. The aim is not to finish The Reset and “drop off a cliff” but to carry the changes that suit you into everyday life.
Prioritise consistency over perfection, says Ferguson. Inevitably, there will be times when your routine goes off the rails. The secret, says Ferguson, is not to hit what she calls the “f--- it” button.
![Rose Ferguson says the aim is to make healthy habits part of everyday life](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000501853260_17891278948680_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqKFWauwmPmEN5zn34pPb9C3uqFFkW70PKKitnWUGuSbY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“People think they’ve ruined everything and spiral downwards, but that’s not real life,” she says. “If you eat something you hadn’t planned, enjoy it and move on. The guilt can be worse than the food.”
Instead, adopt an 80:20 approach. “One bowl of ice cream will not undo your progress; what matters is what you do the majority of the time,” says Ferguson. “Allowing yourself some flexibility makes it less likely one indulgence will lead you to abandon the whole approach.”
If you do feel old habits returning, Ferguson suggests revisiting whichever week of The Reset worked for you – use it as a framework you can return to whenever you need.
The Reset: The 4 Week Plan to Feel Better Than Ever by Rose Ferguson (HQ, HarperCollins) is out now
summary: Nutritionist and functional medicine practitioner Rose Ferguson has created a four-week wellness programme designed to boost energy, improve sleep, and reduce inflammation during midlife. The plan is built around five core pillars: food, sleep, movement, morning light, and stress management, focusing on whole foods, intermittent fasting, and daily habits rather than restrictive dieting. Throughout the four weeks, participants gradually adjust their eating windows, increase plant intake, raise step counts, incorporate strength training, and eventually reintroduce eliminated foods to find a sustainable lifestyle rhythm.
key_points: The four-week reset program focuses on consistency and five core pillars: food, sleep, movement, morning light, and stress management.
Week one emphasizes preparation by eating whole foods, eliminating ultra-processed foods and added sugars, adopting a 12-hour eating window, and getting morning light.
Week two steps up the intensity with an eight-hour eating window, a liquid-only day, increased daily steps, and the introduction of strength training and fermented foods.
Week three involves systematically reintroducing previously eliminated foods like nightshades, eggs, and dairy to test personal tolerance.
Week four establishes a sustainable long-term routine featuring a 12-hour eating window, 10 daily plant portions, 10,000 daily steps, and up to two alcoholic drinks per week.

![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/12/11120948-f9a596a5-7b2e-41ec-8aa6-b9fe5da15e01.jpeg?crop=8:5,smart&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
A man was given just hours to live after a roast dinner led to him developing sepsis.
Udhyam Amin’s recovery was hailed as a miracle by his family, who described him as a “cat with nine lives”.
Mr Amin was soon rushed to the resuscitation room where his blood pH fell dangerously low and he suffered a cardiac arrest.
He was placed on a ventilator in intensive care, with medics warning his family he had developed sepsis and may only have hours to live.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/12/11120941-07067f56-fdd8-4250-b783-d3e36929d957.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Amin’s daughter Parisha Bains, a surgical registrar at Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust, said: “We were told he had gone into sepsis and multi-organ failure. Most of his critical organs had shut down. But he made it through the night and that wasn’t expected.
“It felt like our world had fallen apart. Nothing prepares you for hearing that the person you love may not make it through the day.”
Campylobacter is the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK.
It causes sickness, diarrhoea, tummy pain and fever, and symptoms begin within a few hours or days of eating food that is infected.
It usually gets better when patients rest and replace fluids, but can lead to sepsis in rare cases.
After spending a little over two weeks in an induced coma, Mr Amin is now well and back working.
The former subpostmaster turned businessman has learned to walk and speak clearly again.
Ms Bains said: “His kidneys started to work again and he was gradually weaned off his blood pressure support medication, and from then things improved.
“It’s nothing short of a miracle that he is still with us. We laugh and joke that he’s like a cat with nine lives.
“One of the first things he asked us when he woke up was what date it was because he had to submit his tax returns.
“Now he is back to work seven days a week and enjoying his life again.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/12/11120953-96e7e660-f229-4540-8bbd-98627fc8a03c.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The family have now launched a fundraiser for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity to support the intensive care unit, with £37,000 raised so far.
Read More
Mr Amin is also sharing his story to raise awareness ahead of World Sepsis Day on September 13.
He said: “Words cannot express my gratitude for the exceptional care, compassion and dedication the medical teams showed me during the most difficult time of my life.
“Their skill and commitment saved my life, and I will be forever grateful. I cannot thank them enough for giving me a second chance.”
Molly Simpson, head of charity and fundraising at Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity, said: “Udhyam’s story is both remarkable and inspiring. We are enormously thankful to Udhyam’s family for turning their gratitude into action by raising funds to support St Helier.
“Their generosity will help us enhance the environment, equipment and support available to patients and their loved ones when they need it most.”
Mr Amin is fundraising for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity. Donations can be made at justgiving.com/page/aminfamily.
summary: Udhyam Amin suffered a cardiac arrest and multi-organ failure after developing sepsis from a roast dinner, leaving him with hours to live. Following two weeks in an induced coma and a miraculous recovery, he regained his health, learned to walk and speak again, and returned to work. His family has raised £37,000 for the hospital charity that treated him to express their gratitude.
key_points: Udhyam Amin developed sepsis and multi-organ failure after eating a roast dinner.
He suffered a cardiac arrest and was given just hours to live by medics.
After spending over two weeks in an induced coma, he made a full recovery and returned to work.
His family launched a fundraiser for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity, raising £37,000 so far.

title: Man makes 'miracle' recovery from sepsis caused by a roast dinner
author: Cash Murphy
content:
![Udhyam Amin with his wife Bhavini. Udhyam is wearing a white shirt and holding a glass of bubbly. Bhavini is also holding an alcoholic drink and is wearing a pink top. She has her hand on his shoulder. Both look happy and are smiling to camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/f235/live/8e259e80-add7-11f1-871b-cb14676e811d.jpg)
Amin has expressed gratitude for the "exceptional care, compassion and dedication" shown by the medical teams who cared for him
- Published
A man who was given just hours to live after a pub roast dinner led to him developing sepsis said he has been given a "second chance" at life.
Udhyam Amin, from Kingswood, Surrey, spent more than two weeks in an induced coma in February after what he thought was food poisoning turned out to be sepsis.
Ahead of World Sepsis Day on Sunday, the 64-year-old, now back at work, feels indebted to the medical team at St Helier Hospital in south London.
"Words cannot express my gratitude for the exceptional care, compassion and dedication the medical teams showed me during the most difficult time of my life," he said.
![Udhyam Amin during his hospital stay. He is wearing an oxygen mask and has various wires attached to his body. He is in a hospital bed, wearing a hospital gown.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/3244/live/d82f52f0-add7-11f1-871b-cb14676e811d.jpg)
The 64-year-old, from Kingswood, went to A&E with suspected food poisoning in February after having a roast chicken dinner in a pub
Amin went to A&E with suspected food poisoning in February and was told that he was infected with the bacteria campylobacter, the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK.
It causes sickness, diarrhoea and fever, and symptoms begin within a few hours or days of eating infected food.
It usually improves when patients rest and replace fluids, but can lead to sepsis in rare cases.
Amin was soon rushed to the resuscitation room where his blood pH fell dangerously low and he suffered a cardiac arrest.
Medics warned Amin's family, including daughter Parisha Bains, that he had developed sepsis and may only have hours to live.
She said: "We were told he had gone into sepsis and multi-organ failure. Most of his critical organs had shut down. But he made it through the night and that wasn't expected.
"It felt like our world had fallen apart. Nothing prepares you for hearing that the person you love may not make it through the day."
Bains said it is "nothing short of a miracle" that the former subpostmaster turned businessman is still alive.
"We laugh and joke that he's like a cat with nine lives," she remarked.
A fundraiser for Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity created by the family for the intensive care unit has raised Â£37,000 so far.
