summary: Udhyam Amin, a 64-year-old man from Surrey, made a miraculous recovery from multi-organ failure and sepsis after initially visiting A&E with suspected food poisoning from a pub roast dinner in February. He spent over two weeks in an induced coma and suffered a cardiac arrest, with medics warning his family that he had only hours to live. Amin has since returned to work and expressed deep gratitude for the medical team at St Helier Hospital, while his family has raised £37,000 for the intensive care unit.
key_points: Udhyam Amin developed sepsis and multi-organ failure following a pub roast dinner in February.
He was infected with campylobacter, a common cause of food poisoning that can rarely lead to sepsis.
Amin suffered a cardiac arrest and spent more than two weeks in an induced coma.
His family was initially told he had only hours to live before he unexpectedly survived the night.
Amin's family has raised £37,000 through a fundraiser for the intensive care unit at Epsom and St Helier Hospitals Charity.

title: Depression risk associated with idealized sentiment toward urban places on social media - Nature Cities
author: Yuan; Cunyu; Zhang; Xia; Tang; Luliang; Xu; Danning; Yang; Hong
content:
Abstract
Urban residents face a substantial depression risk globally. Whereas the link between the physical built environment and depression has been extensively studied, the association between subjective environmental perception and depression remains uncharacterized at scale. Here we use social media data for the large-scale quantification of this association. Drawing on the Sina Weibo Depression Dataset, a public corpus of posts annotated for depression-related analysis, we introduce an index to measure place-based sentiment intensity (LooM) and an explainable deep learning framework to analyze 88 types of urban place. We find that depressed individuals exhibit more emotionally mixed expressions. Notably, positive sentiment toward cultural and residential places correlates with higher risk, suggesting longing for an idealized life. These risk signals form systemic patterns, vary across Chinese cities and follow scaling laws with population. Our findings challenge equating positive sentiment with mental health, prompting urban design to address residents’ subjective emotional needs.

title: Porth woman died from cancer after nine-month wait for test results
author: Rowenna Hoskin
content:
![A woman smiles at the camera, she is raising a cocktail glass filled with espresso martini to the camera in a cheers. She has blonde hair and is wearing a white top and neck scarf. She has red lipstick on.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/221/cpsprodpb/2902/live/aa5801e0-adbb-11f1-a1fc-c76e930e8813.jpg)
Sarah Catherine Daniels died at home surrounded by loved ones, her inquest was told
- Published
A mum-of-three died from cancer following a nine-month delay in receiving pathology test results, meaning she did not receive potentially life-extending treatment fast enough, an inquest has heard.
Sarah Catherine Daniels' husband said she "never gave up" trying to fight her rare and aggressive cancer, but died at home in Porth, Rhondda Cynon Taf, aged 43 in April 2025.
Coroner Rachel Knight said the pathology department where a mass from Sarah's ovary had been sent for testing was at the time "completely overwhelmed by demand" following the Covid-19 pandemic.
She told the inquest at Pontypridd Coroners' Court that the delay was "unacceptable" and reduced the chance of successful chemotherapy.
Sarah first presented to her GP aged 39 in October 2021 with "gynaecological symptoms of concern", the inquest was told on Monday.
The matter was escalated by her doctor, resulting in an ultrasound scan on 21 October in 2021 which identified a mass on one of her ovaries. Sarah was then referred to gynaecology in the Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board area.
She was given two surgical options, which included a total hysterectomy or a less invasive procedure to remove the mass.
The full hysterectomy would have triggered an early menopause as well as other effects, so the inquest was told that Sarah opted for the less invasive procedure.
In February 2022 the mass was removed, which did not have the expected appearance of a cancer, but samples were sent to pathology for testing.
![An external view of Pontypridd Coroners Court. It is a two-storey building, with an engraving in the stone which shows it was built in 1913, with tall white windows and a green front door.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/df44/live/0f7dab60-adc6-11f1-82c1-5ff19bf7a2f2.png)
Sarah Catherine Daniels "never gave up", her husband Ben told the inquest at Pontypridd
Giving evidence, Martin Ludlam, a biomedical scientist who worked as the cellular pathology and mortuary service manager at the health board, said the situation at the time was difficult.
He said that during late 2021 and 2022 their workload significantly increased due to many routine appointments being put on hold during the Covid-19 pandemic.
He said they had an insufficient capacity to manage the current demand as well as the backlog.
Ludlam told the inquest that by the end of 2022 the health board was no longer dealing with a backlog in part due to outsourcing, which he said they were still using today.
"This case has highlighted the case that we can never go back to a position where we have a routine backlog again," he said.
Ben Daniels, Sarah's husband, gave written evidence and said when Sarah received her results she was told that her condition was terminal and that her life expectancy was 12 months.
He described how his wife was determined to get better and sought private treatment at the Christie cancer treatment centre in Manchester, which included the removal of her appendix.
Sarah then received follow up treatment at Velindre Cancer Centre in Cardiff which included 10 rounds of chemotherapy and scans.
She got the all clear, but some months later scans revealed that cancer was present.
This time Sarah struggled to have blood markers in the safe remit to receive regular chemotherapy, which meant treatment was "sporadic".
Ben said his wife "never gave up" trying to fight her illness but by January 2025 her health had gotten "progressively worse".
'Incorrectly reassuring'
Dr Kein Yim, a consultant in clinical oncology at Velindre said that in March 2025 it was clear that her condition was declining and a decision was made that she was too frail for any more chemotherapy.
Sarah died at home in Porth on 15 April 2025, surrounded by loved ones.
Mohamed Khalifa, a consultant in obstetrics and gynaecology who leads gynaecological cancer multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings for the Cwm Taf health board, gave evidence about the significance of the nine month pathology delay in Sarah's case.
He said that Sarah had lost time in her cancer treatment due to the delay between surgery and histology. He also said her Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) had been "incorrectly reassuring" to her and her family.
"When she died might have been different if the chemotherapy or other treatment had been started sooner. The delay of [nine] months between surgery and histology was unacceptable," he said.
Knight told the inquest that initial aspects of Sarah's care were dealt with in appropriate time, including her initial GP referral and her MRI scan on November 10.
The coroner said there was "low suspicion" that Sarah had cancer at that stage and that it was "reasonable" that medics did not seek an MRI scan of a wider area like her entire abdomen which may have revealed her appendix cancer.
She said evidence corroborated that the mass did not have the appearance of cancer, and that samples were sent "appropriately" to pathology for testing.
However, she noted that the pathology department was "completely overwhelmed by demand" due to pre and post-Covid factors including staffing and a huge backlog.
Drawing on evidence she stated that the department had begun outsourcing its backlog, but that this was in its infancy. At present she said there had been no "overhaul" of the system, but that a better framework had been established by the health board.
She said she found the nine month delay between Sarah's surgery and result "unacceptable", and noted that the issue was accepted by the health board. She said that Sarah had been living with stage four cancer since October 2021, and that the delay likely impacted her treatment as well as her quality and length of life.
She said the delay reduced the chance of success in cancer control through chemotherapy.
Sarah's medical cause of death was recorded as "metastatic signet ring adenocarcinoma of the appendix".
Although Knight noted that the medical cause of death was "naturally occurring", she opted for a narrative conclusion to reflect the full circumstances of Sarah's death.
Knight apologised to Ben and their children: "I'm sorry you lost Sarah in the way you did. You have shown great dignity throughout the proceedings... What you went though must have been horrendous."
She added it is clear "how loved Sarah was and how missed she is".

An inquest heard that the pathology department was overwhelmed by pandemic backlogs, leading to an unacceptable wait that reduced her chances of successful chemotherapy and life-extending treatment. Coroner Rachel Knight delivered a narrative conclusion, noting that the delay likely impacted Sarah's quality and length of life.

The health board's pathology department was overwhelmed by backlogs and staffing issues following the Covid-19 pandemic at the time of the testing.

title: NHS fuelling obesity by abandoning breastfeeding, says chairman
author: Laura Donnelly
content:
More broadly, Dr Dash suggested efforts to improve public health remained trapped between political fears about the “nanny state” and arguments about poverty.
Drawing on her experience of working with local political leaders, she said attempts to tackle obesity had repeatedly run into objections.
“Every time we tried to get into a conversation about what are we going to do to improve health and tackle obesity, one of the political leaders would say, ‘Oh, nanny state, nanny state, not going near it’,” she said.
At the other extreme, she said, another objection would be “not [being] willing to have any discussion whatsoever about obesity or improving health until we’ve tackled structural poverty”.
She added: “So there we were, two extremes, whole conversation shut down, and unfortunately I think we are still in that world.”
Britain historically among worst for breastfeeding
Health officials recommend that babies are exclusively breastfed for around six months, with breastfeeding continuing after solid foods are introduced.
The latest figures show that by six months, just 26 per cent of babies in England are exclusively breastfed.
International comparisons have historically placed Britain among the worst-performing countries for breastfeeding, although differences in data collection make direct comparisons difficult.
Last year, ministers extended funding for the National Breastfeeding Helpline to provide round-the-clock support, alongside £18.5m for infant-feeding services through family hubs.
Dr Dash, who became chairman of NHS England last year, is a former hospital doctor and senior management consultant who has conducted major reviews of NHS performance.
She said tackling public health was “tricky” because responsibility was shared across multiple bodies, including local authorities, the chief medical officer and other government departments.
But she argued this made it particularly important for the NHS to act where it could make a difference.
Treating conditions such as diabetes once they had developed amounted to intervening “after the horse has bolted”, she suggested, adding: “We’ve really got to get right up front.”
‘Deterioration in diabetes care’
Meanwhile, she warned that deteriorating health had coincided with worsening NHS care for conditions closely associated with obesity.
Diabetes was among the starkest examples, with standards of care falling while obesity and type 2 diabetes became increasingly common.
“To have seen a deterioration in the care that we provide for people with type 2 diabetes is really disappointing,” she said.
The NHS chairman also highlighted international comparisons showing Britain performing poorly on avoidable deaths from cardiovascular and circulatory diseases.
She described the findings as another “wake-up call” after more than a century of improving life expectancy and healthy life expectancy.
Dr Dash linked this to obesity, diabetes and failures to identify and control conditions such as high blood pressure, saying: “That’s what’s letting us down.”
She rejected suggestions that poor outcomes simply reflected a lack of NHS funding, saying standards were not good enough. “At the moment, we’re not providing the level of care that the population that we serve expects us to,” she said.
Country ‘not flush with money’
Health spending had risen significantly, particularly over the past five years, but hospitals had been “flooded” with much of the extra money when much more should be diverted to services in the community, said Dr Dash.
Hospital productivity has recovered over the past year, but remains below its 2020 level despite significant increases in spending.
“It would be hard to find another sector of the economy that had productivity now in 2026 below the level of productivity in 2020,” she said.
Dr Dash said controlling NHS finances was essential because Britain lacked the money to keep increasing spending indefinitely, adding: “We’re not a country flush with money at the moment.”
Catherine Hine, the chief executive of The Breastfeeding Network, said: “It’s great to hear the chair of NHS England highlight the importance of supporting mums and families who want to breastfeed.
“This matters because the evidence consistently shows that despite recent improvements, almost three in four mothers still stop breastfeeding before they want to. This is usually because of challenges that could be addressed with the right support at the right time.”
She said the network provided help through the National Breastfeeding Helpline, run with the Association of Breastfeeding Mothers, 24 hours a day on 0300 100 0212.
summary: NHS England chairman Dr Dash warned that public health efforts to tackle obesity and improve outcomes are hindered by political gridlock and poor early intervention. She highlighted that Britain continues to perform poorly in breastfeeding rates, diabetes care, and avoidable deaths from cardiovascular disease. Furthermore, she noted that despite increased health spending, hospital productivity remains below 2020 levels and more resources need to be directed toward community services.
key_points: Efforts to address obesity and public health are often stalled between fears of a "nanny state" and debates over structural poverty.
Only 26 per cent of babies in England are exclusively breastfed by six months, placing Britain among the worst-performing countries historically.
Standards of care for type 2 diabetes have deteriorated alongside rising obesity rates and poor performance in preventing avoidable deaths.
Dr Dash stated that hospital productivity remains below 2020 levels despite increased funding, emphasizing the need to shift resources to community care.

title: From ‘Ozempic breath’ to hair loss: sorting the science from the hype about weight loss jabs
author: Isabelle Aron
content:
They suppress your appetite so you never feel hungry
FALSE “GLP-1 medications mimic Glucagon-like peptide-1 – one of the hormones involved in appetite regulation. It doesn’t completely suppress hunger, but it is powerful,” says Dr Federica Amati, nutrition lead at Imperial College School of Medicine and author of The Appetite Reset. “The medicine is about 1,000 times stronger than what we naturally produce from our gut,” she explains. As food passes through the gut, cells called L-cells sense the nutrients, which sparks the production of the GLP-1 hormone. Without the drugs, these bursts of GLP-1 production last a few minutes. “It’s a bit like a sparkler. In comparison, the drugs are like a bonfire that roars for a week,” says Amati. Because the GLP-1 hormone stays in your body for longer if you are on the drugs, you feel fuller faster and your appetite gets suppressed, but you will eventually get hungry.
They can cause gastrointestinal issues
TRUE “Nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and vomiting are well-recognised side-effects,” says Dr Adrian Brown, associate professor and specialist dietitian at University College London. “They tend to occur during dose escalation, and most symptoms improve over time.” Eating smaller meals, staying hydrated and limiting fatty foods can help.
“One of the best ways to prevent these side-effects is to prepare your gut, liver and pancreas before you start taking the medications,” says Amati. “If you go into treatment with existing reflux or constipation, it’s only going to get worse.” She advises eating more plants and gradually upping your fibre intake. Once taking the drugs, never push past the point of fullness. “The gastric emptying is so slow that you need to stop straight away.”
They make you forget to drink water
PARTLY TRUE The drugs themselves don’t make you want to drink less, but people can experience this as a side-effect. This is partly because we get a lot of water from food, especially fruits and vegetables. “These drugs massively reduce the amount that you eat – up to 40% reduction in calories,” says Amati. You may also drink less if you’re experiencing nausea, constipation or reflux. “It’s important that you do drink, because dehydration is one of the key reasons why reflux and constipation may be worse,” she says. As well as drinking water, she recommends having hydrating foods and smoothies, especially on the day you take the drugs (typically, the injections are used once a week, while the pills are taken daily), when you can have the most appetite suppression.
They can make you deficient in nutrients
TRUE Taking GLP-1 medication can “substantially reduce food intake, and that creates the potential for nutrient deficiencies if the quality of a person’s diet is poor,” says Brown, who has researched this area. He found that some people on these drugs may not get enough vitamin D, vitamin B12, iron, calcium and protein.
“If your diet was relatively healthy to begin with, that’s fine because you’re just eating less. But this is not true for many people,” says Giles Yeo, professor of molecular neuroendocrinology at the University of Cambridge and an obesity expert. “For those whose diets were not great to begin with, there’s a danger of going into malnutrition. You can’t just inject yourself and hope for the best. You have to think about your diet and exercise.”
Once you come off them you gain weight again
PARTLY TRUE “Obesity is a chronic, relapsing, progressive condition. When medications for obesity are stopped, a person’s body will attempt to regain the weight,” says Brown. “Studies have shown that people can regain about 60% of the weight lost following stopping the medication.”
In fact, one study from the University of Oxford found that people who stop taking GLP-1 medication will return to their original weight within two years. “For a lot of people, these are likely to be long-term or for ever drugs,” says Yeo. “Your appetite is only suppressed when you’re on them. If you stop, your hormonal levels will go back to what they were. You’ll feel as hungry as before, which means the weight will come back.”
While the idea of taking medication for ever might sound scary, Yeo points out that many people take medication for high blood pressure and statins, used for lowering cholesterol, for life. “I think the same is going to be true for these drugs,” he says.
They make you lose muscle and you need to eat more protein while taking them
TRUE “Whenever people lose weight, they don’t just lose fat, they also lose muscle. The key point is whether we can minimise it,” says Brown. “Current evidence suggests that up to 40% of the weight lost with GLP-1 medicine may come from lean mass [bone, muscle and connective tissue] rather than fat alone.”
This is why it’s important to prioritise protein-rich foods and resistance training when taking GLP-1s. “It’s not negotiable – you have to do it if you want to preserve lean mass,” says Amati. “If you have excess fat mass and you engage in resistance training, you will lose fat first because that’s the stored energy source.” She recommends resistance training three times a week, including high-quality protein in every meal, and eating that first.
![Illustration of yellow uninflated balloons forming a circle with three black balloons on top to resemble a face](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/674e619a89170580fbc47f54b9c11919a143cbb7/0_0_4375_3500/master/4375.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Not everyone responds to them in the same way
TRUE “These drugs don’t work for everybody – they’re not a magic bullet,” says Amati. “The data shows that 5-20% of people lose less than 5% of their body weight, so they’re classed as non-responders. If you’re someone who doesn’t have a very sensitive GLP-1 receptor, GLP-1 medications won’t have the desired effect.” While we don’t yet know why this is, Yeo says that it’s only a matter of time before we do.
Anyone should use them to lose weight
FALSE GLP-1 drugs were originally developed for people with type 2 diabetes. Now, they’re also licensed for people with obesity, or people who are overweight and have weight-related health problems. Despite this, many people are using GLP-1s for aesthetic reasons because they’ve become so easily accessible.
“I see a lot of people accessing them to lose weight before a wedding or a holiday,” says Amati. “These drugs are not designed for that.” People taking GLP-1s in this way could end up with a worse body composition, she explains. “It’s much easier to regain fat than muscle, so you could find yourself with increased fat mass compared to before you started. Losing lean mass is not helpful for longevity.”
after newsletter promotion
They could improve your mental health
PARTLY TRUE When it comes to how GLP-1s impact anxiety and depression, Michael Browning, professor of psychiatry at the University of Oxford, says, “The evidence that they’re beneficial is pretty thin, and some studies are ongoing.”
Things are more promising for addiction, particularly with alcohol, where there have been some randomised controlled trials. One of these showed that taking semaglutide (the GLP-1 agonist in Wegovy and Ozempic) reduced the number of heavy drinking days for participants. For other addictions, such as nicotine and other drugs, more research is needed. “There’s work in animals that suggests they might reduce nicotine dependence, but the evidence is not there in humans,” says Browning.
They cause bad breath and smelly burps
MORE RESEARCH NEEDED Is “Ozempic breath” a thing? “There is a lot of anecdotal evidence, but not any epidemiological studies,” says Dr Praveen Sharma, an associate professor at the University of Birmingham’s School of Dentistry.
While there’s no hard evidence yet, it could be side-effects like vomiting and dehydration that lead to a dry mouth, he says. Saliva “keeps the mouth hydrated and the bacteria level low”, so having a dry mouth can mean “you get a proliferation of bacteria, which can result in bad breath”.
As for burps? Dr Lindsey Ann Edwards, senior lecturer in microbiology at King’s College London, says that by slowing gastric emptying, GLP-1 medication can “cause food to remain in the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract for longer, creating more opportunity for the gut microbiome to ferment partially digested food. This microbial fermentation can generate gases which may contribute to unpleasant-smelling or “sulphur” burps.
They can make your hair fall out
TRUE Your body goes through a stress response when you take GLP-1 drugs, says consultant dermatologist Dr Angela Tewari. “That puts stress on the hair, and you can experience telogen effluvium, which is stress response hair loss. It puts your hair into a shedding phase,” she says.
The good news is that this kind of hair loss is reversible. As your body gets used to the medication, this side-effect will ease off, although the pace at which your hair grows back will vary. “It can be an inch a month for some people. Generally, how fast your hair grows is a genetic thing,” says Tewari, who recommends taking the lowest possible dose of GLP-1s and eating food rich in protein, zinc, iron and vitamin C to encourage a healthy scalp.
Your face may get saggy and gaunt
TRUE You may take GLP-1s to change your body, but what do the drugs do to your face? Under your skin, you have a “support system”, explains Tewari. “There’s your collagen, and under that you have a fat layer and a muscle layer. That all makes the skin look plumper.” When you lose the fat layer quickly, the top layer of your skin is still expanded, as it has stretched over time to support the other layers. This means your skin will sag as there is less support underneath, so it can look wrinkled and dull. To counter this, many people end up spending money on injectables, says Tewari. “I wouldn’t jump into any procedures straight away. Allow your body to settle into its new look before you do anything,” she says.
Weight loss isn’t the only health benefit
MORE RESEARCH NEEDED As more people take GLP-1s, researchers are looking at the benefits beyond weight loss. One study found that people on GLP-1s were 30% less likely to develop breast cancer. Another found that patients with breast, lung, bowel or liver cancer who took them were up to 50% less likely to have their cancer spread.
“What’s challenging is disentangling the direct impact of these drugs and the secondary impact of losing weight,” says Dr Simon Cork, associate professor of physiology at Anglia Ruskin University’s School of Medicine. “Obesity increases your risk of at least 13 types of cancer. By reducing your weight, the likelihood of you developing cancer will also be reduced.”
Cork has researched GLP-1s and cardiovascular disease, and found that “the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with obesity taking GLP-1 was reduced by about 14%”. More research is needed, but if there are “weight-independent effects of these drugs”, Cork says the difficulty will be in trying to separate those benefits from weight loss, as some patients won’t need to lose weight.
summary: Weight loss jabs like GLP-1 medications are powerful appetite suppressants that can lead to significant weight loss, but they also carry various side-effects such as gastrointestinal issues, nutrient deficiencies, and muscle loss. While these drugs are generally intended for individuals with obesity or type 2 diabetes, stopping them often results in weight regain, suggesting they may need to be taken long-term. Experts emphasize that proper diet, hydration, and resistance training are essential to mitigate side-effects and preserve lean mass while using these medications.
key_points: GLP-1 medications effectively suppress appetite by mimicking the natural hormone, but they do not eliminate hunger entirely.
Common side-effects include gastrointestinal issues, potential nutrient deficiencies, dehydration, stress-related hair loss, and loss of lean muscle mass.
Stopping the medication often leads to a significant regain of the lost weight within two years, meaning many people may need to use them long-term.
The drugs can cause a gaunt facial appearance and sagging skin due to rapid fat loss beneath the skin.
GLP-1s are licensed for people with obesity or weight-related health problems, rather than for short-term aesthetic weight loss.

title: Customers of UK-owned surrogacy firm in Mexico allegedly face huge bills after insurance denied
author: Helena Horton; Jessica Murray
content:
The UK government has said it is reviewing allegations about a British-owned surrogacy service after surrogates in Mexico who faced health complications including a hysterectomy had their insurance claims rejected.
The Department of Health and Social Care is considering whether the UK-based provider My Surrogacy Journey should remain listed on gov.uk as one of four domestic surrogacy agencies available to intended parents, after its Mexican sister company received complaints.
Emails sent by the chief executive of My Surrogacy Journey seen by the Guardian suggest multiple surrogate women had their insurance claims rejected in Mexico, where the surrogates are based. The emails suggest 300 couples going through a “surrogacy journey” with the company have been moved to a new insurance provider due to the increased risk of claims being rejected.
In the UK, commercial surrogacy is banned and only altruistic surrogacy arrangements are permitted. My Surrogacy Journey has a UK branch which is not-for-profit, and also has for-profit sister companies operating in Mexico and the US, where commercial surrogacy is legal in some states. All three companies have the same owners and chief executives. It is My Surrogacy Journey’s Mexico-based surrogacies which have had insurance issues.
One couple the Guardian spoke to said they paid tens of thousands of pounds to cover the medical costs of their surrogate who had a hysterectomy during birth after her insurance claim was refused.
My Surrogacy Journey was founded in 2021 by the couple Michael and Wes Johnson-Ellis, both from Birmingham, who set it up after having their own children via surrogacy.
The couple, now based in the Cayman Islands, say their company is a “UK surrogacy organisation like no other” with “one of the most enviable advisory boards for a surrogacy not-for-profit organisation” and that it is the “new face of surrogacy”.
The Guardian understands at least five sets of parents say they had to foot the bill for medical costs after insurance claims were refused.
An email seen by the Guardian sent by Michael Johnson-Ellis to the couple whose surrogate had a hysterectomy said: “We have already told you that the insurance companies have been declining some of the claims and we are actively working with the broker to get this issue resolved but you should also consider that they may not be paid out and there is nothing we are able to do to change this ... We appreciate this is not an insignificant sum but this genuinely is out of our control.”
Johnson-Ellis added in the email that the company had switched to a new insurance provider, explaining: “We’re also managing this for 300 other journeys, which is a complex position to be in.”
Lawyers acting for My Surrogacy Journey said the company did not comment on individual cases, but that existing insurance policies were in place and claims continued to be accepted and processed. They said the company was of the understanding that a small number of claims were rejected and was supporting those seeking to resolve claims with an insurer.
It is understood that as part of the surrogacy arrangement intended parents are contractually required to cover any medical costs that may not be covered by an insurer.
The couple who spoke to the Guardian reported being recommended to take the “Mexico option”. The website advertises that those who go to Mexico can have a baby in “under 18 months”. The parents say they were told the UK option can take up to five years, and that the US route is much more expensive. Lawyers acting for My Surrogacy Journey said that intended or prospective parents were provided with information about what the surrogacy process entails, including typical timelines, cost, legal frameworks and practical considerations in a transparent and understandable way, and that the 18-month period is indicative only.
after newsletter promotion
The couple described their dream of having a baby turning into a nightmare when their surrogate developed a serious condition known as placenta accreta, which is when the placenta attaches to the wall of the uterus.
The emails from Johnson-Ellis acknowledge that the insurance provider investigated the birth after the woman’s health complications. One email reads: “As your surrogate’s care took an unexpected turn, this later led to even more scrutiny by the hospital and insurance provider – which we have no control over.”
The parents are considering legal action, and the Guardian understands at least four other couples are reviewing their options.
Phil Brickell, the MP for Bolton West, raised the concerns of a separate couple who had used My Surrogacy Journey. He told parliament during a debate regarding surrogacy on Monday: “Two of my constituents recently travelled to Mexico, where their children were born by surrogacy. Those births were facilitated by a company called My Surrogacy Journey, which is listed on gov.uk. While in Mexico, they had repeated traumatic experiences with the company relating to issues including insurance for their children, accusations of bullying towards staff and repeated efforts to silence any constructive criticism. I understand that other members of this house have received similar complaints.”
Brickell is calling for the government to “take My Surrogacy Journey down from gov.uk pending a review by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority”.
The health minister Diana Johnson said the government was reviewing allegations made regarding My Surrogacy Journey. She said: “The department is looking into the allegations about My Surrogacy Journey. As part of that assessment, the department will consider whether it is appropriate for that company to remain on the gov.uk list of agencies”. A DHSC spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the government was reviewing allegations about My Surrogacy Journey. Lawyers acting for My Surrogacy Journey said the company was in communication with DHSC and it was confident any issues could be resolved.
Dr Bianca Jackson, a surrogacy law expert at Coram Chambers, said the case highlighted by the Guardian seemed “incredibly worrying”. She said: “For the past 13 years, I have acted for intended parents applying for parental orders for children born in many different countries. Though I have come across a plethora of issues with agencies abroad, I have never come across this problem in practice. My experience suggests that this is not a wide or prevalent issue with surrogacy abroad and it is limited to Mexico/the organisation you are investigating, but it is still incredibly worrying.”
The London-based surrogacy consultant Shaun Thomas, who founded The Surrogacy Father after his own experience having children via surrogate, said insurance could get “very complicated”, especially when it involved third-party reproduction like IVF and navigating healthcare systems abroad.
He said intended parents needed to make sure their insurance covered both the surrogate and the baby, adding that some policies did not always include neonatal intensive care unit admission or may exclude certain hospitals.
Lawyers acting for My Surrogacy Journey said the health and wellbeing of surrogates and babies as well as that of intended parents was at the core of its values.
summary: The UK government is reviewing allegations against the British-owned surrogacy agency My Surrogacy Journey after surrogate mothers in Mexico experienced rejected insurance claims for serious medical complications. At least five sets of intended parents have had to pay tens of thousands of pounds out of pocket for medical expenses, including a surrogate who required a hysterectomy. Lawyers for the company stated that existing policies remain in place, claims continue to be processed, and they are supporting those seeking resolutions.
key_points: The Department of Health and Social Care is considering whether My Surrogacy Journey should remain listed on gov.uk following complaints.
Multiple surrogate women in Mexico had insurance claims rejected, prompting the company to switch 300 couples to a new insurance provider.
Intended parents are contractually required to cover medical costs not paid by insurers, leading some couples to pay tens of thousands of pounds.
At least five sets of parents faced unexpected medical bills, with some considering legal action.
Lawyers for My Surrogacy Journey stated that only a small number of claims were rejected and that the company is assisting in resolving them.

title: 'A stroke completely wiped out my ability to speak'
author: Maisie Lillywhite; Nicky Price
content:
![A selfie of a man who looks to be in his 40s. He is smiing and has brown hair which is very short on the sides and curly on top. He is wearing a black polo shirt and a large TV and blue LED lights can be seen behind him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a584/live/d2ac2040-ad2f-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg)
Chris was determined to start walking again after he had a stroke 16 years ago
- Published
A man who had a stroke that "completely wiped out" his ability to speak is encouraging more people living with aphasia to join his support group.
Chris Greenhough could not speak for the first few weeks after having a stroke 16 years ago, and slowly regained the ability after months of rehabilitation and subsequent speech therapy, the latter of which he is still receiving.
Now, Greenhough runs a Say Aphasia group for those also living with the condition which makes it hard for people to communicate, often after a stroke or brain injury.
Colin Lyall, who set up Say Aphasia after his diagnosis, said about 350,000 people in the UK live with the condition.
More from Gloucestershire
According to the NHS, there is no cure for aphasia, but those living with it usually improve with speech and language therapy.
During his rehabilitation, Greenhough said he received half an hour of speech therapy every week, which, he said, was "frustrating".
"I can now walk because I wanted to do it for my kids which all were five and under at the time. I wanted to get better," he said.
"I am continuing to learn different aspects of my speech, I have dyslexia but it's made me learn a different way to speech but it's continuing all the time."
![A group of about 15 people sit inside a boat during a day out for a support group. The group is comprised of men and women - mostly older in age. They are all smiling. Other boats can be seen behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/c10a/live/b6149770-ad14-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Chris (R) says people of varying speech and language abilities come to the support group sessions he runs in Gloucestershire
Greenhough now runs the Say Aphasia group in Gloucestershire, attendees of which have varying speech and language abilities.
The charity was set up by Lyall, who is still unable to read and write after developing aphasia following a stroke 13 years ago.
"It's a fog," Lyall said of aphasia. "After two years, my fog was lifted.
"This is my life. I can't do my job anymore because I can't read, can't write, and it's just too complicated. So, after two years, I decided to do the charity."
Lyall said he focuses on staying positive about the things he can do and his charity, which now has more than 30 support groups across the UK, is one of those things.
![A group of 14 men and women of varying ages sit around a dining table in a cafe, enjoying drinks and talking to one another.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0132/live/86ab0770-ad15-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
According to Say Aphasia, about 350,000 people in the UK are living with the condition
"There's lack of speech, lack of reading, lack of writing, and lack of numbers - there's three people that can't speak at all but they can communicate," Greenhough said of the Gloucestershire group.
"It's a wonderful thing because Colin is passionate about it and so am I - we can do it together."
The Gloucestershire group meets on the first and third Monday of every month at the Malt House Cafe in Stroud, and on second and fourth Monday of every month at St George's Church in Tuffley.
summary: Sixteen years after a stroke completely stripped him of his ability to speak, Chris Greenhough is encouraging others with aphasia to join a support group he runs in Gloucestershire. Greenhough slowly regained his speech through extensive rehabilitation and ongoing speech therapy, despite initial frustrations with limited therapy time. The Say Aphasia charity, founded by Colin Lyall, now operates more than 30 support groups across the UK to help individuals communicate and cope with the condition.
key_points: Chris Greenhough lost his ability to speak following a stroke 16 years ago and continues to learn and improve his speech.
Greenhough now runs a local branch of the Say Aphasia support group in Gloucestershire.
The Say Aphasia charity was established by Colin Lyall, who developed aphasia after a stroke 13 years ago.
An estimated 350,000 people live with aphasia in the UK, a condition with no cure though speech therapy typically helps improve communication.

title: Southampton ovarian cancer patient tumour free after pioneering treatment
author: Alastair Fee
content:
![Caroline Ainslie in a hospital bed she is smiling at the camera. She has a bald head.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/900/cpsprodpb/330f/live/cefca610-acdd-11f1-a91a-5f4222780d03.jpg)
Caroline Ainslie underwent a pioneering treatment
- Published
A former nurse who was told she had inoperable cancer has been declared free of the disease after receiving a pioneering chemotherapy treatment.
Caroline Ainslie, 60, from Southampton, was diagnosed with stage-four ovarian cancer in March after the disease spread to her liver, lungs and other parts of her body.
However, she responded well to initial treatment and became one of the first ovarian cancer patients at University Hospital Southampton to receive hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC).
Her consultant said she was now tumour free and expected to fully recover and go on to lead a normal life.
Caroline's diagnosis could not have been worse.
"I had cancer in my ovary, it was also in my liver and in my lung, so I felt completely and utterly shocked and devastated because I had cancer pretty much everywhere," she said.
"I just thought that was it, I was a going to die, and I didn't have very much life left.
"I thought I would be dead within a year - it was devastating, absolutely devastating."
![Caroline Ainslie being examined by surgeon David Constable-Phelps at University Hospital Southampton. Caroline is on a bed, the surgeon is looking at her scar. There is a nurse in blue.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/59d3/live/3ffb4020-a0a3-11f1-84a9-276d1a8e5a22.jpg)
Caroline was treated by surgeon David Constable-Phelps at University Hospital Southampton
Caroline responded so well to an initial round of chemotherapy, her consultant David Constable-Phelps suggested she undergo a pioneering treatment that involves pouring heated chemotherapy into the body after her cancerous tumours were removed.
Constable-Phelps, a consultant gynaecologist and gynaecological oncology surgeon at University Hospital Southampton, said: "HIPEC is essentially us putting chemotherapy into a carrier solution inside the abdomen.
"Once we've finished the operation and once we've achieved complete clearance of the disease, that solution is heated to 42C (107F) and we circulate that for 90 minutes using a HIPEC machine.
"So that is circulating for 90 minutes to mop up any cancer cells that might remain that are microscopic that of course we can't see with the naked eye."
Caroline's treatment was complicated. The operation took 12 hours â but it was a huge success.
Constable-Phelps said: "It's fantastic. She is currently tumour free.
"I would expect her to fully recover from the operation and have no life-limiting symptoms from the surgery or the chemotherapy and she should go on and lead her life as normal."
![David Constable-Phelps in a white shirt and blue jacket looking at the camera. He has short brown hair and a short brown beard with some grey hairs. He is sat in an office and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1005/live/5125ef30-a0a3-11f1-84a9-276d1a8e5a22.jpg)
David Constable-Phelps carried out the 12-hour procedure at University Hospital Southampton
Caroline, who previously worked at University Hospital Southampton as a divisional head of nursing, said: "At this moment in time I am cancer free and I am absolutely delighted about that.
"It's surreal really because I never would have imagined that I would be in this position, and I'm incredibly grateful to the people who have operated on me and cared for me."
Ovarian cancer is often called a silent killer because its early signs are vague and easily mistaken for common digestive or menstrual issues.
Key warning signs include persistent bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full quickly while eating, and a frequent or urgent need to urinate.
These symptoms are considered silent not because they do not exist, but because they are subtle and often progress before a definitive diagnosis is made.
It is the sixth most common cancer in women, with about 7,500 diagnosed in the UK each year.
Around two-thirds of cases are diagnosed at a late stage, when treatment options can be more limited, and the disease claims more than 4,000 lives annually.
![An operating theatre with people in scrubs around a patient.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/22ef/live/c4abdeb0-a864-11f1-ae45-e9984fc27c77.jpg)
Surgery at University Hospital Southampton using a pioneering treatment known as hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC).
Since establishing its HIPEC service in 2022, UHS has become a national leader in the treatment, recently completing its 50th procedure on patients with a range of different cancers and placing it among the most experienced centres in the UK.
Caroline said: "Hopefully my story inspires other people to realise that actually having a cancer diagnosis does not mean the end of your life.
"It certainly changes it, but there is a great deal of hope in the future because of the advances in treatments."
She is now recovering from surgery and will undergo two further rounds of chemotherapy, while continuing to be monitored closely as part of her follow-up care.
'Transforming lives'
Caroline is now building up her fitness and to celebrate being told she is cancer free she has just booked a ski holiday for next year.
With growing evidence supporting its use in selected patients, more NHS cancer centres are exploring the introduction of HIPEC treatment.
While this case involved ovarian cancer, the treatment is also used for selected patients with other cancers that have spread within the abdomen, including bowel and appendix cancers.
The introduction of HIPEC at University Hospital Southampton was made possible through a donation from Hampshire-based PLANETS Cancer Charity, helping to expand treatment options for patients with ovarian and other cancers.
Neil Pearce, chairman of PLANETS and a retired consultant liver and pancreatic surgeon, said: "We are extremely proud to have been able to fund the use of this revolutionary cancer treatment at UHS, and stories such as Caroline's demonstrate the impact the charity and all our supporters have in saving and transforming lives."
summary: A 60-year-old former nurse from Southampton diagnosed with stage-four inoperable ovarian cancer has been declared tumour free after receiving a pioneering treatment. Caroline Ainslie underwent a 12-hour surgery at University Hospital Southampton, which included hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) to target microscopic cancer cells. Her consultant expects her to fully recover and lead a normal life following the successful procedure.
key_points: Caroline Ainslie was diagnosed with stage-four ovarian cancer that had spread to her liver and lungs.
She received a pioneering treatment called hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) at University Hospital Southampton.
The 12-hour procedure involved removing tumours and circulating heated chemotherapy inside the abdomen for 90 minutes.
Her consultant confirmed she is currently tumour free and expected to make a full recovery.
University Hospital Southampton established its HIPEC service in 2022 and has completed 50 such procedures.

title: Fatigue in teenage girls linked to heavy periods and lifestyle – not iron deficiency
author: Anna Stubbendorff; Moa Wolff
content:
Fatigue is common among teenage girls and can have a substantial impact on their everyday life, including school attendance and social functioning.
Iron deficiency and anaemia are often considered the most probable explanations for the symptoms of fatigue that teenage girls experience. But our recent findings suggest that the cause is more complicated.
We studied 485 Swedish female high school students. Participants completed questionnaires about fatigue, quality of life, menstrual patterns, diet, nicotine use and dietary supplement use. They also provided blood samples to measure haemoglobin and ferritin – key markers to assess iron status. Low ferritin and low haemoglobin levels typically indicate iron deficiency and anaemia, respectively.
In earlier analyses of the same group, we found iron deficiency was present in 38% of participants. It was strongly associated with both heavy periods (reported by 54% of the participants) and eating a diet with little or no meat (reported by 27% of participants).
In our latest study, the group reported experiencing high levels of fatigue. However, our analyses revealed that neither iron deficiency nor anaemia were associated with higher levels of fatigue or lower quality of life.
In fact, the opposite was true. Lower ferritin and lower haemoglobin levels were linked to less fatigue – even after accounting for confounding factors.
Instead, we found that heavy periods were associated with greater fatigue and poorer quality of life. This was true even after adjusting for ferritin and haemoglobin levels.
This suggests that the association between heavy periods and fatigue is not explained by iron deficiency or anaemia. Other consequences of heavy periods – such as menstrual pain, disturbed sleep or missing school, sports and social activities – may instead contribute.
![A teenage girl lies on a couch holding her stomach in pain.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/758750/original/file-20260909-50-4e90m2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
Skipping breakfast, lunch or both meals on one or more days per week was also associated with greater fatigue and poorer wellbeing. Daily nicotine use, including snus or smoking, was likewise associated with greater fatigue and poorer wellbeing.
These are important results because heavy periods, skipped meals and nicotine use are modifiable factors that may be overlooked if iron deficiency is assumed to be the only cause of fatigue.
Understanding fatigue
Our study did not capture everything that might influence fatigue. For example, we lacked information on socioeconomic status, physical activity levels, mental health and sleep – factors that may also be related to fatigue.
We also cannot determine cause or effect. For instance, girls may skip breakfast because they’re tired. Nicotine use may be a marker of other lifestyle factors linked to fatigue – rather than a direct cause of fatigue.
Iron deficiency still matters, however. It’s the leading cause of anaemia worldwide. Iron is essential for transporting oxygen to the organs, for good muscle health and normal brain function.
Teenage girls are particularly prone to iron deficiency because their iron needs increase during growth. Menstruation and dietary habits can further reduce iron stores.
Our research will now evaluate a newly developed five-question screening tool for identifying iron deficiency. We will also continue to investigate which symptoms or other indicators are most useful for detecting iron deficiency, and which treatment strategies work best in this population.
These novel results matters because fatigue in teenage girls is often reduced to a question of iron deficiency. Our findings suggest that the picture is more complex. Heavy periods, skipped meals and nicotine use are common and potentially modifiable factors. Overlooking them may mean missing important opportunities to support teenage girls’ health and wellbeing.
summary: A study of Swedish female high school students found that fatigue in teenage girls is not linked to iron deficiency or anaemia, contrary to common assumptions. Instead, researchers discovered that heavy menstrual periods, skipped meals, and daily nicotine use are associated with greater fatigue and poorer quality of life. Identifying and addressing these modifiable lifestyle factors is crucial for supporting teenage girls' health.
key_points: Neither iron deficiency nor anaemia were associated with higher levels of fatigue or lower quality of life.
Lower ferritin and haemoglobin levels were surprisingly linked to less fatigue.
Heavy menstrual periods were associated with greater fatigue and poorer quality of life, independent of iron levels.
Skipping meals and daily nicotine use were also linked to increased fatigue and lower wellbeing.
Addressing modifiable factors like heavy periods, skipped meals, and nicotine use can help prevent overlooked causes of fatigue in teenage girls.

title: I’d rather risk cancer than drink cold tea
author: Ella Whelan
content:
![A glass cup of hot tea on a table.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501675183_17889627063610_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A glass cup of hot tea on a table.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/09/TELEMMGLPICT000501675183_17889627063610_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
What temperature is your cup of tea? If you don’t know the answer, you could be in, err, hot water. New research from the University of Oxford has found that drinking your morning brew too hot could increase your risk of oesophageal cancer. Using data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women, the researchers concluded that consuming six or more hot drinks per day – or any drink above 65 degrees Celsius – could be dangerous.
Like many, I cannot abide hot drinks that are not hot. I spurn the fancy coffee shops who refuse to produce anything but lukewarm liquids lest they burn the sacred beans, instead seeking out establishments run by Italians and Romanians who understand that there is no other way to drink coffee other than immediately off the hob. In anticipation of Britons across the country suddenly panicking at the kettle, Cancer Research UK put out advice to those “worried” to simply wait “until it’s comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it’s still very hot”. Thank God for experts, eh?
As with all health-scare headlines, the devil is in the detail of this study. Your hot morning beverage is not going to give you cancer – researchers “stress the overall chances of developing this cancer are low”. This is a good thing. Oesophageal cancer is horrendous – my uncle Patrick died of it almost 20 years ago. He liked a hot cup of tea, but he was also a heavy smoker which likely contributed to his illness rather more than his choice of drink. Had Pat known how his life was going to end, would he have changed his habits back then? Perhaps – after all, this is the aim of such panicky research, to scare us into lifestyle change based around “what ifs” about our health.
The thing about cancer is that many of us know someone for whom the diagnosis “made sense” in the context of their lifestyle choices, and others who lived without vice but suffered just the same. Which is the better life – one where all precautions are taken in the name of preventing a rainy day, or one which lives each day for its own sake? The sweet spot is probably somewhere between the two, but we seem to be edging towards a society that wants to live and die by the precautionary principle. This news about hot drinks causing cancer – despite the fact that researchers admit that’s not exactly true – has been discussed on almost every radio, television and news channel this week. We love a scare story, particularly when it comes to the C word.
Around the time that my uncle was dying, Bryan Appleyard published his book How to Live Forever or Die Trying. In it, he detailed a new burgeoning “life-extension” movement, full of people working to stay slightly underweight, experimenting with cryogenic therapy and generally living what sounded like miserable lives. Towards the end, he observes attendees clock-watching at a conference, timing their meals alongside a smorgasbord of pills to aid their plans to live longer. I wonder what Appleyard makes of Bryan Johnson, the vampiric prince of life extension, who looks about as healthy as a teenager after a weekend on Babycham. Johnson might be our modern extreme, but his sacrificial ethos is echoed in much of our approach to health, which tells us to abstain, abstain, abstain.
No one wants to die young – the idea of doing it old and infirm isn’t particularly appealing, either. With research and scientific innovation we now know more about the things that are good for us and the things that aren’t. The question is, what should we do with that information? NHS guidelines seek to create a society which lives without regret, because we’ve eaten the five a day, stubbed out the fags, ordered the 0 per cent beer and left the tea on the counter to cool. Does that sound like a good life to you?
The thing about regret is that it infers you made a choice. What sets us apart as human beings is our ability to do this, to make choices – sometimes bad ones that end in cancer and regret, others that have happier endings. I will not be making myself miserable with cups of tepid tea in the hopes of warding off cancer because I want to choose enjoyment. I start each morning with a nuclear brew – not least because it gives me five minutes untouched on the sofa before my kids start clambering all over me. Whoever said health is wealth never knew the peace that comes with a hot cuppa.
summary: New research from the University of Oxford suggests that drinking six or more hot drinks a day, or any beverage above 65 degrees Celsius, may increase the risk of oesophageal cancer. However, experts stress that the overall chance of developing this cancer remains low and advise simply waiting until drinks are at a comfortable temperature. The author questions the societal shift toward extreme health precautions and lifestyle abstention, choosing instead to continue enjoying piping hot tea.
key_points: Oxford University research indicates that consuming hot drinks above 65 degrees Celsius or having six or more hot drinks daily could increase oesophageal cancer risk.
Cancer Research UK advises people to wait until hot drinks reach a comfortable temperature rather than panicking.
Researchers emphasize that the overall individual chance of developing oesophageal cancer from hot drinks is low.
The article critiques a broader societal trend toward strict precautionary health measures and constant lifestyle abstention.

title: Yeovil Hospital's Hyperacute Stroke Unit closes
author: Dan Ayers; Matt Faulkner
content:
![Six storey building of Yeovil District Hospital. It's the entrance of the hospital building with a big sign on the front.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/8f3f/live/0560ba50-ab73-11f1-9712-a14d469bace4.jpg)
The unit for the most serious stroke cases at Yeovil District Hospital is closing
- Published
Stroke patients requiring urgent care in part of the West Country will be taken to hospitals 20 to 30 miles away from Wednesday, an NHS care board has confirmed.
Yeovil Hospital's emergency hyper-acute stroke unit is closing despite a campaign to keep it open - and patients will be taken to Taunton or Dorchester instead.
Campaigners had argued there was "no logic" in the closure, which they said left patients at risk. Yeovil Hospital will retain its acute stroke provision on site.
Dr Bernie Marden, chief medical officer representing NHS Somerset and NHS Dorset integrated care boards, said they were "committed" to finding the best solution for all stroke patients in Somerset and Dorset.
He said: "We all know that getting timely treatment, and importantly in the right place, is in the best interest of a stroke patient and this system helps us to make that judgement much quicker."
John Falconer, who represents patients in Yeovil and across south Somerset, said: "If you live in and around Yeovil, you will initially be taken to Taunton or Dorchester for immediate treatment - that's not good enough.
"Stroke is a time-critical issue and you need medication as quickly as you can. Because of the delays, patients will be harmed. Clinical outcome will not be as good as it would have been."
More from Somerset
Stroke services are categorised by the NHS as either hyper-acute, where emergency treatment is required within the first 72 hours, or acute, where the stroke is less life-threatening.
A hyper-acute stroke unit treats patients in the first 72 hours following a stroke and provides brain scans and drugs to treat blood clots.
Patients will now been seen at Taunton's Musgrove Park Hospital or Dorset County Hospital in Dorchester.
A new Pre-Hospital Video Triage system is also being introduced across Somerset and Dorset, in which ambulance clinicians will be able to consult stroke specialists via video link while assessing patients.
NHS bosses said the new service would be monitored closely following implementation and would include a range of patient safety measures.
The NHS advice for anyone experiencing a stroke is to call 999 as it is an emergency.
summary: Yeovil Hospital's hyper-acute stroke unit is closing, with urgent stroke patients now being redirected to hospitals in Taunton or Dorchester 20 to 30 miles away. While campaigners and patient representatives expressed concern that the longer travel times could harm patients, NHS officials defended the move as a way to ensure timely treatment in the right place. The hospital will continue to provide acute stroke care on-site, alongside the introduction of a new pre-hospital video triage system for ambulances.
key_points: Yeovil Hospital's emergency hyper-acute stroke unit is closing.
Urgent stroke patients will now be taken to Taunton or Dorchester for immediate treatment.
Campaigners argued the closure puts patients at risk due to longer travel times.
Yeovil Hospital will retain its acute stroke provision on site.
A new Pre-Hospital Video Triage system is being introduced across Somerset and Dorset.

title: 'My cancer spread while I waited 128 days for an op': The cost of England's care gap
author: Chloe Hayward; Hugh Pym
content:
![An older man wearing a black polo shirt, sits at a restaurant table with views of the countryside. He is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/4465/live/866c8070-ac68-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Alan is one of thousands each month who are not being treated within the cancer target timeframe
- Published
Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.
The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex.
"I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.
On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.
Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.
Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2027.
But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.
Now, 69.9% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.
Prof Pat Price, a leading UK clinical academic oncologist, says the government targets "are now simply impossible to hit", after what she describes as a "complete loss of momentum".
Price attributes the current failures to a "complete lack of a plan or accountability".
The plan stated that a new independent cancer board would be established, but it is still not known who will be leading this group.
'Thousands will die unnecessarily'
Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 3,000 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target.
That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type.
Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time".
For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%.
By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist.
He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan.
Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal.
One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets.
Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity.
Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country.
Joined-up care
Diane had a cancerous lump removed from her face at Salisbury District Hospital a few weeks ago, using an innovative procedure, which checks tumour margins are clear while the patient is still in surgery.
That means no follow-up operations, and it allows for complex reconstruction that leaves hardly a trace.
"It's amazing, you literally can't see I had a large cancerous lesion removed from my cheek," she tells the BBC in the waiting room.
Consultant plastic surgeon Neil Wickham checked her face, confirmed a biopsied lump on her arm was benign, and referred her to ENT for a separate lump in her neck.
It is the kind of joined-up care the government's Cancer Plan was meant to trigger in cancer units across England.
![A screengrab of an older woman with shoulder-length wavy hair, wearing a blue striped top and sitting in a hospital corridor.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/60c2/live/62bf3370-ac68-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Diane benefited from an innovative procedure when she had a cancerous lump removed from her face
But over in pathology at the Salisbury trust, head of department Lee Phillips is feeling the pressure. His histology lab receives cancer service biopsies from across the hospital for diagnosis.
"The sheer volume of specimens we have coming in is our problem," he says.
"We need more staff and more kit if we're going to keep up with demand," Phillips says.
Radiotherapy is another bottleneck crying out for staff and kit. Like many trusts, Salisbury has no machine on site, so patients needing daily sessions over one to three weeks must travel up to an hour to Southampton, and sometimes Bath.
Workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks
But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin.
Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers.
"We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can."
Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, University Hospitals Dorset, Milton Keynes University Hospital, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part.
Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement.
"If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan for England, it must match ambition with urgency," said Steve Haines of Macmillan Cancer Support.
He said that "visible progress" was needed on a promise to set up a National Cancer Board to oversee progress on improving waiting times and treatment.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson says the National Cancer Plan "will help more people get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner".
They concedes that "there is more to do, but we are determined to return cancer performance to the standards people rightly expect".
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/f272/live/ef23eeb0-acdf-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.png)
![A thin, grey banner promoting the News Daily newsletter. On the right, there is a graphic of an orange sphere with two concentric crescent shapes around it in a red-orange gradient, like a sound wave. The banner reads: "The latest news in your inbox first thing.â](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/aec3/live/1322d680-5a80-11f1-b682-cf91850925ea.png)
summary: Alan, a 70-year-old lung cancer patient in England, experienced a 128-day wait for his operation after scans were cancelled due to broken machines, allowing his cancer to spread. Across England, cancer treatment performance targets are being missed, with only 69.9% of patients starting treatment within the 62-day timeframe compared to 71.9% previously. Experts warn that a lack of momentum, workforce shortages, and diagnostic bottlenecks are making government targets impossible to hit without urgent intervention.
key_points: Alan waited 128 days for his lung cancer surgery, causing the cancer to spread to his lymph nodes.
Current performance data shows 69.9% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62-day timeframe, down from 71.9%.
For every month a cancer patient waits before treatment, their chance of survival drops by approximately 10%.
Radiotherapy UK analysis indicates that over 3,000 extra patients need to start treatment monthly to meet the government's 2027 targets.
Hospitals face ongoing challenges including workforce shortages, diagnostic bottlenecks, broken equipment, and missed appointments.

title: Got a migraine, acne or ear infection? Go to your chemist first
author: Philippa Roxby
content:
![Young woman holds her head as if she has a bad headache while standing in a pharmacy in front of a pharmacist wearing a white coat](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/ba4b/live/066b5630-ac68-11f1-80f0-9795d1a5edbc.jpg)
- Published
People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first.
Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions - sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections.
Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list.
NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently.
After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen.
"For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said.
Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time".
The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are:
- low frequency migraines in adults
- hay fever or allergic rhinitis in children
- ear infections in adults
- mild to moderate acne in young people and adults
- mild skin infections and scabies
That's in addition to these seven:
- sore throat
- sinusitis
- earache
- insect bites
- impetigo
- shingles
- uncomplicated UTIs
Initially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says.
There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England.
Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations.
The charity the Migraine Trust said it was delighted by the news after calling for more help for migraine care in pharmacies.
Chief executive Rob Music said having this support for people with migraine through their local pharmacy was "a wonderful opportunity for a faster and improved care pathway".
Dr Amanda Doyle, director for primary care and community services at NHS England, said she wanted to make sure that patients can get as much support as possible in their communities, "so they do not have to be admitted to hospital unnecessarily".
But bodies representing pharmacies across England have consistently said that the funding provided by the goverment does not cover the workload for the new plans.
"Pharmacies are still under significant financial pressures," said Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association.
"This shows why the government should go much further and invest in our pharmacy network that has the power to transform people's experience of everyday health issues."
The Pharmacy First scheme started in England in 2024. NHS figures suggest it has delivered 14 million consultations since then, including two million appointments for sore throats and 1.7 million for urinary tract infections (UTIs).
People can be referred to their local pharmacy via NHS111 or by their GP, or just go direct to their high street chemist.
Scotland has a scheme which was seen as the model for England's Pharmacy First - Northern Ireland and Wales also have systems allowing pharmacies to treat patients with certain conditions.
Patients can be treated for 27 different conditions at chemists in Scotland.

Five new conditions—migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections, and badly blocked noses—have been added to the existing list of seven.
