If your porn use feels out of control, however, ideally I’d recommend seeking professional support from an expert sexual-psychotherapist like Silva Neves.
‘You can listen to audio spice during your commute home (on headphones, please!)‘ Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty Images
How can I help my daughters find healthy relationships?
AmongstTheWaves asks: Are my daughters entering a time where love, sensuality and respect are hard to find in the sexual landscape and do you have any advice for parents?
Alix: Lovely human, I really can understand your concern. In a time of Trump and Andrew Tate; non-consensual intimate image abuse and nudification apps; misogyny, manospheres and red pills, it’s easy to be on red alert about your daughters’ safety and feel heartachingly bleak about their romantic futures.
I’d urge you, though, to try not to accidentally infuse your children with a sense of hopelessness about human connection. Instead, teach them that they are absolutely worthy of love, sensuality and respect, and that they shouldn’t settle for less. Model healthy relationships as much as you can at home. Talk to them about consent, and how to set and preserve personal boundaries. When it’s time to discuss safer sex, chat about emotional safety as well as physical safety: what actions and behaviours would make them feel secure, valued, adored, and joyful?
People with sons: please, do the same.
My favourite resources to help guide constructive, compassionate conversations with young people about sex and relationships include the glorious Sex Positive Families, BISH, Brook and Outspoken Sex Ed.
Instilling a sense of sensible caution is vital, but let’s not send our children out into the world feeling jaded about love before they’ve even reached adulthood. There are wonders, still. Such wonders! The more of us who try to raise smart, savvy, self-possessed and self-respecting youngsters who know they can come to us with questions, the more the chances of wonderful love remain high.
Mother and daughter talking, sharing bonding moment outdoors Photograph: VIJ/Getty Images
A good sex life is key to a good life. Want to know how to improve yours, whether that’s practical advice on how to broach the subject of trying something new (and what to do if your partner reacts poorly); how to become more confident at talking dirty or giving constructive in-the-sack feedback; or even how to be intimate with your partner when you’re just plain knackered?
No question is too niche or too embarrassing, too mild or too wild – from how to give great massages and tried-and-tested toys to spend your money on; to how to keep sex comfortable and fun after medical challenges and life changes.
The Filter’s sexual culture and wellbeing expert, Alix Fox answered your questions.
summary: Sex expert Alix Fox answers reader questions about intimacy, covering topics such as food-based play, overcoming communication hurdles in new relationships, and dealing with unpredictable pain during sex. She also offers advice for maintaining intimacy when feeling exhausted from parenting and work, explains why modern sex toys often resemble fruits, and addresses how antidepressant use can impact libido.
key_points: Filling out 'Yes/No/Maybe' checklists together can help new couples communicate their sexual desires and boundaries clearly.
Unexplained and unpredictable pain during sex for seven years should be taken seriously, and consulting a fresh gynaecologist or organizations like The Eve Appeal is recommended.
Scheduling intimacy and creating an erotic 'menu' or practicing 'choreplay' can help busy parents maintain a connected sex life.
The recent trend of fruit-shaped sex toys is largely driven by social media censorship rules that ban realistic depictions of genitalia.
Antidepressants and SSRIs can reduce sex drive and make climax harder to reach, but patients should consult a GP before changing any medication regimens.

title: Eating a handful of nuts each day is linked with lower risk of high blood pressure, our research shows
author: Dagfinn Aune; Shireen Kassam
content:
More than 1.4 billion people worldwide live with high blood pressure (hypertension). It’s the single biggest metabolic risk factor for early death – driving diseases such as heart attacks, strokes, kidney failure and dementia.
Most of these cases of high blood pressure are shaped by how we live and what we eat. This means that making changes to your diet can have a big impact on your risk of developing high blood pressure.
Even small changes can help, as our latest research shows. We found that adding just one serving of nuts into your daily diet is linked with lower hypertension risk.
It’s well known that eating more plant foods is associated with a lower risk of hypertension – but research on the impact of nuts has been limited to date.
Fruits and vegetables are associated with a lower risk of hypertension, with consumption of 800g (ten portions) per day reducing the risk by 11%.
Whole grains – brown rice, oats, wholemeal bread – are similarly linked to lower risk of hypertension. Our research found that the people who consumed the highest amount of whole grains each day had a roughly 26% lower risk compared to people consuming the least.
We have also shown that legumes and soya are associated with a 16% and 19% lower risk of hypertension respectively.
Our latest analysis published in the British Journal of Nutrition, now shows the clear impact eating nuts can have on hypertension risk.
Our study pooled data from 143,000 people – including 20,665 people who had hypertension. We found that eating around a handful of nuts daily (between 30-35g) was linked with a 26% lower risk of hypertension compared to not eating any nuts.
Why plant foods work
Plant foods share a few key characteristics, which may explain why they’re beneficial for the heart.
They are an excellent source of potassium, which helps to lower blood pressure by shedding sodium and relaxing blood vessels.
Plant foods also provide fibre that feeds gut bacteria so they can produce short-chain fatty acids – compounds that are linked to lower blood pressure.
Many plant foods also contain L-arginine and nitrates, which the body converts into nitric oxide in order to widen blood vessels. Plant foods are rich in polyphenols, which have also been associated with lower blood pressure.
Despite nuts being energy-dense, they’re linked to lower obesity rates – thus helping to mitigate another risk factor for hypertension.
These overlapping mechanisms all nudge blood pressure down, and help explain the link between plant-rich diets and lower risk of cardiovascular diseases.
![A person eats a healthy salad made with spinach, nuts, slices of orange and cheese.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/758198/original/file-20260907-60-33fuuq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
But as tempting as it might be to call nuts a heart health “superfood,” their real power lies within a broader pattern of healthy eating. While reductions in hypertension risk are observed with intake of even just one daily serving of nuts, a diet built around several whole plant foods may provide even further benefits.
This is exactly what Dash, Mediterranean and plant-based diets prove. They all work because they put these different plant-based foods on the same plate.
However, it’s worth noting that the studies included in our analysis are observational. This means they show that people who eat more nuts tend to have lower blood pressure, but they cannot fully prove that nuts are the cause.
People who consume more plant foods in their diet also tend to follow other healthy lifestyle habits such as regular physical activity. Although our analysis adjusted for many of these factors, we cannot fully rule their impact out.
But the randomised controlled Dash diet trials, where diet is actually changed to include more vegetables, whole grains and lean protein, are what give us confidence the link is real. Similarly, intervention trials, which compared the effects of multiple different plant-based diets, also show benefits for blood pressure reduction.
There are knowledge gaps to note, too. The nut studies we included in our review did not separate salted from unsalted. Since salt raises blood pressure, the true benefit of unsalted nuts may even be larger than reported.
Most of the data also came from Europe, the Americas and East Asia. Little evidence came from Africa and India. More large studies conducted in a variety of regions will help sharpen the evidence base.
The takeaway is practical and affordable. You don’t need supplements or fads. Fill half your plate with fruit and veg, choose whole grains, build meals around beans and tofu and add a handful of unsalted nuts. These are small habits that add up to a significant reduction in one of our biggest health risks.
summary: Recent research published in the British Journal of Nutrition indicates that eating around a handful of nuts daily is linked with a 26% lower risk of high blood pressure. The study pooled data from 143,000 people and adds to existing evidence that plant-rich diets help reduce cardiovascular disease risks. However, the study is observational, meaning it shows a correlation rather than a direct causal relationship.
key_points: Eating about 30-35g (a handful) of nuts daily is linked with a 26% lower risk of hypertension compared to eating no nuts.
Plant foods help lower blood pressure through components like potassium, fibre, L-arginine, nitrates, and polyphenols.
Other plant-based foods like whole grains, fruits, vegetables, legumes, and soya are also associated with a reduced risk of high blood pressure.
The analysis was observational, meaning it shows an association between nut consumption and lower blood pressure rather than definitive proof of causation.
The reviewed nut studies did not differentiate between salted and unsalted nuts, suggesting the true benefit of unsalted nuts could be even greater.

title: Drinking very hot drinks could triple risk of oesophageal cancer, study finds
author: Denis Campbell
content:
Drinking very hot tea and coffee triples the risk of developing cancer of the gullet, the world’s largest study of the link between them has found.
The findings show that people should let very hot cups of tea and coffee cool down until they are comfortable to drink, in order to reduce their risk of the disease, cancer experts said.
The temperature of the drink and the number of very hot drinks someone consumes increase the chances of getting oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the research found. However, hot drinks do not heighten the risk of getting adenocarcinoma (AC), the other form of oesophageal cancer.
“Consumption of drinks at a ‘very hot’ versus ‘warm’ temperature was associated with a threefold greater SCC risk but not with AC risk, after adjustment for consumption frequency”, according to the study, which was published on Wednesday in the International Journal of Cancer.
“After controlling for drink temperature, daily consumption of six or more versus fewer than six hot drinks was associated with a 71% increase in SCC risk, with little association with AC risk”, said researchers. The study was led by Dr Keren Papier, a senior nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford’s population health department.
The findings are based on analysis of the consumption of hot drinks by almost 980,000 people in the UK – the largest number of people globally in any related studies to date. It followed participants over 14 years to give a long-term picture of their habits and health.
They were asked how they preferred to consume hot drinks. Available answers included “very hot”, “hot”, “warm” and “do not drink hot drinks”. The conclusions were based on people’s estimation of how hot the drinks were that they had consumed rather than their exact temperatures.
The study produced conclusions for a western European population that mirrored similar findings already seen in studies conducted in Asia, Africa, South America and the Middle East, which found that drinking tea or mate – a caffeinated herbal drink popular in South America – at or above 70C increased the risk of oesophageal cancer.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, said in 2016 that hot drinks were “probably carcinogenic to humans” and “one probable cause of oesophageal cancer”. They are thought to heighten the risk of the disease by causing heat damage to the cells which line the oesophagus, which is also known as the body’s foodpipe. Alcohol and smoking are other major risk factors for that type of cancer.
Health authorities could use these latest findings to encourage the public to consume cooler drinks and fewer very hot drinks to help ensure that fewer people are diagnosed with that form of oesophageal cancer, the study team said.
For example, one in seven cases of SCC in the UK “could be avoided if individuals who reported consuming their drinks at a ‘very hot’ temperature instead consumed them at a temperature more representative of the temperature range described as ‘hot’.
The researchers said: “The fact that we observed a clear trend in risk across self-reported temperature categories suggests that further limiting the temperature at which individuals consume their drinks to something well below average for this population may well avoid an even greater proportion of SCC cases.
“This large UK study of middle-aged adults, amongst whom hot drinks are widely consumed, provides clear evidence that temperature and frequency of hot drink consumption represent useful targets for SCC prevention.”
Fiona Osgun, the head of health information at Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, said: “It’s difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool. But if you’re worried, we’d suggest just waiting until it’s comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it’s still very hot.”
However, the charity does not believe that cafes, coffee shops and restaurants should start serving tea and coffee at a lower temperature in order to reduce the risk of SCC.
Muy-Teck Teh, a professor of molecular oral oncology at Queen Mary University of London, said the research’s reliance on self-reported temperatures may have affected the findings.
“A key limitation, however, is that perceived drink temperature is inherently subjective, and it remains unclear whether individuals who tolerate or prefer very hot drinks have altered thermosensation or mucosal sensitivity that might itself reflect underlying biological predisposition to squamous cell carcinoma and lead them to prefer hotter drinks.
“This possibility cannot be excluded and complicates interpretation of causality”, he added.
summary: A large study involving nearly 980,000 people in the UK has found that drinking very hot tea and coffee triples the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Researchers recommend letting hot drinks cool until they are comfortable to consume in order to lower this cancer risk. However, the study noted limitations, including its reliance on subjective, self-reported drink temperatures.
key_points: Consuming very hot drinks triples the risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) but does not heighten the risk of adenocarcinoma.
Drinking six or more hot drinks daily is associated with a 71% increase in SCC risk after controlling for temperature.
The study analyzed data from nearly 980,000 UK participants followed over a 14-year period.
Experts suggest letting hot beverages cool until they are comfortable to drink to reduce potential heat damage to cells lining the oesophagus.
Study limitations include reliance on participants' subjective estimations of drink temperatures rather than exact measurements.

title: British baby given world-first treatment for rare skull condition
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![The new treatment involved an operation using 'super-elastic' springs](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501509861_17888216062200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqslDFZT2LKSpHAwzROxpaz0Wy_sGK6oioMu5BzggyGUY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![The new treatment involved an operation using 'super-elastic' springs](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501509861_17888216062200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqslDFZT2LKSpHAwzROxpaz0Wy_sGK6oioMu5BzggyGUY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A baby boy from Derbyshire has become the first in the world to receive a new type of treatment for a rare skull condition.
Rory Potter, one, was diagnosed with severe sagittal craniosynostosis shortly after he was born – a condition where the skull fuses before birth, which causes it to be long from front to back but narrow from side to side.
Treatment usually involves skull reshaping surgery, which takes place within the first months of life. In the past two decades, this has involved the use of stainless steel springs to widen the gap gradually, giving space for the brain to develop and for new bone to grow.
But now experts have developed new “super-elastic” springs using a special metal called nitinol, a nickel and titanium alloy, with Rory the first patient to have them fitted.
![Rory's parents raised concerns about his head being longer than expected after he was born in April 2025](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501509856_17888216540450_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqzccoJS-E8Wb-wOXrdJto2_lZBRoezaD186OgGOZAjuQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Each spring is custom-designed for the patient and their “super-elastic properties” allow them to adapt more naturally to a child’s growing skull, experts at Great Ormond Street Hospital (Gosh) said.
The springs were developed by experts at Gosh and University College London (UCL).
Using CT scans, the team creates a detailed digital model of each child’s skull to predict how they will respond to surgery. They then design bespoke springs to deliver the right level of force.
Once inserted, the springs will remain in place for several weeks to months, gradually reshaping the skull before being removed.
The new technology means children can avoid longer and more invasive operations and should see a reduction in blood transfusion rates, experts said.
Rory was born in April 2025. His parents, Harry and Jo Potter, from Chesterfield, Derbyshire, raised concerns about Rory’s head being longer than expected.
![Rory received the breakthrough treatment, involving bespoke springs, a few months later](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501509863_17888216707790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNLD3bY7VPsburK0YKqsfIswZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
With sagittal craniosynostosis suspected, Rory was referred to Gosh, where his diagnosis was confirmed. Because his case was severe, medics thought he may benefit from the new nitinol springs instead of the traditional steel springs.
Rory had the 45-minute operation to fit the springs in September and only needed to stay in hospital for one night before returning to Derbyshire to his brother Oscar, three, and the family dog Ada.
Nine weeks later they were removed after his skull reached the desired outcome.
![Rory stayed in hospital for one night, before returning home to Derbyshire to his brother Oscar (pictured)](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501509839_17888219354730_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_Ubenh49j2r2x5KHc9lBttf11FLKtqwYaxK652uKeQE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
His mother Jo, a 36-year-old project manager, said: “Rory is so happy, cheeky and full of energy. You wouldn’t know what he’s been through, he’s just like every little boy and hitting milestones and he will have a great story to tell when he’s older.
“We cannot thank the team enough for the care, compassion and reassurance. Not to mention their dedication to medical science to support and help children thrive.
“Throughout the process, every element was explained so well. We knew what was going to happen and how, we received amazing support from each member of the team.”
![Rory pictured with his father, Harry Potter](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501509842_17888220246760_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqMQ1nOlcuLOwxlDSJLorrMvlZBRoezaD186OgGOZAjuQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Prof Owase Jeelani, a consultant neurosurgeon at Gosh who was part of the team who developed the new springs and led the surgery, said: “Traditional stainless-steel springs are very robust, but they don’t always allow us to fine-tune the force on the skull.
“These new nitinol springs give us much greater flexibility and, in some cases, can prevent the need for further surgery.
“This first surgery is important progress for children with craniosynostosis and so far, we have seen fantastic outcomes.”
![Prof Owase Jeelani said the new 'super-elastic' springs used a special metal called nitinol](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501515480_17888219032110_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqKECXunzJ7sDAQ1sRVMGhWyeHgjik9tvFFp6ltodstQA.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Prof Silvia Schievano, who led the team of biomedical engineers at UCL, said: “This has been many years in the making, with thousands of hours of necessary research undertaken.
“It is a very proud moment to see this technology used in a child with such a positive result. It uplifts the importance of engineering research and clinical care coming together to develop new technologies for improved healthcare.”
![The team behind the research and development of the springs described Rory's success with the treatment as a 'proud moment'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501498206_17888219778410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqc3IxSbjMmXltPISQXxZkAPlZBRoezaD186OgGOZAjuQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Dr Alessandro Borghi, who helped develop the springs and is now at Durham University, added: “It is extremely rewarding to see our research efforts translate into a tangible improvement in the life of a baby.
“This achievement demonstrates the real-world impact that can be achieved through close collaboration between engineering and clinical research.
“We hope this success serves to highlight the importance of investing in and promoting medical technology, showcasing its potential to drive meaningful innovations that improve patient care and clinical outcomes.”
The research work behind the operation was funded by Great Ormond Street Hospital Charity and the National Institute for Health and Care Research Gosh Biomedical Research Centre.
Aoife Regan, from the Gosh Charity, said: “We are so proud to have provided over £1 million of funding for this work via the Face Value project, which aims to improve treatment for children with complex forms of craniosynostosis.
“Gosh Charity is the largest charitable funder of medical research dedicated to paediatrics in the UK and, as part of our commitment to give seriously ill children the best chance, and best childhood possible, we are currently implementing our £70 million research strategy to transform the lives of children through research-led care.”
Prof Marian Knight, scientific director for NIHR Infrastructure, said: “By funding innovative research into treatments such as these ‘memory-metal’ springs, the NIHR enables researchers to help children like Rory receive safer, more precise, and highly personalised care.”
summary: A one-year-old boy from Derbyshire named Rory Potter has become the first patient in the world to be treated for a rare skull condition using new 'super-elastic' springs made of nitinol. Developed by experts at Great Ormond Street Hospital (Gosh) and University College London (UCL), the custom-designed springs adapt naturally to a child's growing skull. Rory underwent a 45-minute operation in September, and the springs were successfully removed nine weeks later after achieving the desired outcome.
key_points: Rory Potter was diagnosed with severe sagittal craniosynostosis, a condition where the skull fuses prematurely before birth.
He is the first patient globally to receive treatment using new custom-designed 'super-elastic' springs made from nitinol, a nickel and titanium alloy.
The new technology, developed by Gosh and UCL, allows for more precise force and helps children avoid longer, more invasive operations.
Rory's surgery took 45 minutes, required a one-night hospital stay, and his custom springs were successfully removed after nine weeks.

title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk
author: Michelle Roberts
content:
![A woman reaches her hand out to pick up a steaming hot mug which is shiny and green-coloured](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/779f/live/b37430c0-aaa8-11f1-9eba-7de947fa7cd1.jpg)
- Published
Regularly drinking beverages like tea and coffee at very hot temperatures increases the risk of cancer of the food pipe or gullet, known as oesophageal cancer, UK research suggests.
Researchers say the findings, external, from a study of nearly a million people, make this the largest to date to establish the link.
In the study, people who had their drinks "very hot" had around a three times higher risk of the cancer than "warm" tea or coffee drinkers - although experts stress the overall chances of developing this cancer are low.
Steaming hot liquid can damage the cell lining of the food pipe on the way down to the stomach.
Scalding hot brews
The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk.
Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women.
Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say.
Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F). Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C.
The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature.
Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool.
"But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said.
Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer.
But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk."
A separate study, external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above.
According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C.
Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee.
Small overall risk
The researchers suggest that around one or two in every 10 oesophageal cancers could be avoided if people stopped drinking very hot beverages.
Squamous cell oesophageal cancer is rare, affecting a few thousand people a year. In the UK, around a 1% of the popularion has a lifetime risk of being diagnosed with this type of cancer.
So even if scalding hot drinks might increase someone's risk, the chances of them developing the cancer are still low.
And there are other factors, such as smoking, which are a bigger risk for oesophageal cancer.
Fiona Osgun from Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, stressed: "The most important ways to reduce the risk of this cancer type are not smoking and cutting down on alcohol."
Symptoms of oesophageal cancer can include heartburn, indigestion or a pain in your throat or chest, along with weight loss.
summary: UK research from Oxford University involving nearly a million people suggests that regularly consuming very hot beverages, such as tea and coffee at 65 degrees Celsius or above, increases the risk of oesophageal cancer. Steaming hot liquids can damage the cell lining of the food pipe, and consuming six or more hot drinks per day further raises the risk. However, experts emphasize that the overall chances of developing this rare cancer remain low, and factors like smoking and alcohol pose greater risks.
key_points: Drinking beverages at 65 degrees Celsius or above increases the risk of oesophageal cancer by around three times compared to warm drink consumers.
The study by Oxford University analyzed data from nearly one million middle-aged men and women.
Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk of food pipe cancer.
Experts recommend waiting a few minutes for hot drinks to cool to a safer temperature before consuming them.
Smoking and alcohol remain much bigger risk factors for developing oesophageal cancer.

title: Husband of Crawley woman who died at 32 in cancer drug plea
author: Matt Graveling; Tanya Gupta
content:
![Fionnuala Quinlan-Bennett is seen in a hospital treatment area. She is sitting upright in a hospital bed. A cooling cap is fitted to her head and tubing is attached to medical equipment. A large mug, books and personal belongings are visible nearby. Medical monitoring equipment and hospital furnishings can be seen in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/f17a/live/0ad27cc0-abab-11f1-8e72-a346833ed029.jpg)
Fionnuala Quinlan-Bennett died in June after cancer spread to her bones and liver
- Published
The family of a woman who died from breast cancer aged 32 are calling for a life-extending treatment to be made available on the NHS in England.
Fionnuala Quinlan-Bennett, from Crawley in West Sussex, died in June after being told the disease had spread to her bones and liver.
Her family say a drug called Enhertu, available in Scotland and several other countries, could have given her more time.
Cancer charity Breast Cancer Now said making Enhertu available could help about 1,000 women in England. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) said discussions had resumed with the manufacturer and NHS England.
![An outdoor wedding portrait showing Fionnuala Quinlan-Bennett and Nathan Bennett standing side by side in front of a softly blurred background of trees and greenery. She is holding a bouquet of pale blue, white and pink flowers and wearing a light-coloured wedding outfit with a veil. He is wearing a blue checked suit jacket, patterned tie and white rose buttonhole. Sunlight filters through the trees behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/9296/live/15935350-abab-11f1-8e72-a346833ed029.jpg)
Fionnuala's husband, Nathan, said his wife found it difficult knowing there was a treatment out there she could not have
Enhertu is a combination of a targeted therapy drug called a monoclonal antibody and a chemotherapy drug called deruxtecan, according to Macmillan cancer support.
Fionnuala's husband, Nathan Bennett, said it had been difficult for his wife to know a treatment existed which she could not access.
"Her exact words were, 'It's painful knowing that this drug is available and out there, but not available to me'," he said.
Before her death, Fionnuala had asked family and friends to honour her memory by embracing life.
She said there were still children to teach, countries to explore and books to read.
"If you want to honour my memory, go out into the world with a smile on your face and make a difference," she said.
![A close-up selfie shows two people and a beagle outdoors. The dog occupies much of the foreground with its face close to the camera. Fionnuala is wearing glasses and is on the right of the image, while Nathan appears behind the dog. Green woodland vegetation fills the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/936c/live/232ac980-abab-11f1-8e72-a346833ed029.jpg)
Fionnuala wanted her family and friends to honour her memory by embracing life
Holly Heath, head of policy and evidence at Breast Cancer Now, said: "There is still an opportunity for this drug to become available on the NHS so no-one else misses out on the chance to extend their lives.
"This group of women don't have time to wait. We need a sense of urgency, we need pace and we need a deal to be done now."
A NICE spokesperson said: "In 2024, we concluded that, at the price offered by the company, the treatment was not cost effective, as the cost was too high relative to the benefits it would provide to patients.
"However, following the US-UK trade deal announced in December 2025, NICE is now applying a new, higher threshold for cost-effectiveness decisions.
"In light of these changed circumstances, discussions between NICE, the company, and NHS England have resumed, with the aim of reaching a commercial agreement that would make Enhertu available."
![A close-up indoor photograph shows Nathan and Fionnuala seated together at a table. Nathan is leaning towards Fionnuala and kissing her on her cheek. Fionnuala is wearing a sleeveless pink floral top and has long hair. Wooden furniture and decorative wall hangings are visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/cb6b/live/30a39420-abab-11f1-8e72-a346833ed029.jpg)
Fionnuala's family do not want other women to miss out on the treatment
Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: The family of Fionnuala Quinlan-Bennett, a 32-year-old from Crawley who died of breast cancer in June, is campaigning for the life-extending drug Enhertu to be made available on the NHS in England. Enhertu is currently accessible in Scotland and other countries but was previously deemed not cost-effective by NICE. Following recent changes, discussions between NICE, the manufacturer, and NHS England have resumed to reach a commercial agreement.
key_points: Fionnuala Quinlan-Bennett died at age 32 after breast cancer spread to her bones and liver.
Her family and charity Breast Cancer Now are calling for the life-extending drug Enhertu to be provided on the NHS in England.
Enhertu is already available in Scotland and several other countries.
NICE previously rejected the drug for being not cost-effective, but discussions have resumed following changed circumstances.

title: More teenagers getting flu vaccination is 'vital'
author: Julia Gregory
content:
![A close-up of someone's arm as they get a flu vaccination injection.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/0db3/live/b5867bd0-aba1-11f1-8e72-a346833ed029.jpg)
Health bosses say a "concerted effort" is needed to get more teenagers vaccinated
- Published
More than 96,000 children aged four to 16 across Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly did not get flu vaccines last winter, with more older children missing out, according to government figures.
Just over half of children aged four to 16 in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly had a flu vaccine last winter, with 53.1% of children vaccinated in Torbay, 56% in Plymouth and 60.4% in Devon, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.
Dr Fiona Neely, UKHSA consultant in health protection, said children of primary and secondary school age were "among the biggest spreaders of the virus" and it was "concerning" fewer older pupils were vaccinated.
She added: "It's vital we turn this around."
'Concerted effort'
She said: "Young children, along with children of any age who have other illnesses such as asthma and other lung conditions, heart, liver or kidney problems, are at the highest risk of developing complications and being hospitalised with flu.
"Unvaccinated teenagers can still become seriously unwell, and they can spread flu into the wider community, to younger siblings and grandparents.
In Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, 44.5% of secondary school age children were vaccinated, with 51.1% in Torbay, 51.6% in Plymouth, and 52.8% in Devon.
Neely said it needed a "concerted effort" to boost the number of teenagers getting vaccinated.
'A hospital admission'
Dr Matthew Dominey, the immunisation lead for NHS England South West, said: "Flu can be a serious illness for children and can lead to complications which may require a hospital admission.
"The vaccine is usually given at school, so we urge parents and carers to return their consent forms promptly to ensure their child can get protected ahead of winter."
Immunisation teams would be moving from school to school in the South West up to around early December and younger children, aged two and three could have a receive a flu vaccine from their GP surgery, health bosses said.
Across the UK, the vaccine is estimated to have prevented 52% of children from having to visit their GP and 68% from being hospitalised, the UKHSA said.
Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.
summary: Health officials are urging a concerted effort to increase flu vaccination rates among teenagers in Devon, Cornwall, and the Isles of Scilly after tens of thousands missed out last winter. Experts emphasize that children are major spreaders of the virus and that unvaccinated teens risk serious illness as well as transmitting the disease to vulnerable family members. NHS and UKHSA representatives recommend that parents promptly return school consent forms to ensure children receive protection before winter.
key_points: Over 96,000 children aged four to 16 in Devon, Cornwall, and the Isles of Scilly did not receive flu vaccines last winter.
Health officials note that secondary school-aged children are among the biggest spreaders of the flu virus.
Unvaccinated teenagers are at risk of severe illness and can spread the virus to younger siblings and grandparents.
Parents and carers are urged to promptly return school consent forms so children can be vaccinated before winter.

title: Northern Ireland cancer wait times 'dangerously long', says patient
author: Niall Blaney
content:
![A man with grey hair wearing a grey 1/4 zip](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/cc9e/live/94038d20-aad6-11f1-aa35-df10e5ff32f4.jpg)
John McClean said waiting for medical outcomes meant he was "constantly on a knife-edge"
- Published
A man who has been fighting incurable cancer for seven years has said increased times between scans and results are becoming "dangerously long" for himself and other patients.
John McClean said waiting for medical outcomes meant he was "constantly on a knife-edge". A lack of radiologists in Northern Ireland meant scans had to be sent to Australia to be analysed, leading to further delay, he said.
Campaigners, survivors and experts have gathered at Stormont to call on the executive to make a commitment to reduce the cancer death rate by 15% by 2040.
The Department of Health (DoH) said while cancer waiting times are "not where we want them to be", work is "underway to improve performance".
McClean is backing the manifesto by Cancer Research UK.
The 51-year-old Antrim man was originally diagnosed with skin cancer but later developed tumours in his brain.
![A group of people standing on the steps of Stormont. They are holding up various blue and pink placards promoting cancer care.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/6a41/live/e03755d0-ab8c-11f1-aa04-efbf6a882854.jpg)
Campaigners, survivors and experts have gathered at Stormont to call on the executive to make a commitment to reduce the cancer death rate by 15% by 2040
The Longer Better Lives campaign - being launched at Stormont on Tuesday - says the move would prevent around 5,900 cancer deaths between now and 2040.
Among its key recommendations are the urgent tackling of NI's "unacceptably long cancer waiting times", targeted lung screening, extending the age range of the bowel screening programme to 50-74 year olds, and quicker access to tests and scans to detect cancer.
'I'm constantly fearful'
![A man with grey hair wearing a grey 1/4 zip and jeans. He has a black and white dog and is holding a purple lead](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9e7a/live/7cb36190-aad6-11f1-aa35-df10e5ff32f4.jpg)
McClean has been fighting incurable cancer for seven years
McClean underwent stereotactic radiosurgery, which is a precise form of radiotherapy that delivers a high dose of radiation to a targeted area within the brain.
He also received neurosurgery after three tumours were discovered in his brain. A fourth tumour was discovered in 2024, which required radiotherapy.
He said he was living well with cancer, but receiving quicker scan results would reduce his high level of stress.
"I'm constantly fearful... my anxiety levels are very high all the time and the waiting lists are a big part of that, because once I have a scan I am always more anxious until I get the results," he said.
"There have been times when I've got the results and it's like I relax, because I know that there's going to be a plan.
"I've been able to do my job, but the anxiety is actually what's holding me back at the minute and that makes my life, my working life, much more difficult."
McClean, who documents his story on YouTube, praised his medical team and said the blame for the state of cancer services in Northern Ireland "is Stormont's fault".
'Unacceptable cancer outcomes'
![Michelle Mitchell. She has blonde shoulder-length hair, wearing a green corduroy blazer, blue top and gold necklaces.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1c22/live/5b9b46b0-ab8c-11f1-aa04-efbf6a882854.jpg)
Michelle Mitchell, from Cancer Research UK, says waiting times for cancer care in Northern Ireland are "unacceptable"
Cancer Research UK is calling on Northern Ireland's political parties to prioritise cancer services in their manifestos ahead of next May's Assembly election.
It said more cancers could be prevented through implementing the Tobacco and Vapes Act, providing better support to stop smoking and increasing the uptake of HPV vaccinations to protect against cervical cancer.
The charity has also urged the NI Executive to introduce minimum unit pricing on alcohol and restrictions on less healthy food and drink promotions.
Its Chief Executive Michelle Mitchell said waiting times for cancer care in Northern Ireland are "unacceptable".
"We really can set an ambition to save 5,900 lives by 2040 and reduce cancer deaths by 15%. We believe that's possible and we think political action and support across all the parties is necessary to make that happen."
She said there was also an economic benefit to preventing deaths as a result of cancer as fewer people would be forced to leave employment and there was "a real opportunity to turn the tide on unacceptable cancer outcomes in Northern Ireland".
'Radiology outsourcing'
In a statement, the Department of Health said it was "committed to reducing waiting times across the system and embedding long term changes that deliver better outcomes for all patients".
"However, the absence of a three-year budget makes a major transformation of the healthcare system harder to deliver, and the minister has called for more certainty on the department's budget position to help plan for the future."
In relation to scans being sent to Australia to be analysed, the department said the increased reliance on "radiology outsourcing" had been driven primarily by growing demand across radiology services.
"Ongoing difficulties in recruiting radiologists have impacted reporting capacity while CT scanning has seen demand increase by 10% annually, adding further pressure to in-house capacity. Outsourcing enables services to continue to provide opportunities for patients to receive scans," it said.
summary: Cancer patient John McClean and health campaigners have criticized Northern Ireland's cancer waiting times as dangerously long, contributing to severe patient anxiety. A lack of local radiologists has forced scans to be sent to Australia for analysis, further delaying results. Campaigners are calling on the executive to commit to reducing the cancer death rate by 15% by 2040.
key_points: John McClean, a 51-year-old fighting incurable cancer, stated that waiting times for scan results are dangerously long and cause high anxiety.
A shortage of radiologists in Northern Ireland has led to scans being outsourced to Australia for analysis, causing additional delays.
Campaigners, survivors, and experts gathered at Stormont to support a Cancer Research UK manifesto aimed at reducing cancer deaths by 15% by 2040.
The Department of Health stated that waiting times are not where they want them to be, citing recruitment difficulties and a lack of a three-year budget as barriers to transformation.

title: Why I’ll never give up alcohol
author: Tim Spector
content:
![Tim Spector drinking a low-alcohol beer](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501521077_17887790218650_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqoGbZwtdBNwcvkKZqZUEDO0Wy_sGK6oioMu5BzggyGUY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Tim Spector drinking a low-alcohol beer](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501521077_17887790218650_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqoGbZwtdBNwcvkKZqZUEDO0Wy_sGK6oioMu5BzggyGUY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The worst hangover of my life was about 10 years ago in Kazakhstan. The night before I was due to give a talk at a university, I was invited to a supper which involved a never-ending supply of toasts and vodka. I initially tried to avoid top-ups, but the dean sitting next to me was drinking it with abandon and was half my size – and foolishly I tried to keep up with him.
It kicked off the most uncomfortable 24 hours of my life. When I woke up the next morning, I could barely stand. The local cure of horse milk kefir didn’t help. I was hot, nauseous and only just managed to get through the talk I was there to deliver to 1,000 students.
While I haven’t touched a spirit since, I’m still a dedicated drinker. Five days a week, I’ll usually have one or sometimes two glasses of wine or small beers. Although there are exceptions, I generally stay roughly within the 14 units of alcohol recommended by the NHS (seven pints of low-strength beer or just under seven standard 175ml glasses of wine).
For someone of my generation, this is cutting back. I drank significantly more as a student and while working as a doctor, when I would come home from work desperate for a double gin and tonic and would routinely surpass the 21 units men used to be told was acceptable.
I think my current drinking pattern is the sweet spot for my own health and don’t currently see myself ever quitting it, though never say never.
![Tim no longer drinks spirits, instead opting for wine, beer or non-alcoholic drinks](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501521076_17887790218771_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Alcohol has been unfairly demonised
It’s important to point out the dangers of alcohol: it raises the risk of liver disease, stroke and cancer.
One study showed that 4.1 per cent of new cancers globally could be accounted for by drinking. While epidemiological studies (which look at how often diseases occur in groups of people and why) are quite consistent, showing that both light and heavy drinking raise the risk of breast cancer, for example, genetic studies that remove many biases are less convincing for light drinking.
While I think the campaign has been absolutely correct on heavy drinking and binge drinking, it has become too heavy-handed on light or occasional drinking and stating there is no safe level of alcohol. I don’t think low-level drinking, under 14 units per week, should be demonised, though I’m very unpopular with some colleagues for my views.
There is too much focus on this one aspect of our lifestyle, while others are ignored. Your overall diet, your activity levels, stress and sleep are arguably just as, if not more, important areas to focus on, provided your alcohol intake is within the recommended limit.
This is especially the case when it comes to ultra-processed food. Although direct comparisons are tricky, eating it regularly appears to me much more harmful than having a glass of wine five days a week, but nobody is banning junk food or even putting health warnings on it, even in children. To single out alcohol and ignore ultra-processed food is, in my opinion, not backed by science.
When research highlights the harms of light drinking, the point is never made about what people will have instead. If you discourage someone from having a glass of wine, will they have a Coca-Cola, Fanta or Monster energy drink instead? These types of drinks increase the risk of heart disease, diabetes and early death by around 10 per cent per daily can. In that case, it may be slightly healthier to have a small glass of wine, especially if worried about type 2 diabetes or living longer.
The health benefits of alcohol
1. A lower risk of heart disease
Research continues to show that wine in moderation has a mild protective effect against heart disease. This effect is still hanging around in studies. Scientists think it’s due to bias, but can’t get rid of it.
The latest study (as yet not peer-reviewed), presented at the American College of Cardiology’s Annual Scientific Session, looked at 340,000 people from UK Biobank for ten years and found that moderate wine drinkers, who had around one glass per day, had a 21 per cent lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease compared to people who never or rarely drank wine. A slightly increased risk was found for light beer and spirit drinkers.
These studies are observational, so we can’t show causality and don’t know exactly why wine might be beneficial for heart health. However, my guess is that it’s down to compounds called polyphenols.
2. It may protect against dementia
There is some weak evidence to suggest that moderate wine drinking may protect against dementia, possibly because the plant compounds it contains support our blood vessels. However, the evidence is stronger that too much alcohol definitely increases the risk of dementia. There’s a bit of a tightrope to walk on, so don’t rely on your wine to help your brain.
3. Drinking with friends could help you live longer
One of the major factors for living healthier for longer and reducing your risk of heart disease is maintaining social contacts and avoiding loneliness. This is another reason alcohol might protect health indirectly, as people tend to drink alcohol socially with others. Stronger social connections can increase your likelihood of survival by up to 50 per cent, and poor social connection is associated with roughly 30 per cent higher risk of heart disease and stroke.
This is another reason why saving Britain’s pubs is so important. It’s not just so people can keep drinking alcohol; they are social hubs. The two do go hand-in-hand.
How to drink sensibly
Have alcohol-free days
Lots of people quit alcohol for a month as a challenge but then go back to heavy drinking afterwards. I’m not a huge fan of this approach, as it encourages the idea that alcohol is fun and being abstemious is not. It’s much better to have a routine of some alcohol-free days each week. I find that Sunday and Monday work well for this, as they provide a bit of a reset before going into a new week.
However, if you’ve never gone for one month without alcohol, it can be helpful to try. I did it once after colleagues told me they experienced huge improvements in their sleep, mental state, work and productivity. I didn’t notice any of these benefits myself, but I appreciate it can be very individual.
Swap to non-alcoholic drinks sometimes
I increasingly opt for alcohol-free beers several times a week, either on days I’m not drinking or by alternating them with standard beers. It’s much easier to do this now that the quality and range of alcohol-free beer is so much better, more pubs stock them and I always keep the fridge stocked so I have the choice. Creating the right environment is important. Studies suggest that having a supply of alcohol-free alternatives reduces alcohol consumption. And don’t forget kombucha as an alternative; some pubs have it on draught.
Have yogurt before you drink
Some research suggests that having yogurt can offset some of the negative effects of alcohol and help you recover faster from a hangover, possibly because the microbes in dairy help to break down the alcohol. Have a yogurt or cheese before you leave, instead of picking up a kebab on your way home.
Be good at stopping
I’m generally pretty good at stopping after two or three drinks, and having your own cut-off is definitely advisable. I’m determined never to have the Kazakhstan experience again, but it is clear that binge drinking or having more than two or three drinks too often will likely harm your health.
I don’t see myself ever quitting alcohol completely, though as alternatives improve, my body changes with age and the science becomes clearer, I may change my mind.
summary: The author shares his personal drinking history, explaining that while he avoids spirits after a severe hangover, he remains a dedicated moderate drinker within NHS guidelines. He argues that light, occasional drinking has been unfairly demonized compared to ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks, and that moderate wine consumption may offer health benefits related to heart disease and social connection. The article concludes with practical tips for sensible drinking, such as having alcohol-free days, swapping to non-alcoholic options, and knowing when to stop.
key_points: The author typically consumes one or two glasses of wine or beer five days a week, staying roughly within the NHS recommended 14 units per week.
He believes low-level drinking has been unfairly demonized while more harmful lifestyle factors, such as ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks, are often ignored.
Observational research suggests moderate wine drinking may offer mild protective effects against heart disease and dementia, potentially due to polyphenols.
Drinking socially with others can indirectly improve health and increase longevity by reducing loneliness and strengthening social connections.
Sensible drinking strategies include incorporating alcohol-free days, choosing alcohol-free alternatives, eating yogurt before drinking, and setting a personal cut-off limit.

title: Mother tells how nail infection led to diagnosis of baby son’s brain tumour
author: PA Media
content:
A mother has spoken of how her son narrowly survived a brain tumour that medics discovered only as they looked into a tiny fingernail infection.
Sam Sharp, 39, gave birth to her son in 2020.
Just 11 days later, Joey, from Penicuik, Midlothian, was taken to hospital after he struggled to feed, lost weight and developed jaundice that would not let up.
He also began twitching intermittently.
Doctors investigated a small infection in one of his fingernails and an ultrasound revealed it was a brain tumour causing his symptoms.
Ms Sharp, an orthopaedic nurse, said: “Joey had only been home for a week and we were having visits from the midwife and health visitor every day because his newborn jaundice wasn’t improving, he wasn’t feeding well and he’d started losing weight.
![Joey in hospital with his mother](https://news.stv.tv/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ea06f3aa39a4338ed55520f6bbaa0227-1788761055.jpg) PA Media
“He was also having tiny spasms while feeding but, at the time, the midwives couldn’t quite work out what was causing them.
“Once we were in hospital, doctors noticed what looked like a tiny infection in one of his fingernails. It was so small, almost like a grain of sand under the nail. We had no idea then that within hours we’d be facing every parent’s worst nightmare.”
Joey underwent three brain surgeries and nine rounds of chemotherapy afterwards, with two operations to remove the tumour, and a third to help alleviate the scar tissue that remained, which had prevented drugs from treating his seizures.
At this point, he suffered from more than 30 epileptic seizures a day, and needed feeding tubes to eat.
He took part in clinical trials to help researchers gain a better understanding of chemotherapy treatment for babies.
Ms Sharp said: “We were told that without surgery that day, Joey was unlikely to survive.
“I can still remember that conversation as though it happened yesterday. Because it was during the Covid pandemic, my husband Steven had already been sent home under the hospital restrictions, so I was sitting there alone with our tiny baby while doctors explained what they’d found.
![Joey with Sam, Steven and sister Carly](https://news.stv.tv/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/38bee2b99abd5b675a853372e3d1f7a0-1788760967.jpg) PA Media
“As a nurse, I understood enough to know how serious the situation was, but nothing prepares you for hearing words like that about your own child.
“Thankfully, the hospital staff made sure my husband was allowed back in before Joey was taken to theatre. Watching your newborn baby disappear through those theatre doors is something no parent should ever have to experience.”
Specialists, who took samples of the tumour, discovered it was a glioblastoma, an aggressive and incurable form of brain cancer.
But on August 4 2021, towards the end of his treatment, the family received the news they had hoped for.
Ms Sharp said: “Joey was in the children’s day ward receiving his final chemotherapy when our consultant walked over to us. I remember she had tears in her eyes.
“It was an open ward with lots of other families with very sick children around us, so she couldn’t celebrate loudly, but she quietly told us Joey’s latest scan showed no evidence of disease.
“We’d been preparing ourselves to hear that he would probably need more surgery after chemotherapy, so hearing those words was overwhelming. For the first time in months, we felt like we could finally breathe again.”
Now aged five, the youngster has cerebral palsy, with little use of his right hand, wears a leg brace and uses a wheelchair for longer distances.
Despite his circumstances, his mother says he has a love for life, enjoying swimming and spending time with his siblings, eight-year-old Carly and one-year-old Robbie.
He has also started school.
Ms Sharp said: “Joey is our little ray of sunshine. He’s the kindest, funniest and most loving little boy you could ever meet. He fills every room with laughter and never lets anything hold him back.
“Watching him walk through those school gates was incredibly emotional, not just for our family but for the many doctors, nurses and therapists who have supported him since he was only 11 days old.
“He approaches life with so much determination and happiness. The bond he now shares with his sister, Carly, and brother, Robbie, is incredible.”
Ms Sharp called for more investment in brain cancer research from the Scottish Government, with a deadline of 2029.
She has also signed up for the Edinburgh Marathon next year, with donations to go to the Scottish Brain Tumour Research Centre of Excellence in a bid to find a cure for glioblastoma.
![Joey’s surgery scar](https://news.stv.tv/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/5fa44b0d5a2992b2034cc4507425594f-1788761014.jpg) PA Media
Ms Sharp said: “More research means better treatments and, ultimately, more families getting the chance to watch their children grow up.
“I hope the work taking place at the Scottish Centre of Excellence will help improve outcomes for anyone facing this devastating diagnosis in the future.”
Scotland’s Health Secretary Angela Constance said: “My heartfelt wishes go to Ms Sharp for sharing her son Joey’s brave battle to overcome brain cancer.
“The Scottish Government shares their desire to further improve cancer survival and is taking action to improve the awareness and earlier diagnosis of cancers in Scotland. I would encourage anyone with unusual or persistent symptoms to contact their GP practice.
“We published our cancer strategy for Scotland in 2023, with a focus on less survivable cancers, such as brain tumours and improving their outcomes.
“We are also the only nation in the UK to have a dedicated cancer strategy for children and young people, with work under way to renew this.
“We welcome innovation in cancer care and continue to consider emerging evidence on new treatments and technologies to ensure patients can benefit from clinically effective advances.”
Dr Karen Noble, director of research and policy at Brain Tumour Research, said: “No family should have to face the uncertainty Sam and her family experienced when Joey was diagnosed at such a young age.
“We urgently need greater investment in research into childhood brain tumours.”
Follow STV News on WhatsApp
Scan the QR code on your mobile device for all the latest news from around the country
![WhatsApp channel QR Code](https://news.stv.tv/wp-content/themes/stvnews/static/images/whatsapp-qr.png)
summary: A mother from Penicuik shared how her newborn son, Joey, survived an aggressive brain tumour that was discovered after doctors investigated a tiny fingernail infection. Joey underwent three brain surgeries, nine rounds of chemotherapy, and clinical trials to treat the glioblastoma and resulting seizures. Now five years old, Joey has started school and shows no evidence of disease, prompting his mother to advocate for increased brain cancer research funding.
key_points: Joey was diagnosed with an aggressive brain tumour called a glioblastoma at just 11 days old after doctors investigated a fingernail infection and newborn health issues.
He endured three brain surgeries, nine rounds of chemotherapy, and suffered from numerous daily epileptic seizures before completing his treatment.
A scan in August 2021 showed no evidence of disease, and Joey is now five years old and has started school.
His mother is calling for greater investment in brain cancer research and plans to run the Edinburgh Marathon to raise funds.

title: Probing the proteome at cellular scale
author: Eisenstein; Michael
content:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
Rapid technological advances are allowing researchers to identify thousands of proteins in individual cells, revealing the hidden mechanisms underlying development and disease.
Single-cell samples arrayed on glass slides for analysis by mass spectrometry. Credit: Andrew Leduc
When a fertilized mammalian egg divides, it yields two seemingly identical daughter cells. Some of their descendants generate the diverse organ systems of the embryo, while others form extra-embryonic tissues that sustain the developmental process.
In 2025, researchers used a cutting-edge technique known as single-cell proteomics (SCP) to show that even in the two first-generation cells, this division of labour is already established1. Nikolai Slavov at Northeastern University in Boston, Massachusetts, who co-directed the study with fellow cell biologists Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz and Tsui-Fen Chou at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, says that the protein contents of these two cells, which were termed ‘alpha’ and ‘beta’, reveal distinct properties and fates. “Beta cells were more likely to give rise to healthy embryos than the alpha cells,” he says, whereas alpha cells typically formed extra-embryonic tissues. The team could trace these identities back to fertilization.
Other questions are also yielding to the technology. Researchers now recognize, for instance, that many of the most clinically significant events in the formation of tumours originate from individual cells camouflaged in the chaotic tumour environment. “Single-cell proteomics may help us understand why patients have different outcomes due to tumour evolution, immune responses and cell differentiation — all driven by cellular heterogeneity,” says Yu-Ju Chen, a mass spectrometrist at Academia Sinica in Taipei.
Just a few years ago, protein biologists largely dismissed the possibility of single-cell proteomics — profiling thousands of proteins in individual cells — as the stuff of science fiction. “I’m almost on the record as saying, ‘not in my lifetime’, because it seemed to be so far off,” says Matthias Mann, a proteomics researcher at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in Martinsried, Germany. But over the past decade, SCP has become not only possible but practical — and scientifically informative. Mann himself is now an avid practitioner, using SCP to study illnesses ranging from liver conditions to Alzheimer’s disease. The bar to entry remains high, however, and the need for expensive equipment, deep expertise and methodological precision to process cell-scale volumes of protein still limits the potentially transformative impact of this technology.
Precious cargo
Biology is already deep in the single-cell era, but most such analyses focus on the transcriptome. Profiling gene expression at the level of the individual cell can provide valuable information about a cell’s identity or physiological state. But researchers cannot necessarily predict the protein contents of a cell from its RNA alone — not every RNA gets translated, and numerous factors shape the timing and extent of protein production from a given transcript. Many disease mechanisms can best be understood by surveying the protein contents — for example, the pathology of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease is strongly linked to aberrant aggregates of protein. “The proteome reflects the current state of the cell,” Mann says.
To survey that state, proteomics researchers typically work in bulk, pooling and analysing thousands or millions of cells using mass spectrometry (MS). This technique uses specialized instruments that break samples down into ionized pieces, which are then analysed in terms of their mass and charge. The resulting ‘fingerprint’ enables precise identification of the molecule from which the fragment originated, and researchers can routinely detect 10,000 or more distinct proteins per sample. But this is an averaged perspective that can obscure the underlying biology. “Are they really reflecting what’s going on in all cells or is it just a small population of cells where you see dramatic changes?” asks Jesper Olsen, a mass spectrometrist at the University of Copenhagen. “These are things we have not really been able to address before.”
Enter single-cell proteomics
In some ways, the technology should be simpler than its transcriptomic analogue. Protein is more stable than RNA is, and more abundant. “With RNA, we count zero, one, two, three [copies] most of the time; with proteins, we count 100, 500, 10,000,” says Slavov. But transcriptomics researchers can boost the cellular RNA signal by using the PCR amplification technique. No such tool exists for the proteome, and researchers must learn all they can from a few hundred picograms of material.
Getting a robust and informative signal from such tiny quantities requires a highly sensitive mass spectrometer — but sample preparation poses a more formidable challenge. “The raw sensitivity was there … but the sample prep was optimized for bulk level,” says Ryan Kelly, a biochemist at Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah.
Matthias Mann’s Deep Visual Proteomics strategy adds spatial data to single-cell proteomics.Credit: Axel Griesch/Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry
In 2018, a team led by Slavov demonstrated an important first step towards broad proteomic coverage at the single-cell level2. The researchers developed a sample preparation and analysis workflow called SCoPE-MS (single-cell proteomics by mass spectrometry), in which they chemically labelled proteins in individual cells of interest and then mixed these with an excess of unlabelled ‘carrier’ cells. This limited protein loss from the target cells and made protein identification easier, enabling the detection of more than 1,500 proteins across eight individual cells. “We essentially gained about four orders of magnitude in sensitivity,” he says.
Slavov recalls that the publication of his results was met with scepticism, but other groups soon replicated them. And importantly, a second group led by Kelly published an independent approach to SCP that same year, using a sample preparation device called the nanoPOTS chip (nanodroplet processing in one pot for trace samples) to identify 670 proteins in small numbers of individual cells3. “The whole point of those early papers was, ‘this is real signal from single cells’,” says Kelly. “It’s not a question any more.”
A growing crowd
Since then, the field has advanced at a remarkable pace. Jennifer Van Eyk, a clinical proteomics researcher at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, California, says that her team has developed a workflow that can consistently identify 1,500–2,000 proteins per cell. “The biology we’re seeing is just unbelievable,” she says.
And deeper coverage is possible. In 2025, two independent studies inventoried more than 5,000 proteins per cell — a figure that is already being surpassed. Olsen, who led one study4, says his group has work under review in which they identify up to 7,000 proteins in individual cells. And Karl Mechtler, a proteomics researcher at the Research Institute of Molecular Pathology in Vienna, who co-directed the other study5, notes that with some larger cells, “you can get up to 8,000 or 9,000 proteins”.
Many SCP laboratories now rely on the cellenONE, a device commercialized by Cellenion in Lyon, France, that makes it possible to isolate individual cells from a culture or tissue sample while also imaging them. That allows users to record each cell’s shape and size, which matter because cells can vary considerably in volume and protein content.
Downstream processing steps have also been optimized, minimizing sample loss and preventing cross-contamination that could confound interpretation of the data. Although chemical labelling of proteins was a key step in Slavov’s 2018 publication, many groups have adopted unlabelled approaches that are simpler and faster. For example, Kelly’s team developed a single-step process in 2023 that remains its go-to protocol6. And Chen and her collaborator at Academia Sinica, Hsiung-Lin Tu, have integrated the full sample preparation process into a compact microfluidic device. Known as the SciProChip, it performs all the necessary steps in nanoscale volumes of liquid7. “The chip substantially improved our sensitivity, reproducibility and quantitation accuracy,” says Chen.
The SciProChip uses microfluidics to capture, count and process individual cells for analysis.Credit: Hsiung-Lin Tu and Yu-Ju Chen
Advances in MS instrumentation have also propelled the field. Popular options include the Orbitrap Astral machines from Thermo Fisher Scientific in Waltham, Massachusetts, and the timsTOF Ultra line from Bruker in Billerica, Massachusetts. These systems employ different strategies to detect and quantify proteins that would be invisible with older technology, but can cost around US$1 million. “We can quantify much more sensitively, much more deeply, and at high throughput even more proteins in single cells,” says Slavov. However, he notes that the more affordable, older-generation systems remain effective for profiling high-abundance proteins.
The biggest hurdle is speed. Most SCP pipelines top out at a few hundred cells per day — orders of magnitude lower than the throughput of transcriptomics studies. This is mainly because of the need to separate cellular peptides by size before MS analysis. Going faster can mean sacrificing precious data, says Kelly: “When we switch from 288 samples per day to 500 samples per day, we do see a big hit in our proteome coverage.”
Multiplexing offers one solution, in which individual cells are labelled such that the data from each can be disentangled even after the cells have been pooled for processing and analysis. For example, the labelling strategy Slavov used in 2018, based on MS-resolvable ‘tandem mass tags’, can resolve dozens of samples in parallel. But labelling adds complexity to sample preparation and can confound data analysis. “In the end, you end up getting actually quite a low identification rate from the peptides compared to a label-free experiment,” says Olsen.
