summary: Single-cell proteomics (SCP) has rapidly evolved from a seemingly impossible concept into a practical and powerful technology capable of identifying thousands of proteins in individual cells. By overcoming major hurdles in mass spectrometry sensitivity and sample preparation using specialized techniques like microfluidic devices and carrier cells, researchers can now reveal hidden cellular mechanisms in development and disease. Despite remaining challenges such as high equipment costs and limited sample throughput, SCP is providing unprecedented insights into cellular heterogeneity and biological function.
key_points: Single-cell proteomics (SCP) allows researchers to profile thousands of proteins in individual cells, overcoming the limitations of bulk analysis and transcriptomics.
Early methodological breakthroughs in 2018, such as SCoPE-MS and the nanoPOTS chip, proved that robust proteomic signals could be extracted from tiny cellular samples.
Recent technological advancements have enabled studies to inventory between 5,000 and 9,000 proteins per individual cell.
Major current hurdles for the technology include the need for expensive equipment, high methodological precision, and relatively low processing throughput compared to transcriptomics.

title: Bovine TB: Gaps in evidence about impact of vaccinating badgers
author: Craig Duggan
content:
![A young badger standing among grass and vegetation outdoors. It has the distinctive black-and-white facial markings associated with European badgers, including two dark stripes running from the nose over the eyes toward the ears. Behind the badger there appears to be earth, rock, or a burrow entrance, consistent with a woodland or countryside habitat.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/963/cpsprodpb/aec4/live/0bf6f3b0-aaa7-11f1-9eba-7de947fa7cd1.jpg)
The Welsh government is "renewing" its approach to eradicating bovine TB
- Published
There are "significant gaps" in knowledge and evidence about the effect of vaccinating badgers in Wales against bovine tuberculosis (TB), according to researchers.
A team from the British Ecological Society's Wales policy group, along with staff from Cardiff and Aberystwyth universities, argue the gaps reduce the effectiveness of this method of trying to deal with the disease.
Vaccination is part of a programme to eradicate bovine TB in Wales, but it is a controversial topic.
The Welsh government said it was "renewing" its approach to eradicating bovine TB.
There have been calls for alternative methods to vaccination for controlling the infection among cattle, such as badger culling, as they can carry the disease and transmit it to cattle.
Cattle are regularly tested for the presence of the infection and are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers.
![A group of black-and-white dairy cattle housed inside a livestock building. Several cows are standing side-by-side in feeding stalls along a concrete feed barrier. The animals are positioned closely together, with their heads extending through metal rails.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/953/cpsprodpb/d50f/live/8edf18a0-aaa4-11f1-9eba-7de947fa7cd1.jpg)
Cattle are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers of bovine TB
The call for more monitoring comes in a new policy briefing by researchers.
They are calling for increased monitoring of the vaccination's impact, a review of the evidence, and collaboration with farmers "to ensure the greatest possible impact" from the programmes.
In their policy briefing, they say "major questions remain about how many badgers are being vaccinated, what impact vaccinating badgers is having on disease levels in cattle, and how confidence in vaccination can be improved among farmers and veterinary professionals".
Dr Niall McKeown, a lecturer in the department of life sciences at Aberystwyth University and vice-chair of the British Ecological Society's Wales policy group, said the infection "remains one of the biggest animal health challenges facing Wales".
"Badger vaccination should not be presented as a stand-alone route to eradicating bovine tuberculosis," said McKeown.
"There is strong evidence that BCG vaccination protects badgers, but evidence that operational vaccination programmes reduce disease in cattle remains limited.
"Any cattle-level benefit is likely to depend on sustained and sufficiently extensive vaccination coverage alongside effective cattle controls."
He emphasised it was not simply more vaccination that was needed "but vaccination that is better targeted, measured and evaluated".
"By combining non-invasive genetic monitoring with sett surveys, camera traps and movement data, we can estimate local badger numbers, check the proportion of the population reached and identify significant gaps," he added.
![A sign for Aberystwyth University. It is a metal sign with a yellow background, with the text in black. There is also a logo for the university on the sign, which is a shield featuring two dragons in the top half, and an open book in the bottom half.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a1a5/live/3bc23640-aaa7-11f1-9eba-7de947fa7cd1.jpg)
Researchers say bovine TB remains "one of the biggest animal health challenges"
A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "We are renewing our approach to eradicating bovine TB in Wales, focusing on three main elements: cattle, people, and wildlife.
"This work will be evidence-based and science-led, taking into account advice from the programme board and the technical advisory group, while ensuring that value for money remains a core consideration in decision-making."
Last month, Llyr Gruffydd, the minister responsible for agriculture, said there was a need to "look at a range of solutions".
He said the "picture varies from farm to farm" and that a "wide range of options" were being considered.
His comments came as the Welsh government announced the extension of two projects aiming to eradicate bovine TB.
The project began as a pilot scheme introduced in two areas - Pembrokeshire, where there is a very high number of TB cases, and parts of north Wales - but there was no intention to expand this to other areas.
In August 2024, a new board was established by the government to try to eliminate the disease.
summary: Researchers from universities and the British Ecological Society report significant gaps in evidence regarding the effectiveness of vaccinating badgers against bovine TB in Wales. The policy briefing highlights major questions about vaccination coverage, its impact on cattle, and the need for better monitoring and farmer collaboration. The Welsh government states it is renewing its science-led approach to eradicating the disease by focusing on cattle, people, and wildlife.
key_points: Significant knowledge gaps reduce the effectiveness of badger vaccination in tackling bovine TB in Wales.
Researchers call for increased monitoring, evidence reviews, and collaboration with farmers and vets.
Evidence that operational badger vaccination programmes reduce disease in cattle remains limited.
The Welsh government is renewing its approach to eradicating bovine TB, focusing on cattle, people, and wildlife.

title: Concern about 999 process before Surrey teen's meningitis death
author: Craig Buchan
content:
![An emergency services call handler sitting at a desk with a headset on taking a call](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/270c/live/41a38d30-47f2-11ef-b89a-7f3a998111a9.jpg)
Oliver Shelley's parents had rushed him to hospital as an ambulance was not dispatched following their 999 call
- Published
A coroner has raised concerns about emergency call handling after the death of a teenager from meningitis.
Oliver Shelley died in July 2024 aged 17 from meningococcal septicaemia. His parents had rushed him to East Surrey Hospital in Redhill as an ambulance was not dispatched after their 999 call.
Surrey assistant coroner Dr Karen Henderson wrote, after an inquest in February, of concern about the lack of a sepsis pathway on the computer system assisting call handlers.
South East Coast Ambulance Service (Secamb) said it was "committed to continuing to learn from Shelley's death and listening to all patients and families".
At February's inquest, a jury found Shelley's parents had phoned emergency services at 14:51 BST on 22 July 2024, reporting he had meningitis symptoms.
An ambulance was not dispatched so they took him to hospital themselves, arriving shortly before 16:00.
The teenager had a "widespread rash and evidence of septic shock and organ dysfunction", according to the report, and he "continued to clinically deteriorate".
He died seven-and-a-half hours after being admitted to hospital.
![An infographic titled âWhat are the signs of meningitis?â listing symptoms that can appear suddenly and in any order. It includes illustrations for: fever shown with a thermometer; vomiting depicted by a person leaning forward; severe headache shown with red lines around the head; a rash on an arm; a stiff neck illustrated by someone touching their neck; dislike of bright lights shown with an eye shielded by a dark band; drowsiness or difficulty waking shown with a person resting a head on a hand; and seizures illustrated by a figure lying on their side. Text at the bottom notes: âYou do not always get all the symptoms.â Sources: NHS, CDC](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/248a/live/07bcc710-21dc-11f1-a79a-77e93010d956.png)
During the 999 call, the handler began to triage the call but was unable to prioritise any of the symptoms on the NHS computer software, according to the coroner's report, external.
Henderson wrote that Shelley's parents were told "a call back was scheduled within 20 minutes", but it instead came one hour and 41 minutes later.
She said call handlers find it "challenging to triage individuals when multiple signs and symptoms were present in relation to a possible sepsis diagnosis" on the system.
Having a "dedicated sepsis algorithm" would assist responding to callers and managing cases, according to the prevention of future deaths report.
A further concern raised was that call handlers' official job title - emergency medical advisors - could be "misleading the public" as staff have "no qualifications in medicine or nursing".
In its formal response to the coroner, external, NHS England said the concerns raised "have been listened to and reflected upon".
The organisation said its programme "would screen for potential sepsis" in a range of situations and that both sepsis and meningitis were "addressed within core training".
"Trained clinicians are available at all times to provide immediate advice" to call handlers, it said.
NHS England added that Secamb had "implemented a number of improvements", including clearer rules for escalating calls to clinicians and better staff training.
Jo Turner, Secamb's interim chief nursing officer, said the service's "deepest sympathies remain with Oliver's family" and it was "extremely grateful to them for working so openly with us".
"Their involvement has helped us better understand what happened and implement necessary improvements to our systems, processes and training," she said.
Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Surrey on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Seventeen-year-old Oliver Shelley died from meningococcal septicaemia in July 2024 after his parents rushed him to the hospital when an ambulance was not dispatched following their 999 call. A coroner raised concerns regarding the lack of a specific sepsis pathway on the computer software used by emergency call handlers and noted that the job title "emergency medical advisors" could be misleading to the public. In response, NHS England and the South East Coast Ambulance Service stated they are implementing improvements, staff training, and better systems for escalating calls.
key_points: Oliver Shelley died from meningococcal septicaemia in July 2024 at the age of 17.
An assistant coroner highlighted a lack of a sepsis pathway on computer systems used by 999 call handlers.
Shelley's parents drove him to the hospital themselves after an ambulance was not dispatched following their emergency call.
The coroner noted that the job title "emergency medical advisors" may mislead the public since staff lack medical or nursing qualifications.
NHS England and the South East Coast Ambulance Service stated they have implemented improvements and enhanced staff training following the incident.

title: Cravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work?
author: Nicola Davis
content:
When Mercedes was told by her doctor that she could be prescribed GLP-1 weight loss jabs in 2024, she broke down. “[When] she said yes, I cried in her office. And I didn’t really stop crying for a week,” she said.
“Finally, after being overweight my entire life, this was going to save me. My struggle, my burden, my shame was finally going to come to an end.”
But as time went on it was hope, not weight, that fell away.
“I was on [Ozempic] for nine months. And then I went on Wegovy for four months, then Contrave [an oral, non-GLP-1 medication], and then Mounjaro, and that was for a few months, and then nine months ago I started on Zepbound,” said Mercedes. “Nothing has worked.”
A recently retired teacher in her 50s, Mercedes is among a small proportion of people for whom the powerful new weight-loss drugs, championed by celebrities for their transformative effects, do not work.
Ozempic, a type 2 diabetes medication, and Wegovy, which is licensed for weight loss, both contain a drug called semaglutide that mimics a hormone that occurs naturally in our bodies: GLP-1. These medications reduce the rate at which food is emptied from the stomach, suppresses appetite and increase the production of insulin – meaning many people lose weight.
Mounjaro and Zepbound, also now household names, have an even greater weight-loss effect. They both contain the drug tirzepatide which mimics both GLP-1 and another hormone.
The excitement around such “GLP-1s” has been hard to miss: the medications have grabbed headlines, with clinical trials suggesting they can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight. Studies suggest they could help with conditions ranging from heart problems and addictions to fatty liver disease. In some cases experts say the effects may not be entirely related to weight loss.
But not everyone experiences the benefits. Between 9% and a third of participants in clinical trials lose less than 5% of their body weight – depending on the type of drug and dose used.
Now researchers are trying to work out why – something they say could help doctors tailor the use of the drugs, maximise cost-effectiveness and reduce side-effects.
For Mercedes, the impact of non-response has been profound.
“Aside from the fact that it’s not working and that it’s so expensive, to say it’s hard on the self-esteem is a humongous understatement,” said Mercedes, who lives in Canada. “It’s been a real struggle, with shame and regret and big bills and disappointment that my own body is not working the way it should.”
Prof Alexander Miras, an obesity expert at Ulster University, said the efficacy of the drugs could not be blamed on patients. “If the drug does not reduce hunger and food intake for someone, it is just not going to work,” he said.
Mercedes said she has tried hard to stick to lifestyle changes alongside the medications but, for her, the jabs did not suppress constant, intrusive thoughts about food.
“I just thought: ‘No, I’ve got to get somewhere … I’m going to die of obesity’,” she said. “I was really strict with myself for a month – but the cravings, which I can only call like heroin withdrawal … it’s just overwhelming. And the food talk never ended.”
The extreme effort paid off, to an extent. “I can honestly say I lost 20 pounds in that month, but not because of the medication,” she said.
Mercedes is certainly not alone: the Guardian has heard from dozens of people for whom GLP-1 medications have had little effect.
Yury K, 57, also from Canada, said he tried a number of weight loss programmes before starting Wegovy for obesity. He exercises about five days a week, mainly with kettlebells, and does not eat junk food or fast food.
While Yury said he saw some improvements in his blood sugar levels and cholesterol while using the medication, as well as a reduction in food noise and appetite, he found his weight barely changed.
“I started Wegovy at about 242lb and, after six months, I was still about 242lb. My weight can fluctuate a little because of water, but essentially there was no meaningful weight loss,” he said. He also experienced unpleasant side effects, including constipation and sensitive skin.
“There is so much discussion about GLP-1 medications as if they work for everyone, and that was not my experience. When you put in the effort with diet and exercise, take the medication exactly as prescribed, and still see little benefit, it is difficult not to feel disappointed,” he said.
Lucille*, 53, who is based in Luxembourg, told the Guardian she has been taking GLP-1 medications for four years – initially to help with insulin resistance – starting on a daily injection of a GLP-1 medication called Saxenda, before switching to Ozempic.
Yet despite being effective at first, Lucille says the medications no longer help her lose weight – even after switching to Mounjaro and taking the highest dose. “It’s as if nothing is having an effect any more,” she says. “The Mounjaro 5mg [dose] is outrageously expensive and so far none of these medications have been approved by my health insurance,” she adds.
At present, the reason for such variations in response remains unclear. “The short answer to why some people don’t respond is we don’t really know,” said Miras.
He said research had suggested factors such as motivation, intelligence, education and socioeconomics did not predict how patients would respond to GLP-1 medications.
But other characteristics might do. “We know, for example, that age plays a role – so older people lose less weight. Sex plays a role – men lose less than women,” said Miras. “[And] people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight compared to people without.”
Studies have also suggested ancestry might have an impact, with the medications most effective in people of European ancestry, and least effective in people of African American ancestry.
Dr Mahesh Umapathysivam, an endocrinologist and clinical researcher at Adelaide University in Australia, said it was plausible that hormones could have an effect too.
“There is growing evidence that oestrogen alters GLP-1 response. We see that with the difference between male response and female response. Also, we know from some of the physiological studies that time of menstrual cycle also alters GLP-1 response,” he said.
“Finally, the use of menopausal hormone replacement therapy – which contains oestrogen – is associated with greater weight loss in semaglutide users.”
Then there is the matter of genetics. A recent study highlighted the potential role of a genetic variant that affects receptors in the brain upon which the drugs work.
“People carrying the genetic variant, we found lose about an extra 0.76kg (1.6 lbs) on average, and people who carry two copies of the variant double that,” said Adam Auton, vice-president of human genetics at the 23andMe Research Institute, and the senior author of the study.
“For people with two copies, this accounts for about 10% of the weight people might expect to lose on these medications.”
Umapathysivam and colleagues have recently published a study into two genetic variants that affect the production of an enzyme, known as PAM, that modifies many hormones including GLP-1. The team found people with such variants appear to show resistance to GLP-1.
“GLP-1 resistance simply means a given amount of GLP-1 has less effect on the body,” Umapathysivam said. “The implication for treatment is that a certain dose of GLP-1 in someone with resistance might mean less weight loss, less glucose lowering, less insulin secretion or less slowing to the gastric emptying.”
Despite emerging research, it is not yet possible to accurately predict who will respond to weight loss jabs and who won’t.
But there are reasons for people like Mercedes to be hopeful. A series of promising new drugs are in development. “Another option is to change patients to a non-GLP-1 based drug called Mysimba [the UK brand name for Contrave]. It works in the same parts of the brain, but just slightly differently and therefore may be worth trying,” said Miras. “It is not available in the NHS, just privately.”
For some who struggle to lose weight with GLP-1 medications, weight-loss surgery may be the only option left. And, Miras says, “[A] lack of response to GLP-1 based drugs does not predict lack of response to [bariatric] surgery.”
And for those who lose little to no weight on GLP-1 medications, the message is clear. “It’s not your fault and it’s not the drug’s fault either, this is purely luck,” said Miras. “I’ve seen it before, it’s not very common, but it does happen.”
Mercedes began GLP-1 medications with huge amounts of hope and expectation. “There was just so much publicity around it. So many people [using the drugs said]: ‘Oh, I forgot to eat lunch,’ that I suppose subconsciously I just sort of ignored the prospect that … the drugs didn’t work,” she said.
“I wish I knew if there were other people out there, like me, for whom [GLP-1s] are just not effective at all.”
*Some names have been changed
summary: While powerful GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Mounjaro help many people lose significant weight, a small proportion of patients experience little to no effect. Clinical trials show that between 9% and a third of participants lose less than 5% of their body weight. Researchers are actively studying why non-responses occur—pointing to potential factors such as age, sex, genetics, hormones, and ancestry—though experts emphasize that lack of efficacy is not the fault of the patient.
key_points: Between 9% and a third of clinical trial participants lose less than 5% of their body weight using GLP-1 medications.
Experts state that non-response is not a patient's fault, but rather a matter of biology and luck.
Emerging research suggests factors like age, sex, ancestry, hormones, and genetics may influence how a person responds to the drugs.
Alternative treatments, such as different medications or bariatric surgery, remain options for individuals who do not respond to GLP-1 jabs.

title: Being a carer 'nearly broke me' but love 'carried me through'
author: Emma Stanley
content:
![Ellen and Terry in winter coats and knitted hats embrace outdoors at night by an illuminated fountain, with city buildings and lights in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/6ca1/live/c8126580-a7a4-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Ellen Miller said she "knew something was very wrong" when her husband Terry started to act differently
- Published
Ellen Miller said she started to notice changes in her husband Terry's behaviour in 2016.
She said his driving had become erratic, and though he was a keen cook, he was no longer able to prepare a Sunday roast - something which had been an "unshakeable family ritual" for many years.
But the change that troubled Ellen most was Terry's growing disengagement from their relationship.
"He just didn't seem bothered anymore," she said.
'I knew something was very wrong'
Ellen, from Blackpool, said she decided to carry out her own test to see what would happen.
She said: "I deliberately didn't speak to him to see what would happen.
"It was three days before he said anything to me.
"We'd had a fantastic partnership and he'd been my rock for decades so I knew something was very wrong."
Ellen and Terry went to the GP numerous times from 2017. But it was 2023 before he got his diagnosis - vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease.
"Because Terry wasn't experiencing memory problems it took quite a while, and a few visits to persuade the GP to do a memory test," Ellen said.
![Ellen and Terry pose together indoors for a photograph, standing close with one arm around the other's shoulders](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/a911/live/14e30220-a7a5-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Ellen and Terry were married for 32 years
Their story is far from rare. Research published by Alzheimer's Society, external found families affected by dementia were being forced to put their lives on hold as they waited for a diagnosis.
A survey of more than 1,000 carers showed that for respondents in the north west of England, nearly four in 10 (37%) waited more than six months for a diagnosis after first seeking help.
The dementia charity said this had "devastating consequences" for carers' work, finances and mental wellbeing.
The charity is now calling for a new nationally-recognised standard that would mean patients get an accurate diagnosis and care plan within 18 weeks of a GP referral.
'Terry always knew who I was'
Ellen knew they needed to make adaptations to their home and to prepare for Terry's condition to worsen over time.
The family put in handrails and floor lighting, but he still suffered a lot of falls in the following years.
His memory, though, stayed intact.
"Terry always knew who I was," Ellen said. "He was even able to tease and make jokes with my brother about football the weekend before he went into hospital for the last time."
Terry died in 2025.
Since his death, Ellen has taken up volunteering on the board of the Dementia Carers Matter charity - something that has given her great comfort.
"Caring nearly broke me," she said, "but I've also found solace in walking and playing music.
"My dad played trombone and when I took Terry to a Christmas concert in Blackpool during his illness and heard a cornet solo, it moved me to tears.
"I was inspired to return to music myself after many years and now play trombone in my local brass band.
"The support and love from that community has carried me through."
summary: Ellen Miller noticed behavioral and personality changes in her husband Terry starting in 2016, though he was not officially diagnosed with vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease until 2023. Following years of making home adaptations and caring for Terry, who passed away in 2025, Ellen found solace in volunteering and playing the trombone in a local brass band. Her experience reflects broader issues highlighted by the Alzheimer's Society regarding long waits for dementia diagnoses and the heavy toll on carers.
key_points: Ellen Miller first noticed changes in her husband Terry's behavior in 2016, including erratic driving and emotional disengagement.
Despite multiple GP visits starting in 2017, Terry did not receive a diagnosis of vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease until 2023.
Research by the Alzheimer's Society shows many families wait months for a diagnosis, prompting calls for a new 18-week standard from GP referral.
Terry passed away in 2025, and Ellen subsequently found support and comfort through volunteering and joining a local brass band.

title: The sleeping x eating secret: 15 ways to better rest, a healthier diet – and a happier life
author: Rachel Dixon
content:
A study published in the journal Nature Health last month found that food choices and meal timings have “immediate and measurable effects” on sleep. It was just the latest in a growing body of research into the link between diet and rest. Here is the latest science on what to eat for better sleep – and how sleep deprivation can affect your dinner the next day.
What should I eat for a good night’s sleep?
While there isn’t “a special sleep diet” that will guarantee eight undisturbed hours, a Mediterranean-style diet comes closest, says Dalhia Campbell, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association. She describes it as “a balanced, varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, wholegrains, lean proteins and healthy fats to help stabilise energy and support the hormones involved in sleep”.
Prof Marie-Pierre St-Onge is the director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University in New York, and the author of Eat Better, Sleep Better. Her research into “plant-forward” diets, including the Mediterranean diet, is investigating why they are beneficial for sleep. She says this could be due partly to the phytonutrients in plant foods, which have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds, and partly to nutrients that feed the gut microbiome and are involved in gut-brain communications. “That could play a role in improving sleep through helping people quiet their minds,” St-Onge says.
Are there any specific sleep-promoting foods?
![A chopping board with halved and whole kiwi fruit](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/33c6fd27c405f4127dea2ef1d452f5f6f6f5330a/1249_0_6247_5000/master/6247.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“It is best to look at your overall diet rather than focusing on one particular food,” says Campbell. “The latest UK diet and nutrition survey shows that fewer than 17% of adults meet the ‘five a day’ recommendation. Improving fruit and vegetable intake supports general health and sleep.”
But once you’ve nailed your five a day, are any fruit and veg better than others? “There’s quite a bit of research showing tomatoes, tropical fruits such as bananas and pineapples, and oranges have benefits for sleep,” says St-Onge. “Nuts and seeds, especially pistachios and walnuts, and wholegrains can contribute to better sleep as well.”
Emerging studies show that kiwis may have some benefits, says Dr Sammie Gill, a senior nutrition scientist at the British Nutrition Foundation, but the evidence is limited so far. There is also early research into tart cherries: “A recent systematic review indicated that consumption may help improve sleep duration, sleep efficiency or sleep onset time,” she says. “That said, the science remains limited and inconsistent.”
Do I need more protein?
![Overhead view of a large group of food with high content of healthy proteins. The composition includes salmon beef fillet, chicken breast, eggs, yogurt, mussels, chick peas, pistachios, cheese, brown lentild, beans, shrimps, canned tuna, pumpkin seeds, soybeans among others.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/72b0acf0ca25d54c0f52f45ac05b7b828fc9ab74/8_0_6627_5304/master/6627.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Diets higher in protein have also been associated with better sleep. “Proteins are important because they provide a source of tryptophan, which is essential for producing serotonin and melatonin, which are important for sleep,” says St-Onge. Tryptophan is one of the nine essential amino acids that your body can’t make on its own, so it has to come from your diet. All animal proteins and many plant proteins contain tryptophan. “In the US, people talk about turkey all the time, like, ‘That’s why you fall asleep at dinner on Thanksgiving,’” says St-Onge. “But food is not an instantaneous process – it’s not like you pop a pill and two hours later it gets to exactly where it needs to get.”
If you do want to try tryptophan-maxxing, Gill says other sources are “dairy, eggs, fish, seafood, meat, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and legumes. Tryptophan-containing foods have been linked with improved sleep outcomes – such as total sleep time and sleep efficiency – compared with controls.” So having a warm milky drink before bed makes sense? “There isn’t strong research showing that warm milk helps with sleep, but that shouldn’t stop you from having milk as a bedtime option,” says Gill.
What foods will keep me awake?
“Foods that are low in nutrients and high in fats and sugars are less likely to support good sleep,” Campbell advises.
St-Onge conducted research on this topic in France. “We showed that people who consumed more ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of insomnia symptoms. We’ve also shown that women who consume foods that have a higher glycemic index – the types of foods that tend to raise your blood sugars to a greater extent than others – have a higher risk of developing insomnia.” According to Diabetes UK, high GI foods include refined carbohydrates such as white bread, potatoes, doughnuts, bagels, sweets, sugar-sweetened breakfast cereals and sugar-sweetened drinks. As well as added sugars, St-Onge would avoid foods high in salt.
Does caffeine help or hinder?
![A middle-aged woman with short gray hair sleeps peacefully in bed, covered with a light blanket, her hand to her face, in a room bathed in bright morning sunlight.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/348904b60e243ca7dc9471cb687deaae2f47a1bc/0_0_8306_5217/master/8306.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Caffeine is a double-edged sword,” says Gill. “Plenty of studies have shown that caffeine in moderate doses [up to 400mg/four cups of coffee a day] can have a positive effect on cognitive performance, memory and alertness. But at higher doses, it can trigger anxiety, irritability and restlessness.”
Four coffees may sound an awful lot to some. “The effects of caffeine vary from person to person – some people are more sensitive to its effects. How you respond to caffeine is partly determined by your genetics,” she says. But however much you drink, the main thing is to do so in the morning. “Caffeine has a quarter-life of around 10-12 hours, meaning that if you consume it at lunchtime, a quarter of the caffeine is still in your body close to midnight, which can disrupt sleep.” Cutting it out by lunch “can lead to noticeable improvements in sleep quality and quantity”.
As you get older, you may find the after-dinner espresso you once enjoyed is now keeping you awake. “Your ability to metabolise caffeine changes as you age,” says St-Onge. “It’s important to keep track and evaluate every so often. If you’re starting to see that your sleep is changing, you might want to make adjustments related to intake of caffeine or timing of the last caffeinated beverage.”
How about alcohol?
![Closeup of the hands of people toasting with pints of beer](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/96eea5cfc7bb3709f95c0607269377de356a778f/1152_0_6827_5464/master/6827.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Many people think a drink or two helps them fall asleep – and they are right. But that doesn’t mean it’s a sleep aid. “Alcohol is a sedative – it does not prompt natural, ‘true’ sleep,” says Gill. “While it may help you fall asleep faster, it significantly disrupts the quality of your sleep. Alcohol, even in low amounts, reduces REM sleep, which is important for emotional processing and memory consolidation.”
What’s more, “alcohol interacts with several neurotransmitters that are important in the regulation of sleep and can trigger awakenings during the night, which can make you feel tired the next day”. It can also make acid reflux worse, adds Campbell. So much for the trusty nightcap.
How long should I leave between dinner and bed?
![Young man sleeping peacefully in bed](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e2e4895055dd0d06c8742c74cfdedbc337689e51/281_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Studies have found that later meals are generally linked to lower-quality sleep,” says Gill. “A recent trial found that eating dinner one hour before bedtime was linked with reduced sleep continuity and stability.” And you may find it harder to drop off in the first place, says Campbell, as your body is busy digesting your meal.
St-Onge cautions that going to bed on a full stomach also increases your risk of heartburn and acid reflux. “As a general rule, wait two to three hours after a meal,” she says. If you already suffer from acid reflux, NHS advice is to avoid food for up to four hours before bed. Beware of that late-night cuppa, too, says St-Onge: “If you’re drinking much too close to bedtime, you’ll need to wake up to use the bathroom.”
But I hate going to bed hungry!
“It’s OK to have a light snack after an early dinner if you’re feeling hungry – going to sleep on an empty stomach can disrupt sleep, too,” says Gill. “The key message is: don’t go to bed too full or too hungry.”
“Choose a light, nutritious option such as yoghurt with fruit and nuts, or wholegrain toast with nut butter and banana,” says Campbell. “That’s better than grazing on biscuits and chocolate.”
Why am I ravenous when I haven’t slept well?
![Hand holding a spoon, eating a bowl of choco Krispies](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5462c2f75d11fde3b0d046f418e0661a50bf2c04/466_0_3385_2708/master/3385.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
This is partly down to your body’s hunger signals. “Some research suggests that sleep loss can alter appetite hormones such as leptin [which signals fullness] and ghrelin [which stimulates appetite],” says Gill. “One study showed that one night of inadequate sleep can increase ghrelin levels and decrease leptin levels.” As a result, “poor sleep is associated with increases in energy intake, mainly from snacking, especially on foods higher in fat and carbohydrates. One review found that people who are sleep-deprived consume an average of 385 calories extra the following day compared with controls.”
St-Onge’s research has found this hormone effect varies by sex: “Ghrelin tends to rise before a meal, signalling hunger. We’ve shown that it increases to a greater extent in men who haven’t had sufficient sleep.” In sleep-deprived women, on the other hand, leptin – “the satiety signal” – is suppressed. But the result is the same: overeating.
It’s not just about ghrelin and leptin. “I always tell people that we don’t necessarily eat because we’re hungry, right? People have many reasons to eat, and eat despite lack of hunger,” says St-Onge. She says our brain reward centres are affected by how much sleep we’ve had the night before, and the “hedonic signals – the things that make food more appealing – tend to be more intense after a period of short sleep. So you’re more susceptible to reaching for appetising or pleasurable foods.” Who hasn’t chosen the pain au chocolat over the porridge after a bad night?
Does this mean poor sleep will make me gain weight?
In the long term, it certainly increases the likelihood. “Studies show that people who regularly sleep less than six hours tend to gain more weight over time, and increasing sleep to seven or eight hours can help with appetite regulation,” says Campbell. As well as disrupted hunger hormones, there are a number of explanations. “Observational studies show those who don’t get enough sleep tend to eat less fruit and vegetables, more sugar, less protein and less fibre. Staying up late at night also means that you might get peckish and be more tempted to snack. And when tired, we may be less motivated to be active and to cook from scratch, relying more on quick, less nutritious foods and fizzy, sugary drinks.”
Does the time I go to bed affect what I eat the next day?
![Young woman waking up in bed, stretching, smiling](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f178c905c9f29b7de08a915f74f92e674f8f433e/846_0_6726_5381/master/6726.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Most of the research focus is on chronotype [your body’s natural preference of when to sleep and wake] – if you have a late chronotype versus an earlier chronotype,” says St-Onge. So is it better to be an early bird or a night owl? “Typically, people with earlier chronotypes tend to have more healthful diets and exercise more,” she says. Plus, “people who have an earlier chronotype have an easier time getting adequate sleep duration because their sleep is more aligned with the societal clock”. Unfortunately for late risers, chronotypes are thought to be largely genetic.
I do shift work – how can I eat and sleep well?
“Shift workers report less healthy diets compared with day workers, and shift work is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes,” says Campbell. She suggests “eating the main meal before a night shift, and choosing lighter, nutrient-rich foods overnight”. This is easier said than done, says St-Onge. “It’s difficult because it’s a whole culture that needs to change – people tend to bring in treats to have in the middle of the night.”
Should I take magnesium?
![Hands holding a variety of supplement pills in various shapes, colours and sizes](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9e80fb88069b2f220c2a04c142c8b3dfab273db2/0_0_4791_3833/master/4791.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Try science-backed sleep strategies first, focusing on regularity, timing, temperature and lighting,” says Gill.
Campbell agrees: “Rather than looking to supplements, it’s more helpful to look at the bigger picture. Take a look at sleep routine, stress levels, alcohol and caffeine intake, activity levels, and any underlying health issues that might be affecting rest, such as sleep apnoea, menopause symptoms or frequent night-time waking.”
If you’ve sorted your diet, exercise, sleep hygiene and general health, however, there is some weak evidence that magnesium may help. “Observational studies have linked magnesium with sleep-promoting effects, whereas limited gold-standard trials report mixed results,” says Gill. “A recent randomised controlled trial in adults with self-reported poor sleep quality supplemented with magnesium glycinate found modest improvements in insomnia severity. Another study showed that supplementation with magnesium threonate improved sleep quality and daytime alertness in people with self-reported sleep problems.”
Do I need added vitamins?
B vitamins and vitamin D are also commonly believed to help with sleep – are supplements advisable? “B vitamins are abundant in the diet – typically, people don’t have any deficiencies in those,” says St-Onge. “Vitamin D is something that could be problematic, especially if you don’t drink fortified dairy products. We can produce vitamin D from sunlight, but in some populations the sun is not sufficient, so that could be something that could be supplemented.” In the UK, government advice is to consider taking vitamin D in autumn and winter.
What about melatonin?
“Melatonin is a hormone that helps regulate the body’s sleep-wake cycles,” says Gill. “It’s often called the ‘hormone of darkness’ because its levels increase as evening approaches, signalling to your brain and body that it’s time for sleep. Rather than acting like an on-off switch, melatonin works more like a dimmer switch – preparing your body for sleep without directly causing it.” So should insomniacs take supplements? “Melatonin supplements are most effective for shifting the timing of your sleep, rather than as a routine, everyday sleep aid,” says Gill. “Melatonin can also be really helpful for managing jet lag. When used at the right time, melatonin can help fool the brain into thinking it’s night-time.”
summary: Recent research highlights the significant connection between diet, meal timing, and sleep quality. Eating a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet rich in plants, lean proteins, and specific nutrients can support better rest, while ultra-processed foods, caffeine, and alcohol can disrupt it. Additionally, poor sleep negatively alters hunger hormones and brain reward centers, often leading to increased calorie intake and weight gain the following day.
key_points: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in fruit, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats is closely linked to better sleep.
Consuming ultra-processed foods, high-glycemic foods, and caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime can impair sleep quality and continuity.
Waiting two to three hours after a meal before going to bed helps prevent digestion issues and acid reflux.
Sleep deprivation alters appetite hormones like ghrelin and leptin, causing sleep-deprived individuals to consume more calories and crave high-fat or sugary foods.

title: Cancer survivors living with chemo hair loss celebrate resilience
author: Nicola Bryan
content:
![Rhiannon looking into the camera with a thoughtful expression on her face. She is almost completely bald.  She has a silver hoop nose ring and silver heart stud earrings.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/8707/live/b0f024f0-a097-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.jpg)
Rhiannon is one of 11 Welsh women who have been photographed for The Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD campaign
- Published
When Rhiannon Thomas lost her hair during chemotherapy just weeks after having a mastectomy, her confidence was at an all time low.
But being photographed for a campaign that celebrates the resilience of women living with breast cancer helped her find an inner strength she never knew she had.
"For the first time I feel I look pretty, I look confident and strong," said the 36-year-old mum.
"It's surprising the strength you find when you go through such a hard time."
![Rhiannon is wearing pajamas and sitting in a chair in hospital holding two cuddly toys.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/addd/live/5bf4de00-a61e-11f1-bb6f-e5db02d232fa.jpg)
Rhiannon Thomas recently completed her chemotherapy
Rhiannon, a mother to two daughters aged 14 and nine, was diagnosed with breast cancer after finding a lump while in the shower in November last year.
"I had an absolute breakdown," said the teaching assistant.
"Like, how do you tell your children? I was so scared to just tell them."
Since then she's had a mastectomy, chemotherapy and is currently having radiotherapy.
When her hair began falling out during chemotherapy she decided to shave her head, but wanted to make it as positive an experience as possible for her children.
She encouraged her youngest to play at being a hairdresser and do whatever she wanted with a scissors before getting the shaver out.
"I was like, 'just cut whatever you want because it's going anyway'," said Rhiannon.
"I wanted to make something hard joyful for my children and for myself because I didn't want them to see me upset, and my daughter loved it."
![Rhiannon, her partner and two daughters standing in front of a Christmas tree.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/7da8/live/562aef00-a61e-11f1-bb6f-e5db02d232fa.jpg)
When Rhiannon was diagnosed with beast cancer her first thought was her children
Footage captured on her phone shows the family laughing at home in Abertridwr, near Caerphilly, as her daughter gets creative with the scissors.
But afterwards, in private moments, the radical change to her appearance was hard.
"I remember looking in the mirror and like just crying because it's just you know we don't recognise yourself," she said.
Rhiannon was brought to tears recalling the look on her parents' faces when they first saw her after her head had been shaved.
She took to wearing a head wrap whenever she left the house.
![Sam has her face in her hands and looks into the camera. She is bald, wearing a black T-shirt and has a tattoo on her forearm.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3866/live/3c175e60-a776-11f1-993c-a325009c1935.jpg)
Sam Gronow-Walters says she is proud of her portraits
All this sounds very familiar to mental health nurse and mother-of-two Sam Gronow-Walters.
The 44-year-old has also lost her hair though breast cancer treatment.
Her cancer is incurable.
She was first diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer, external five years ago, which was successfully treated with intravenous chemotherapy, a lumpectomy and radiotherapy, followed by oral chemotherapy.
But seven months later she found another lump and tests showed it had returned.
A mastectomy followed and she was told she was cancer-free.
In 2024, she was told it had spread to her lung. Last July, tests showed it had spread to her liver and lymph nodes.
"You've got to keep going," said Sam from St Athan in the Vale of Glamorgan.
"You've just got to do whatever you can because I want to see my kids grow up."
![Sam is in profile and running her hand over her bald head. She is wearing a black T-shirt and has a tattoo on her forearm.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9396/live/406b9d50-a776-11f1-993c-a325009c1935.jpg)
Sam was diagnosed with breast cancer five years ago
Like Rhiannon, when she felt she had no option other than to shave her head, Sam's thoughts were immediately how to make it easier on her children, a daughter aged 20 and a son aged 13.
Her son requested she have her head shaved with a bit left at the front in homage to Brazilian footballer Ronaldo's memorable hairdo at the 2002 World Cup - and she obliged.
"To me that that's quite a happy memory, so he'll see that even when I'm poorly I can still have fun, can still smile and I can still make my children happy and laugh," she said.
Again, she was concerned about the impact her new appearance would have on her children.
"I used to ask my son when I took him to school, 'do you mind if I don't wear a hat?'" recalled Sam.
"He was like, 'why would I care?'."
![Sam and her son after having her head shaved. Her young son  is wearing a football kit. She has just hair at the front of her head remaining and is wearing a black hairdressing cape.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/b176/live/62445f10-a83f-11f1-b3a7-d5de760fef6e.jpg)
Sam agreed to have her hair styled like Brazilian footballer Ronaldo's memorable hairdo in the 2002 World Cup finals
Rhiannon and Sam first met after signing up to be part of breast cancer charity Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD Wales campaign.
The project celebrates the courage and confidence of women who have lost their hair through breast cancer.
Alongside nine other Welsh women they spent a day in Cardiff being photographed by Dutch photographer Caroline Sikkenk.
The photos will be displayed at London's Piccadilly Lights next month.
![Sam at an event with her husband and children. They are all smiling. She is wearing a black and white print top and has a blonde bob.Her son and husband are wearing white shirts and ties. Her daughter has long blonde hair and is wearing a red top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/5e4b/live/6b717aa0-a5ec-11f1-8348-fb0cb1cd9761.jpg)
Sam says her husband and children help her stay positive
Both women had been nervous about being photographed but said the experience couldn't have been more joyful.
"It was like we'd all known each other before meeting that day, and we still keep in touch now," said Sam.
Rhiannon had never spoken to another women who had lost her hair during cancer treatment.
"I just felt really safe and not judged," she said.
![Rhiannon and Sam standing on a residential street, smiling at the camera. Both have bald heads. Rhiannon is wearing a white T-shirt and Sam is wearing a black and white print dress.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/2a74/live/bcaf3cc0-a5e9-11f1-a019-f3ea5e194221.jpg)
Rhiannon, Sam and the other women who took part in the campaign have stayed in touch after the photoshoot
Seeing the photos for the first time was emotional for both.
"I was like, 'oh wow'," said Rhiannon, who was proud of the courage it had taken to be photographed at such a vulnerable time.
Sam barely recognised herself.
"I was like, 'wow, that's not me'," she said.
"I was quite proud to show them to my family to say, 'oh, this is me'."
![Lisa has her arm around Rhiannon and both are looking at the camera and smiling.  Lisa has spiky bright pink hair and her head shaved at the sides. She is wearing a white T-shirt.  Rhiannon is bald and wearing a denim jacket.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/1617/live/e2c47e80-a5e8-11f1-a019-f3ea5e194221.jpg)
Lisa Allen from The Pink Ribbon Foundation, on the right pictured with Rhiannon, says a community has grown around the project
BOLD began in 2022, when Lisa Allen from The Pink Ribbon Foundation met photographer Caroline Sikkenk at a breast cancer conference.
Caroline had spent years photographing women who had experienced hair loss through illness.
"What struck us about her photographs was that these women weren't being shown as patients," said Lisa. "They were strong, beautiful and completely themselves."
The first BOLD shoot took place in 2023.
"What we hadn't anticipated was that we would create a community," said Lisa.
She said the impact often began before a photograph has been taken.
"We set up a WhatsApp group beforehand, so by the time the women arrive they already feel they're going through it together.
"The friendships and support that grow around it last long after the photograph is taken."
Both women said taking part in the project had given them a new-found strength and sense of optimism.
"I feel like my confidence and my positivity just got stronger from the photo shoot," said Rhiannon.
"I walked out of there just so confident and I felt so free and just like I don't have to hide."
Gone are the head wraps and proudly showing her shaved head has become "the new normal".
For Sam, the photoshoot helped her find self-acceptance.
"This is me now - I wouldn't have long hair again," she said.
"Hair loss doesn't define who I am. It's just a symbol that I'm getting through this and I am strong."
If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.
summary: Eleven Welsh breast cancer survivors, including Rhiannon Thomas and Sam Gronow-Walters, participated in The Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD campaign to celebrate resilience despite experiencing hair loss from chemotherapy. The campaign involves portraits taken by Dutch photographer Caroline Sikkenk, which will be displayed at London's Piccadilly Lights. Participating in the project fostered a supportive community and helped both women find newfound confidence, strength, and self-acceptance.
key_points: Rhiannon Thomas and Sam Gronow-Walters are two Welsh mothers living with breast cancer who lost their hair during chemotherapy treatments.
Both women intentionally turned their head-shaving moments into playful experiences to ease the emotional impact on their children.
The BOLD campaign, organized by The Pink Ribbon Foundation and photographer Caroline Sikkenk, celebrates the resilience and strength of women experiencing hair loss from illness.
Portraits of the 11 Welsh women from the campaign are set to be displayed at London's Piccadilly Lights.
Participating in the project created a lasting support community that helped the women build confidence and embrace their new normal.

title: Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months
author: Andrew Gregory
content:
A genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure alive for a record nine months and successfully acted as a “bridge” to a human transplant in a world first.
Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list.
Kidney transplantation provides the best survival and quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease, but global demand for human organs far exceeds supply.
Surgeons in the US successfully transplanted a kidney from Wilma, a Yucatan miniature pig, into Andrews, after genetically engineering it to be compatible with his immune system.
The kidney kept Andrews free of dialysis for a record nine months, the longest period ever recorded, before it began failing and he received one from a dead human donor. It was also the first time a pig’s kidney had been used as a temporary “bridge” to a human transplant.
Details of the breakthrough, which offers hope to millions of people whose kidneys have failed, were published in the Lancet medical journal.
Andrews, from New Hampshire, described the pig kidney transplant as a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” He was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog, Cupcake, he said.
![Surgeons in blue surgical gowns, with back to the camera, are gathered around the patient during the procedure](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6ea68ef7e5688e00a970bbae2341b0e1768fd641/0_0_4800_3202/master/4800.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Transplanting genetically engineered pig organs has long been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. But the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days when the patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft survival beyond two months, according to the Lancet.
Before the transplant in January 2025, Wilma the pig had received 69 edits to her genome. Some of these were designed to dodge viruses that might pose a risk to humans, while others made the organ more compatible with humans, reducing the odds of immune rejection.
The team behind the transplant at Mass General Brigham, a non-profit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, said Andrews successfully lived with the genetically edited kidney for 271 days before receiving a human kidney from a donor.
His case represents the longest dialysis-free survival following pig kidney xenotransplantation in a living human, and the world’s first transition to human kidney transplantation, the team said.
“The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” said Dr Leonardo Riella, of the Center for Transplantation Sciences and the Division of Nephrology at Mass General Brigham. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.
“Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap – initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right.”
![Andrews sits in a chair sipping a drink from a paper cup, as Brodner kneels in front of him](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2884b597acd0172ead0b8958c88934b392413273/0_0_4800_3202/master/4800.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
After roughly six months, damage developed in the pig kidney’s blood vessels which progressed to organ failure and the kidney was removed nine months after transplantation.
After several months back on dialysis, Andrews received a kidney from a dead human donor, which worked well during six months of follow-up, according to the Lancet.
There were no new antibodies against human tissue detected, indicating the pig kidney had not made it harder for the human kidney transplant to work successfully. No pig viruses or other pig pathogens were detected at any point.
The team cautioned that this was a single patient with no comparison group, and that the outcome reflected careful patient selection and intensive specialist care that may not be available elsewhere.
Further clinical trials such as the one Andrews participated in will be needed. But the success opens the door to pig kidney transplants as a bridge for other people facing long waits for a human kidney, they said.
“The patients are the true pioneers here,” Riella said. “By stepping forward and being willing to participate in these early stage studies, they are advancing the science. Without their trust and courage, we would not be able to do what we do.”
summary: A genetically modified pig kidney successfully kept a 66-year-old end-stage kidney disease patient alive for a record nine months without dialysis. The procedure served as a world-first temporary bridge to a subsequent human kidney transplant after the animal organ began failing. Details of the breakthrough, performed by a team at Mass General Brigham, were published in the Lancet medical journal.
key_points: Tim Andrews received a kidney from a genetically engineered Yucatan miniature pig named Wilma, which had 69 genomic edits.
The pig kidney functioned successfully for 271 days, marking the longest dialysis-free survival following a xenotransplantation in a living human.
After the pig kidney began to fail due to blood vessel damage, Andrews successfully received a kidney from a human donor.
Researchers noted that xenotransplantation could help address the global shortage of human organs by acting as a bridge for patients waiting for human transplants.

title: Alzheimer’s drug to be offered to people without symptoms in bid to prevent onset
author: Holly Bancroft
content:
An Alzheimer’s drug will be offered to people without symptoms who are at high risk of the disease in an NHS trial that is unique in Europe.
The trial will give the drug Trontinemab to those at high risk of Alzheimer’s to see if the disease can be delayed or prevented, it has been reported.
Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust are the first in Europe to join the trial, which will recruit 1,600 healthy adults aged 55 and 80 internationally, the BBC said.
Participants from the UK will be tested to make sure they are not showing signs of memory loss, and will also under go a blood test to see if they have p-tau217 - a biomarker that can predict the development of Alzheimer’s.
The drug Trontinemab, which has been developed by Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche, is delivered into the vein directly through an IV bag.
It targets amyloid plaques, which are build-up of amyloid protein that clumps in the brain, the Alzheimer’s Society said.
The build-up of this protein can slow down brain cell function, and eventually kill them, the charity said.
Previous trial results published by Roche show that trontinemab can clear amyloid in patients.
Professor Ramin Nilforooshan, chief investigator for the trial, told The Telegraph: “For decades, research has focused on treating Alzheimer’s disease after symptoms appear.
“PrevenTron (the name of the trial) addresses a different question - whether we can act earlier, before symptoms begin.”
He added there was still uncertainty about the treatment, saying: “I’m not saying this trial is magic. It’s an investigational medicine. We need to wait and see: will it work or not?”
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia in the UK and it is a progressive condition, meaning the symptoms get gradually worse over time.
It is most common in people over the age of 65, and affects an estimated one in 14 people over this age, according to the NHS.
This rises to one in six people over the age of 80. There are estimated to be 982,000 people with dementia in the UK, the Alzheimer’s Society says.
summary: An NHS trial is offering the Alzheimer's drug Trontinemab to healthy high-risk individuals without symptoms to test if the disease can be delayed or prevented. The international trial, named PrevenTron, involves recruiting 1,600 adults aged 55 to 80 who will be screened for memory loss and the p-tau217 biomarker. Developed by Roche, the intravenous drug targets amyloid plaques in the brain that disrupt cell function.
key_points: Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust is the first in Europe to join the international PrevenTron trial.
The trial will recruit 1,600 healthy adults aged 55 to 80 who show no signs of memory loss.
Participants will undergo blood tests to check for p-tau217, a biomarker that can predict Alzheimer's development.
The drug Trontinemab, developed by Roche, targets and clears amyloid plaques in the brain.
Previous research focused on treating Alzheimer's after symptoms appeared, whereas this trial aims to act earlier.

title: Cardiff student who 'brushed off' sore throat developed sepsis
author: Catriona Aitken; Nelli Bird
content:
![A girl with curly dark hair, wearing a white dress and black graduation cap and gown. She is stood in front of a flowerbed of pink flowers, with trees and people in the background, and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/788/cpsprodpb/746d/live/f6018bc0-a96a-11f1-b850-096ea2f533db.jpg)
Elle Black was in her first year at Cardiff University when she developed sepsis as a complication of quinsy
- Published
When Elle Black woke up the morning after a night out in February 2024, she felt dreadful.
The 21-year-old, who was in her first year at Cardiff University, believed her sore throat and flu-like symptoms were a hangover and initially "brushed it off".
But the following day she was being treated in hospital for sepsis, external, a serious reaction to an infection which can be life-threatening. Doctors told her if she had waited another day things could have been "quite different".
Elle is now urging other young people to be aware of the symptoms of sepsis, while the charity Sepsis Research said it was important to never dismiss symptoms that are severe or getting worse.
"I got home in the early hours of the morning and the back of my throat started to hurt, which I thought was strange because I didn't have any other symptoms yet," recalled Elle, who graduated this summer with a degree in journalism, media and culture.
"I took some ibuprofen, shrugged it off, went to sleep. I woke up the next day absolutely exhausted, no energy, really high fever."
![Two girls sat in the stands at a rugby stadium, smiling at the camera and holding pints. The one on the left is brunette, the other blonde, and they are both wearing black puffer jackets.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1408/cpsprodpb/c1ca/live/fc097730-a843-11f1-b3a7-d5de760fef6e.jpg)
Elle (left) had been out enjoying the Six Nations with friends before she fell ill
Elle, who is originally from Warwickshire, went to get brunch with her parents as planned, but "alarm bells were ringing" because her tonsils were swollen and she was unable to eat, so she booked a private GP appointment for later that day.
The doctor diagnosed her with laryngitis, external and prescribed antibiotics.
"I was so drowsy, so confused, almost delirious," she recalled.
She said she did not remember much about the following day, but has been told she called her mum and said "I can't feel my legs".
"I got to hospital, triaged within 15 minutes, it was all amazingly quick."
![A girl with long dark hair in two plaits. She is wearing a grey hoodie and has one arm raised above her head with an IV needle in it. She is wearing glasses, and is smiling as she looks at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/bc7c/live/9afdcf80-a849-11f1-80f8-c33181935c5a.jpg)
Elle spent two days in hospital receiving IV antibiotics
Elle had developed quinsy, external - a complication of tonsillitis where a pus-filled abscess grows between your tonsils and the wall of your throat - which turned into sepsis, external.
She spent two days at the University Hospital of Wales (UHW) but went on to "make a full recovery", which she credits to attending hospital quickly, telling staff she believed she had sepsis, and a fast-acting medical team.
"[The doctors] said if I'd left it another day, it could have been quite different," said Elle.
"You don't really hear about sepsis in this context," she added.
"It was strange for my parents to hear this had happened to their daughter. My mum says it's the scariest thing she's ever gone through.
"They didn't expect me to look so dreadful, they'd never seen my like that. I was completely pale, clammy. They are quite traumatised by it."
She added: "I was exhausted for a couple of weeks after and I was a little bit out for it for a couple of months, just really tired, it does take it out of you. But, other than that, I'm OK.
"They acted quickly and I got to the hospital quickly, but it's so different for everyone."
What is sepsis and what are the symptoms?
Sepsis is a serious reaction to an infection that can be life-threatening which develops very quickly.
Common symptoms are:
- A high fever, or swinging between feeling very hot and very cold
- Inability to keep food or fluids down
- Extreme drowsiness or difficulty staying awake
- Intense or unusual muscle pain
- A sore throat or tonsillitis that suddenly worsens
- A feeling that something is seriously wrong
![A family of four stood in a row with a pink flowerbed and trees behind them, all smiling and looking at the camera. Left to right: a middle-aged man with grey hair wearing a white shirt and grey suit jacket; a young woman with long dark hair wearing a white dress and black graduaiton cap and gown; a young woman with long dark hair wearing a yellow floral-patterned dress and sunglasses on her head; and a middle-aged woman wiht short brown hair, wearing a pink and white paisley-pattern dress and sunglasses on her head.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/b6e1/live/14bd8640-a849-11f1-834b-c1f68897b4b3.jpg)
Elle graduated this summer and says she hopes sharing the experience which "traumatised" her family will encourage other students to seek medical advice
In the UK, there are 48,000 sepsis related deaths each year, according to the UK Sepsis Trust., external
The charity Sepsis Research said the condition "rarely announces itself clearly".
"It often develops from infections that seem familiar and manageable, which is why it can be so easily overlooked," it added.
"Drowsiness, nausea, exhaustion and feeling generally dreadful after a night out are symptoms many students might put down to alcohol, lack of sleep or freshers' flu.
"Elle's experience shows why it is so important not to dismiss symptoms that are severe, getting worse, or feel out of proportion to what you would normally expect."
Elle will be running the London Marathon for the charity Sepsis Research next year, and is urging anyone who thinks a hangover might be something more to seek medical advice.
"With something as dangerous as sepsis, there's not too many stories where it's OK and it all works out. It's just so scary how fast it is.
"It really does put things into perspective. It's not always a hangover, sometimes it's something worse."
More top stories
