  - Published1 day ago
 ![A mound of soil and earth in a field. A woman looks up at it](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/2acc/live/0ae9b080-a885-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.jpg)
- ![Rob Brydon smiling at the camera. He had brown hair and wearing a brown jacket. There's a big pink butterfly sign behind him with Dolly written in yellow.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/148d/live/97a28e60-a87c-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.jpg)
summary: Elle Black, a Cardiff University student, initially mistook the severe sore throat and flu-like symptoms of quinsy and sepsis for a hangover. After rapidly deteriorating and becoming delirious, she spent two days receiving intravenous antibiotics at the University Hospital of Wales and has since made a full recovery. She is now urging other young people not to dismiss severe or worsening symptoms as mere hangovers or freshers' flu.
key_points: Elle Black developed sepsis as a complication of quinsy during her first year at Cardiff University.
She initially dismissed her high fever, exhaustion, and sore throat as a hangover from a night out.
Doctors told her that waiting another day to seek treatment could have resulted in a life-threatening outcome.
The charity Sepsis Research emphasizes the importance of not ignoring symptoms that are severe or disproportionate to expectations.
Elle plans to run the London Marathon for Sepsis Research to raise awareness about the condition.

title: Essex mum thought she would die from maternal sepsis
author: Alice Cunningham
content:
![A woman in a selfie-style image who is smiling at the camera. She has wavey blonde hair and she is standing in front of a brick wall.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/d81d/live/a2f9e510-a92b-11f1-bb81-8fbd2d2d397c.jpg)
Poppy Gibson was pregnant when she first started to feel unwell and was later found to have sepsis
- Published
Poppy Gibson had only just given birth when she thought she was going to die.
Eleven years ago, while pregnant with her second baby, she developed pain in her side which doctors thought could be the baby putting pressure on her lung.
Doctors then feared Poppy, from Rayleigh in Essex, was ill with pneumonia and decided to induce her at 36 weeks.
While her baby was healthy, her condition worsened and after suffering from seizures, doctors realised she had sepsis, with her husband Richard told to prepare for the worst.
"I can still remember overhearing the doctor... he told my husband to prepare for death," the now 36-year-old said.
"Although I couldn't communicate, I remember looking at him and he was crying, and he never cried.
"I just thought, I know he'll take care of my boys for me."
She has only been able to talk about her experience in the past two years and for September's Sepsis Awareness Month, she shared her story to raise awareness of the illness that can affect anyone.
![A woman sits in a chair with a baby lying on her lap looking up toward her. The woman has red hair that has been tied back and she is wearing a pink T-shirt. She has various medical tubes attached to her hand. The baby wears a multi-coloured babygrow.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/65c2/live/97fba890-a784-11f1-b2d5-535b3b3d379f.jpg)
Poppy also had hallucinations including one where she imagined she had given birth in a medical tent in the desert
At about 34 weeks pregnant, Poppy began experiencing shortness of breath and said "something felt different" compared with her previous pregnancy.
An X-ray found a shadow on her left lung.
"I'm only 5ft so it could have just been the strain on the body, but they were worried that it either could be from compression from carrying a large baby, (or) it could be pneumonia," she explained.
Poppy was given pneumonia medication, but nine days postpartum, she went into septic shock and had seizures.
![A man and woman take a selfie with the camera angled slightly below them. The man has dark hair and a dark beard. He is wearing a grey T-shirt. The woman has blonde hair that has been tied up.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/a596/live/876a46a0-a921-11f1-b98a-59841fe45d46.jpg)
Poppy told her husband Richard to look after their children if she died from sepsis
An MRI revealed an abscess on her left kidney that had become septic and it was drained while she also had two blood transfusions.
She described knowing she might die as "terrifying".
"When I finally started feeling better, I wasn't the person that I was when I went in," she continued.
"My milk supply had dried up and when [my baby] could finally come visit, he was a stranger."
Poppy said the hardest part had been her mental recovery. She still worried about even minor cuts for herself and her children.
![A man and woman with their arms around each other smile at the camera. Behind them is a park area with a pond. The man has short grey hair and is wearing a blue shirt with white shorts. The woman has blonde hair with some pink dye in the ends. She wears a white T-shirt, floral scarf and blue jeans. She is also wearing sunglasses.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/039f/live/8ae95d60-a783-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Sue Puddefoot was close to death after contracting sepsis twice with her husband Mark stating it was touch and go
Three years ago, Sue Puddefoot, 62, from Saxmundham, Suffolk, went into Ipswich Hospital for a hip replacement.
Surgery went well and she recalled still feeling pain around her hip, but the doctors said she could go home.
Her husband Mark noticed she looked "absolutely awful" and doctors decided to test for an infection where her blood markers came back extremely high.
Doctors believed she had suffered a septic shower, where bacteria or toxins from an infected site are released into the bloodstream, rapidly triggering sepsis.
Due to being so unwell, Sue missed her son's wedding.
"It's really strange because I don't think it's actually hit me, it didn't hit me what I'd been through and the severity of it," she said.
Sue recovered, but quickly went downhill again, feeling very cold and shaking despite a normal temperature.
Doctors believed she had a second septic shower and Mark said "it had been very touch and go".
She had seven blood transfusions and years on she suffered from some memory loss and struggled to regulate her body temperature.
"I hadn't known anyone that had sepsis before," Sue said.
"It's worrying that there's so many people that haven't heard of it."
![A graphic showing the signs of Sepsis](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/7bd3/live/739e0650-034c-11f1-b7e1-afb6d0884c18.png)
According to the UK Sepsis Trust charity, sepsis affects about 245,000 people a year causing 48,000 deaths each year.
It occurs when the body overreacts to an infection or an injury, and it starts to damage its own tissues and organs.
It can affect anyone and in adults symptoms include, external slurred speech or confusion, shivering, passing no urine in a day and feeling like you are going to die.
In children they could have very fast breathing, be convulsing, be very lethargic or have a rash that does not fade when you press it.
Meanwhile maternal sepsis, which develops during pregnancy, childbirth or in the months following, has a 10% mortality rate in the UK, external.
![A woman with brown curled hair smiles at the camera. She is wearing a dark top and the background behind her is blurred.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/60d1/live/fbfce560-a785-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Amy Breslin, a maternal sepsis specialist, said it was able to mask itself extremely well as other conditions
Amy Breslin is a midwife and a maternal medicine consultant for the UK Sepsis Trust. She said maternal sepsis typically masks itself extremely well.
She said it could be difficult for mothers to know what was normal and what was not, but stressed it was OK to signal when they felt unwell.
"We really want people to be able to trust their instincts and act quickly," she said.
"So whether you're pregnant, have had a miscarriage or termination, given birth recently or if you feel seriously unwell, don't assume that it's part of what you're going through, and just ask, 'Could it be sepsis?'."
Prof Ramani Moonesinghe, NHS England's deputy medical director, said it was "vital" the NHS had an "ambitious plan" to tackle the illness and urged everyone to be aware of the signs.
"Key to tackling sepsis is catching it early â the longer sepsis goes undetected the less chance a person has to survive or make a full recovery," she added.
"That's why the NHS will be trialling new wearable devices that will allow people's vital signs to be monitored at home â so that if they deteriorate, they can get tested and treated faster."
Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.
summary: Poppy Gibson developed maternal sepsis following the birth of her second child, an ordeal that left her with lasting mental and physical recovery challenges. Sue Puddefoot also suffered from severe sepsis twice following a hip replacement surgery, resulting in ongoing health issues. Experts highlight the importance of early detection, noting that sepsis affects approximately 245,000 people a year in the UK and can mask itself as other conditions.
key_points: Poppy Gibson was induced at 36 weeks due to suspected pneumonia before going into septic shock and suffering seizures from an abscess on her kidney.
Sue Puddefoot suffered two separate bouts of sepsis involving septic showers following a hip replacement surgery.
Sepsis affects about 245,000 people in the UK annually and causes 48,000 deaths.
Maternal sepsis has a 10% mortality rate in the UK and can easily mask itself as other pregnancy-related conditions.
The NHS plans to trial new wearable devices to monitor vital signs at home for faster sepsis detection and treatment.

title: Wakefield boy starts school after spending Christmas in coma
author: David Spereall
content:
![A four-year-old boy stands against the black front door of a house. He is wearing a school uniform, comprising a blue jumper and a white polo shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/81af/live/241e0440-a7a7-11f1-a7ad-37a1f7dc081c.jpg)
Oliver started primary school earlier this week
- Published
A four-year-old boy has started school this week, less than a year after he spent Christmas in a coma.
Oliver, from Wakefield, was in Leeds General Infirmary for five months after he was diagnosed with a type of blood cancer in 2025.
Despite the brutal side effects he suffered, doctors managed to successfully treat Oliver and he is now in remission, having left hospital on New Year's Day.
The young pupil's mum, Cora, said it was "extra special" watching her son start his reception year.
Oliver fell ill on Mother's Day last year and was subsequently diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, which had affected his abdomen, spine, brain fluid, kidneys, and liver.
He underwent intensive chemotherapy, which left him with red-raw ulcers on his mouth and a depleted immune system, which meant he had to be kept in isolation.
![A small boy lying in a hospital bed with a tube protruding from his nose. He is wearing an orange t-shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1fd3/live/4bdeb6a0-a7a7-11f1-a7ad-37a1f7dc081c.jpg)
Oliver spent five months in hospital
Cora, 33, said: "Last year was absolute hell. The cancer snatched so much away from Oliver and from all of us.
"We went from having an energetic little boy who loved trains and going to the park, to watching our son puffed up with steroids, losing the ability to walk and at one point stuck in a coma for a month, desperately fighting to stay alive."
Although he needed physiotherapy to help him walk again and his sight has been permanently affected, Oliver is now cancer-free.
Cora added: "Every parent gets emotional about their child starting school, but it is extra special seeing how excited Oliver is to make friends and learn how to read and write. We'll never take moments like this for granted."
![Two women and a small boy sit in a fast-food restaurant eating. They are all smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/068b/live/464e7700-a830-11f1-b808-43cdd10f38ce.jpg)
Oliver enjoys spending time with his parents, Cora and Helen
Cora and Oliver's other mum, Helen, said they wanted to share their family's story as part of a Blood Cancer UK campaign, which is highlighting the special moments the disease can take away, as well as the ones made possible due to successful treatments.
Symptoms of blood cancer can include fatigue, unexplained bruising, recurring infections, and pains in the bones and joints.
Matthew White, the charity's director of engagement, said: "We want to showcase the amazing resilience of those who adapt to these moments or celebrate once they have come through treatment, and to pay tribute to the researchers who are helping people recover from cancer or live a better quality of life.
"We want to raise awareness so people understand the devastating impact it can have and support us to fund the research that gives children like Oliver a future."
summary: A four-year-old boy from Wakefield named Oliver has started primary school, less than a year after spending Christmas in a coma following a blood cancer diagnosis. After undergoing intensive treatment, including five months in the hospital, he is now in remission. His mothers shared his story as part of a Blood Cancer UK campaign highlighting the impact of the disease and the importance of successful treatments.
key_points: Oliver was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma last year and spent five months in Leeds General Infirmary.
He endured a month-long coma, intensive chemotherapy, and required physiotherapy to learn how to walk again.
Oliver is now cancer-free, in remission, and has started his reception year at primary school.
His family shared their experience to support a Blood Cancer UK campaign raising awareness of the disease.

title: Families hit by long waits for dementia diagnosis
author: Dominic Hughes; Camilla Horrox
content:
![A picture of a father and son. The younger man wears a pale grey shirt and the older man wears a navy shirt with his arms crossed. Both look relaxed and happy.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/768/cpsprodpb/4cf8/live/ca44b320-a615-11f1-9a0e-e95c171695e2.jpg)
Michael Fathon with his father, Jim, who was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease at the age of 69 in 2022
- Published
Hundreds of families say they have had to wait months or even years for a dementia diagnosis for a loved one.
Such long delays have an impact on their own work, finances and mental health, a survey for the Alzheimer's Society charity reveals.
The charity is calling for a national standard that would mean someone with dementia would receive an accurate diagnosis within 18 weeks of being seen and referred by a GP.
That would put dementia on a similar footing as other major health conditions, including cancer.
"He could have had medication sooner"
Michael Fethon says his dad, Jim, waited 18 months from their initial appointment with a GP before being diagnosed.
It was a delay that took its toll on Jim - and on Michael, who eventually had to give up his job to care for his dad.
"I think my dad felt beside himself because he was experiencing symptoms. It wasn't just memory loss."
Michael says his father struggled to drive, shop and, eventually, even to walk.
"It almost spiralled in that 18 months of his condition, gradually getting worse.
"If we'd have had a diagnosis sooner, he could have started medication sooner, and whilst the medication doesn't cure dementia, it acts to sort of slow it down and eliminate the severity of it."
Agonising waits
In the survey, more than a thousand families and carers of people living with dementia revealed that nearly half of them waited for more than six months for an accurate diagnosis after their first visit to a GP.
Michelle Dyson CB, of the Alzheimer's Society, says a diagnosis can really help families access support and plan for the future.
"Too many families spend months, and sometimes years, waiting for answers while their dementia progresses.
"It is like trying to plan a journey without knowing where you are going or when you will arrive.
"You would never accept someone being diagnosed with cancer and then left to work out the next steps on their own."
Dementia does not wait, and neither should diagnosis, she added.
![Two adults sit side by side in a restaurant booth, leaning slightly towards one another as they face the camera. The person on the left, Keith, wears rectangular glasses, a dark purple jumper and a checked shirt, while the person on the right, his wife Sue, wears glasses and a bright blue knitted sweater. The image is closely framed around the two seated figures.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/953e/live/5c8d6b20-a637-11f1-8438-7134607e7611.jpg)
Keith and Sue first met when they were 15, and have been married since 1969.
Sue's story
Keith and Sue Andrews first met when they were 15, and they've been married for 57 years.
Sue's condition has deteriorated so much that she now lives in a home.
Keith says they had to wait almost a year for a diagnosis, which was difficult.
He says life became more maneagable, once they knew for sure.
"I won't say it's easy, but you know where you're going, and you know where you're heading and you feel a lot more confident in what you're doing.
"Because you know you're doing the right thing, but before that diagnosis, you don't know if you're doing the right thing or what to do even.
"And it's a horrible time, a horrible time."
Like Keith, 9 out of 10 families surveyed said that a formal diagnosis made at least one aspect of life easier.
That included understanding symptoms and behaviour, supporting the person living with dementia, accessing information or speaking to healthcare professionals.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said:
"This Government is determined to strengthen the support that is available both to individuals affected by dementia, and the family members who look after them.
"We are bringing forward the timetable for Baroness Casey's commission on reform of the social care system, and we are appointing a new dementia tsar to help lead our work in that area, as recommended by Baroness Casey."
"We are also implementing a new action plan for unpaid carers to ensure that they receive the support and recognition they deserve for the selfless work they do."
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d048/live/80825d90-55a8-11f1-b682-cf91850925ea.png)
![A thin, grey banner promoting the News Daily newsletter. On the right, there is a graphic of an orange sphere with two concentric crescent shapes around it in a red-orange gradient, like a sound wave. The banner reads: âThe latest news in your inbox first thing.â](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/73cd/live/b1be3060-a697-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
summary: Hundreds of families face waits of months or years to receive a dementia diagnosis for their loved ones, negatively impacting work, finances, and mental health. A survey by the Alzheimer's Society reveals that nearly half of families wait more than six months for an accurate diagnosis. The charity is now calling for a national standard to ensure dementia diagnoses occur within 18 weeks of a GP referral, putting it on par with conditions like cancer.
key_points: Nearly half of surveyed families waited more than six months for an accurate dementia diagnosis after visiting a GP.
Long diagnostic delays negatively impact families' mental health, finances, and ability to work, according to the Alzheimer's Society survey.
The Alzheimer's Society is calling for a national standard to provide a dementia diagnosis within 18 weeks of GP referral.
Nine out of ten families reported that a formal diagnosis ultimately made at least one aspect of life easier.
The Department of Health and Social Care stated it is committed to strengthening support for individuals with dementia and their families.

title: Hartburn headteacher opens park after MND diagnosis
author: Jim Scott
content:
![Claire Park, who is in a wheelchair and wearing a floral dress, is next to her husband, Matthew. Together, they are holding silver metal scissors and are getting ready to cut a red ribbon, which is at the entrance of the new wooden playground. In the background is one of wooden fences, and a large shed.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/0d9f/live/4f0214a0-a881-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.png)
An ankle injury led to Claire Park's motor neurone disease diagnosis
- Published
A head teacher, whose ankle injury turned out to be motor neurone disease (MND), has fulfilled a dream to open an Â£89,000 playground at her former school.
Claire Park had to retire from Hartburn Primary School in Stockton after being told she has MND, a condition which causes muscle weakness, in January 2025.
Her husband Matthew likened the condition to a game of "whack-a-mole", with new health challenges appearing every day, but said the family remained positive.
Former colleagues, friends and businesses raised more than Â£100,000 to grant the former head's years-long wish to refurbish the playground, and provide funds for the awareness charity the MND Association.
![A photograph which shows Claire Park before her diagnosis. She is smiling and is standing between two pupils on each of her side who are wearing mortar boards and school uniform. Two of the girls, on the right of the picture, are blowing party whistles. They are all in front of a large blue sign which has several languages, welcoming people to the school.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/6d76/live/63ffebc0-a881-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.png)
Claire had been head teacher at the school since 2020
Speaking via artificial intelligence, which uses old recordings of her voice, she said she had wanted to open the park years before her diagnosis.
"When I was head teacher I had a vision for this space and wanted to create somewhere really special for our children," she said.
"That vision was something I cared deeply about, so to come back today to see it become a reality is especially special to me."
The playground features a shed, flower beds, climbing frames and astroturf and has been named Mrs Park's Park.
Jill Ellison, the school's chair of governors, said it was a "dream come true".
![A section of the new play park, which includes a bench around the trunk of a tree, six large boxes on top of wooden decking, and three main patches of astroturf linked by pebble-patterned paving. In the background is the school's existing play area which is separated with a low, metal green fence.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/34a5/live/838dec80-a881-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.png)
The new park cost about Â£89,000 which was fundraised by the community
Matthew Park said MND had been a "very difficult" disease to deal with.
"There's a new symptom, new challenge every day and we adjust, try and find a rhythm and then the next day there's another one that crops up that we have to adjust and deal with."
He said he no longer considered it a "rare disease" as it was clear "there's a lot of people affected".
summary: Claire Park, a former head teacher at Hartburn Primary School who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease in January 2025, has fulfilled a long-held dream by opening a new £89,000 school playground. Former colleagues, friends, and local businesses raised over £100,000 to fund both the playground—named Mrs Park's Park—and the MND Association. Speaking via an AI tool using recordings of her voice, Park expressed gratitude for seeing her vision become a reality.
key_points: Claire Park retired as head teacher of Hartburn Primary School following a motor neurone disease diagnosis in January 2025.
Community fundraising raised over £100,000 to build the £89,000 playground and support the MND Association.
The new playground, named Mrs Park's Park, features climbing frames, astroturf, a shed, and flower beds.
Park spoke at the opening ceremony using an artificial intelligence voice tool created from old recordings of her voice.

title: Warning issued as mosquitoes carrying Zika virus found breeding in London
author: Emily Bashforth
content:
![Dengue fever vector, mosquito biting hand.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_148501552-863f.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
An invasive mosquito species has been found breeding in some south east London homes.
The Aedes aegypti species is known to transmit viruses including dengue, chikungunya, and Zika.
This is the fourth time they’ve been detected in the UK in recent years, but the first time they’ve been identified as reproducing.
Consequently, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has increased surveillance and activities to trap and destroy the larvae.
Fortunately, the risk to the public is low, as, despite the five heatwaves we’ve had this year, health experts assure that the UK climate is too cold for the species to survive long-term.
There is currently no evidence of humans becoming infected by the insects.
![FILE - In this Jan. 27, 2016, file photo, an Aedes aegypti mosquito known to carry the Zika virus and the Dengue fever, is photographed through a microscope at the Fiocruz institute in Recife, Pernambuco state, Brazil. In a statement on Friday, Oct. 14, 2022, the European Medicines Agency is recommending that a dengue vaccine made by the Japanese pharmaceutical Takeda be authorized, in a move that could provide a new tool for millions worldwide against the potentially fatal disease. (AP Photo/Felipe Dana, File)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_129431206-cec9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Typically located in tropical and subtropical regions, the mosquitoes are believed to have been transported in baggage. They were found via the Mosquito Watch scheme, which compiles and detects reports of mosquito species in the UK.
Dr Jolyon Medlock, head of medical entomology at UKHSA, said: ‘There is no evidence that these mosquitoes have caused human infections, and importantly, to date, there is no evidence of the mosquitoes or larvae being detected in nearby public areas.’
The Nuffield Department of Medicine at the University of Oxford also called the finding ‘important’ but urged people not to be alarmed.
What is Aedes aegypti, and how can you recognise it?
Also known as the yellow fever mosquito, the Aedes aegypti species is dark-bodied and approximately four to seven millimetres in length.
You can recognise it by white bands on its legs and a lyre-shaped (a string instrument) white marking on the upper surface of its thorax.
Latest London news
- Met Police refuse to say if they are investigating London upskirting website
- Man, 32, dies after 'violent attack' at major London station
- Londoners can hail a limited Uber Wayve robotaxi after new trial starts
To get the latest news from the capital, visit Metro's London news hub.
![Insect repellent. Woman tourist applying mosquito repellent on hand during hike in nature. Skin protection against tick and mosquito bite](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_302821257-a330.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
It is native to North Africa but has become commonly invasive in other temperate regions.
The species prefers to rest in dark indoor spots, and eggs can survive for several months in dry conditions before hatching once submerged.
Females lay eggs in damp containers where water accumulates, such as buckets, vases, tyres, and roof gutters.
What is Zika virus?
Zika virus is transmitted by a bite from an infected mosquito. It is usually found in South and Central America, the Caribbean, the Pacific islands, Africa, and Asia.
Many cases are mild, but it can lead to hospitalisations in some and complications if someone is pregnant.
As explained by the NHS, symptoms of the Zika virus tend to last between two days and a week, although some people have no symptoms.
![(FILES) An Aedes aegypti mosquito is kept in a cage for researchers to collect their eggs, at a laboratory of biotech company Wolbito do Brasil, in Curitiba, Parana state, Brazil on March 19, 2026. The world's largest breeding factory for the mosquitoes -- nicknamed "wolbitos" after the Wolbachia bacterium they were injected with to block the transmission of dengue -- is located in the southern city of Curitiba. The anti-dengue mosquitoes have been introduced to 15 countries, but nowhere have they protected as many people as in Brazil -- an estimated six million people since 2011, when scientists first began testing the method. (Photo by Nelson ALMEIDA / AFP via Getty Images)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_299777781-39fd.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Signs include:
- high temperature
- headache
- sore, red eyes
- swollen joints and joint and muscle pain
- lower back pain
- rash and itching all over the body
While there are no specific treatments, you should rest, stay hydrated, and take pain relief.
In pregnancy, blood tests and ultrasounds may be arranged, as serious problems before and after birth can arise.
You should speak to your midwife or doctor about risks and concerns.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_45650449-158c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Do the mosquitoes carry other viruses?
Aedes aegypti can also transmit dengue, which can cause high fever and flu-like symptoms. These often get better on their own, and severe cases are rare.
- 
	![Man faces prison after killing his newly found biological father Tributes have been paid to a man who died following an incident on Christmas Eve.Officers were called to The Queen?s Head, in Willington, just after 4.45pm following reports a man was unconscious inside the pub.Despite the best efforts of the emergency services, the man was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.Today, he has been named as 61-year-old Steven Shevels from Crook.In a statement, his family said: ?We are heartbroken to announce the tragic death of Steven, who was taken from us far too soon.?He will be deeply missed by all of his family and friends.?A 36-year-old man was arrested on Christmas Day and taken into custody, where he was charged with manslaughter.Martin Greensmith was remanded into police custody before his appearance at Newton Aycliffe Magistrates? Court on Saturday (December 27).He was released on bail to appear at Durham Crown Court on Tuesday, January 27.A man is facing prison time after he killed his own dad just hours after discovering he was his biological father.Steven Shevels, 61, died after hitting his head on the concrete floor of the beer garden of the Queen?s Head pub, in Willington, County Durham, on Christmas Eve last year.Martin Greensmith, 37, admitted pushing Mr Shevels but denied manslaughter.Following a seven-day trial at Teesside Crown Court this week, a jury found him guilty.Picture: Durham Constabularyhttps://www.durham.police.uk/news/durham/news2/2025/12.-december/man-who-died-in-christmas-eve-pub-incident-is-named/](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SEI_310394523-4b48.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- First picture of man who died after jumping in canal while being chased by police
- Procession led by horses and Lamborghini for first A66 crash funeral
- Dad and daughter tied mum's body to paving slab with washing line and threw it into canal
Again, symptoms tend to ease within 10 days, and dengue is not otherwise found in the UK. You cannot catch it from another person.
Symptoms of severe dengue are:
- severe tummy pain
- repeatedly being sick
- fast breathing
- bleeding gums or nose
- fatigue
- being unable to relax (restlessness)
- blood in your vomit or poo
As for Chikungunya, this is another mosquito-borne viral infection which also manifests as high fever and joint pain.
Most recover within one or two weeks, but joint pain can be persistent. It is spread by female Aedes mosquitoes.
Get in touch with our news team by emailing us at webnews@metro.co.uk.
For more stories like this, check our news page.
summary: An invasive mosquito species known to transmit viruses like Zika, dengue, and chikungunya has been found breeding in south east London homes for the first time. Although this marks the fourth time the insects have been detected in the UK, health experts assure that the public risk is low because the UK climate is too cold for them to survive long-term. The UK Health Security Agency has increased surveillance and is working to trap and destroy the larvae, with no current evidence of human infections.
key_points: Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can transmit Zika and dengue, were found breeding in south east London homes.
This is the first time the species has been identified reproducing in the UK, though it is the fourth time they have been detected.
The UK Health Security Agency has increased surveillance and is actively trapping and destroying the larvae.
Health experts state the public risk is low because the UK climate is too cold for the species to survive long-term, and there is no evidence of human infections.

title: Medical breakthrough as man lives for nine months with pig kidney
author: Jane Kirby
content:
Man kept alive by pig kidney for nine months in world first
![Man kept alive by pig kidney for nine months in world first](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/03/22/01M1K4E1VQJVEQYH48MB2BJ2GX.jpg?quality=75&width=83&auto=webp 83w>)
Medical breakthrough as man lives for nine months with pig kidney
- Tim Andrews, 66, has become the first person to live without dialysis for nine months after receiving a genetically modified pig kidney transplant.
- The pioneer procedure, conducted at Mass General Brigham in January 2025, served as a temporary bridge until Mr Andrews received a human donor kidney.
- Published in The Lancet, the milestone marks the longest recorded dialysis-free survival following a pig-to-human kidney transplant in a living patient.
- The genetically edited organ functioned for six months before blood vessel damage occurred, with researchers detecting no pig viruses or pathogens during the trial.
- Lead author Dr Leonardo Riella said xenotransplantation could help address the severe global organ shortage crisis by providing a vital alternative for patients.
summary: Tim Andrews, 66, became the first person to live dialysis-free for nine months after receiving a genetically modified pig kidney transplant in January 2025 at Mass General Brigham. Published in The Lancet, the procedure served as a temporary bridge until he received a human donor organ. Researchers reported that the genetically edited kidney functioned for six months before blood vessel damage occurred, with no pig viruses or pathogens detected.
key_points: Tim Andrews lived for nine months without dialysis using a genetically modified pig kidney.
The pioneering procedure took place at Mass General Brigham in January 2025.
The pig kidney served as a temporary bridge until Mr Andrews received a human donor kidney.
The genetically edited organ functioned for six months before experiencing blood vessel damage.
No pig viruses or pathogens were detected during the trial.

title: Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief
author: Neha Gohil
content:
Mental health organisations have “failed to acknowledge” the risk of violence from a minority of people with severe mental illnesses, the chief executive of Mind has said ahead of the closure of the inquiry into the Nottingham attacks.
Dr Sarah Hughes, who has led mental health charity Mind for four years and has worked in the sector for almost four decades, said charities had shied away from addressing the risk of violence due to the fact it had increased the stigma and harassment around people with mental health conditions.
The inquiry into the Nottingham attacks is examining the events leading up to 13 June 2023, when 19-year-old students Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and 65-year-old caretaker Ian Coates, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.
In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.
The public inquiry has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.
The inquiry heard how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, repeatedly refused to take medication, and was sectioned four times in the space of two years. During her evidence, Calocane’s mother described the mental health system as “so broken”.
![Dr Sarah Hughes, chief executive officer of Mind](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e006ba1f4f66324a5057580da4a949b0224bf904/576_0_6142_4912/master/6142.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Speaking exclusively to the Guardian, Hughes said charities specialising in mental health had to become “more comfortable” with discussing the risk of violence that could exist from a minority of people with mental health illnesses.
Hughes’s comments come after the charity Mind held a roundtable with experts in Westminster to discuss the role mental health services needed to play to keep the public and patients safe.
“We, as a charity sector, have failed to acknowledge that violence does happen in some circumstances,” she said. “As a sector, [we] have held the narrative that the majority of people don’t commit violent crime. However, some do and the consequences are grave.”
Hughes added: “My feeling is that we haven’t always been able to articulate the topic of violence and mental health well to the public and ultimately, we have softened the truth. Stigma and discrimination are incredibly harmful, however our efforts to reduce them have, at times, meant that some of the most difficult topics have been brushed under the carpet. That’s why it’s so important to bring together a wide range of experts and experiences to have an open and honest conversation.”
Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was killed by Calocane, said she welcomed the statement by Hughes. “I do feel like danger to others has been almost deliberately quietened down in the conversation in the past,” she said.
Webber said there had not been enough acknowledgment from mental health organisations of the risk of violence.
“It could be a really powerful voice for the charities to have that difficult conversation, and to not be fearful of saying about the risks of violence toward others, and that people that are mentally ill, like Calocane, can and do go on to kill.
“Obviously the vast majority of people with mental health issues in this country are completely safe … but if somebody’s dangerous, they’re dangerous.
“Had the risks in Calocane’s case been understood, then I genuinely believe we wouldn’t be having this conversation today.”
after newsletter promotion
![Celeste Calocane giving evidence](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/81aee70d6960c22088314220c48300cbe0643490/570_0_2700_2160/master/2700.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Seena Fazel, a professor of forensic psychiatry at the University of Oxford who attended the event by Mind, said a minority of people with mental illnesses perpetrate violent acts and high-quality research on schizophrenia had “converged on the same picture”.
“People with schizophrenia do have an elevated risk of violence compared with the general population, even after accounting for socioeconomic factors, but the absolute risk is small. Only a minority will commit a serious violent act,” he said. 
 “That risk increases when other factors are present, particularly drug or alcohol problems, a history of violence, or having been a victim of violence themselves. The important point is that treatments we already have, and which are widely available, can bring that risk down.”
Hughes, who said she had experienced violence when she was a mental health practitioner from people experiencing psychosis, said many in the sector feared that addressing such issues could increase stigma and discrimination, and that could lead to dangerous health outcomes.
“We are incredibly frightened of deepening that stigma and discrimination because we know how dangerous it can be,” she said. “This could risk going back to a more restrictive approach. My view is that’s not the answer, but stigma creates a pathway to that as being the only solution to this problem.”
Hughes said this meant the sector had “shied away” from difficult conversations around violence. “The public, I think, are more ready [and] we’ve got to get our act together,” she said. “Even within Mind there was a reluctance internally and we had to really talk it though.”
Hughes said Mind is set to introduce its mental health strategy, which will call for better support and treatment for those with severe mental illnesses, as well as address matters of public safety.
This includes ensuring an adequate number of beds in hospitals, assertive outreach, and accountability and communication with services.
“I hope that by us having these conversations openly we can both make sure that the people we’re advocating for know that we’re doing this safely with their consent, but equally, the public and families and victims know that we recognise that we have to come together to solve this problem,” Hughes said.
“Crucially, there is a role for Mind – and the sector as a whole – to show that patient and public safety are not mutually exclusive. Both are possible if we want to change our mental health system so people can get the right care before or after reaching crisis point,” she added.
summary: Dr Sarah Hughes, the chief executive of the mental health charity Mind, stated that mental health organizations have failed to acknowledge the risk of violence from a minority of people with severe mental illnesses. Speaking ahead of the conclusion of the inquiry into the Nottingham attacks committed by Valdo Calocane, Hughes explained that charities previously shied away from this topic to avoid increasing stigma and discrimination. Emma Webber, whose son was killed in the attacks, welcomed the statement, noting that the danger posed to others had been quietened down in past conversations.
key_points: Mind chief executive Dr Sarah Hughes stated that the charity sector has failed to acknowledge the risk of violence from a minority of people with severe mental illnesses.
Mental health organizations previously avoided discussing violence due to fears of increasing stigma, harassment, and discrimination against patients.
The remarks preceded the closure of the inquiry into the Nottingham attacks, where Valdo Calocane fatally stabbed three people and attempted to kill three others.
Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was killed by Calocane, welcomed Hughes's comments and agreed that the danger to others was previously downplayed.
Mind is set to introduce a new strategy calling for better support, treatment, hospital beds, and public safety measures.

title: Alzheimer’s trial to test drug on people without symptoms to see if it can be prevented
author: Donna Ferguson
content:
People without memory loss will be offered an experimental Alzheimer’s drug that could stop the development of the condition before dementia symptoms emerge.
Healthy middle-aged people deemed to have a higher risk of developing the condition will be eligible to participate in the trial, which is being run by an NHS trust as part of an international clinical trial aiming to prevent dementia.
The first European participants in the trial, which is recruiting about 1,600 people aged 55 to 80 from around the world, will be screened on Monday by the Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust.
Participants from across the UK will be tested to check that they have no memory problems, before being offered a blood test to assess whether they have p-tau217, a biomarker that can predict cognitive decline and the development of Alzheimer’s.
Previous research found people with the highest levels of p-tau217 had an estimated 78% chance of developing cognitive impairment within 10 years.
Research has also showed that blood tests measuring p-tau217 could identify Alzheimer’s disease with up to 95% accuracy.
The phase III trial, called the PrevenTRON study, will investigate whether prescribing a new drug, Trontinemab, to participants who have elevated levels of p-tau217 and meet the trial criteria can stop dementia developing in the first place.
Trontinemab, which was developed by the Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche, attacks amyloid plaques, a toxic protein that builds up in the brain and slows down – and eventually kills – brain cells.
It has been hailed as a groundbreaking drug after early research found that it cleared amyloid plaques in nine out of 10 people with early-stage Alzheimer’s or mild cognitive development within 28 weeks, meaning that one of the key characteristics of Alzheimer’s was removed.
Prof Ramin Nilforooshan, consultant psychiatrist and chief investigator for the PrevenTRON trial, said the study demonstrates how researchers are shifting their focus from cure to prevention: “For decades, research has focused on treating Alzheimer’s disease after symptoms appear. PrevenTRON addresses a different question, whether we can act earlier, before symptoms begin.”
Through research and trials such as PrevenTRON, he said there was the potential to help millions of people affected by Alzheimer’s.
However, he stressed in an interview with the Telegraph the experimental nature of the treatment.
after newsletter promotion
“I’m not saying this trial is magic. It’s an investigational medicine. We need to wait and see: will it work or not?” he said.
At least 15 hospitals and clinics across the UK are expected to take part in the study by the end of the year, with recruitment led by the Surrey and Borders Partnership Trust.
The trial is expected to last four to six years. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either Trontinemab or a placebo, and will then be monitored to see how quickly they develop any signs of dementia.
Alzheimer’s disease is thought to develop inside the brain up to 10 years before people typically seek treatment for memory problems.
It affects around one in 14 people over the age of 65 and one in six people over the age of 80.
Those interested in being screened for the trial can contact the Surrey and Borders Partnership research team on 01372 216584 or at research@sabp.nhs.uk.
summary: An international clinical trial called the PrevenTRON study is testing an experimental Alzheimer's drug called Trontinemab on healthy middle-aged individuals without memory loss to see if the condition can be prevented. Run in the UK by the Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust, the trial targets people aged 55 to 80 who have elevated levels of the p-tau217 biomarker. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either the drug or a placebo over a four-to-six-year period to monitor whether the treatment stops dementia from developing.
key_points: The phase III PrevenTRON study aims to test if the drug Trontinemab can prevent Alzheimer's before symptoms emerge.
The international trial is recruiting about 1,600 people globally aged 55 to 80 without memory problems.
Participants will undergo blood tests to screen for p-tau217, a biomarker that can predict cognitive decline.
Trontinemab, developed by Roche, targets and clears amyloid plaques in the brain.
At least 15 UK hospitals and clinics are expected to participate in the trial, which will last four to six years.

title: Surrey and Borders trust joins Alzheimer's prevention drug trial
author: Craig Buchan
content:
![A blue gloved hand points a middle finger at a screen showing a collection of black and white scans of cross-sections of the brain. They look like white ovals where the outline of the skull is visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/8a41/live/c22eb870-a85e-11f1-ae45-e9984fc27c77.jpg)
The clinical trial is recruiting 1,600 healthy adults aged 55 to 80 internationally
- Published
An NHS trust says it has become the first in Europe to join a trial examining if a new drug can delay or prevent the onset of Alzheimer's.
Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust is offering the drug Trontinemab to people at high risk of developing the disease and is the third site worldwide to do so.
The clinical trial is recruiting 1,600 healthy adults aged 55 to 80 internationally, with the Surrey and north east Hampshire trust recruit participants from anywhere in the UK.
Alzheimer's disease, external is the most common form of dementia and accounts for 60% to 80% of the country's dementia cases, according to the NHS.
The progressive condition affects multiple brain functions. Symptoms typically develop gradually over many years and eventually become more severe.
The new drug attacks a sticky gunk called beta amyloid that builds up in the spaces between brain cells in Alzheimer's disease.
Researchers will use blood tests to identify people who are most likely to benefit from participating in the trial, the trust said.
Prof Ramin Nilforooshan, consultant psychiatrist and chief investigator for the trial, said research had "for decades" focused on treating Alzheimer's after symptoms appeared.
The trial "addresses a different question, whether we can act earlier, before symptoms begin", he said.
"We are very excited for the potential to help millions of people affected by Alzheimer's disease."
An estimated 982,000 people are living with dementia in the UK, according to an Alzheimer's Society report, external.

summary: Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust has become the first in Europe to join an international clinical trial testing the drug Trontinemab for Alzheimer's prevention. The study aims to recruit 1,600 healthy adults aged 55 to 80 who are at high risk of developing the disease. The drug targets beta amyloid buildup in the brain, allowing researchers to investigate whether intervention can occur before symptoms begin.
key_points: Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust is the first in Europe and the third site worldwide to join the trial.
The clinical trial is testing the drug Trontinemab to see if it can delay or prevent Alzheimer's onset.
The international study is recruiting 1,600 healthy adults aged 55 to 80.
The drug works by attacking beta amyloid, a sticky substance that builds up between brain cells in Alzheimer's patients.
Researchers are using blood tests to identify participants who are most likely to benefit from the trial.

title: What went right this week: the good news that matters
author: Gavin Haines
content:
A new ‘superhuman’ tool for spotting heart disease, France slowed down fast fashion, and a near-extinct species bounced back, plus more good news
This week’s good news roundup
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-1148177972-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
Software that can detect heart disease in seconds could help change the trajectory of the condition for millions of people, experts said this week.
The new tool, developed by Imperial College London, scans electrocardiograms (ECGs) for information that human cardiologists are unable to see.
ECGs record electrical activity in the heart and have long proved reliable in helping cardiologists diagnose heart attacks and abnormal rhythms. But even the most experienced among them are unable to detect signs of heart disease in ECG data. For that, they must carry out echocardiograms, which many patients wait months for – valuable time lost that could be spent seeing treatment.
“We looked at the ECGs to see if we could do things that are superhuman,” said Imperial’s Dr Arunashis Sau. “Not things that clinicians can already do, but things that no cardiologist, no matter how expert, can do.”
A trial involving 67,000 patients found that the tool successfully correctly identified up to 81% of patients who had heart failure and 90% of those who had heart valve disease. The results were presented at the European Society of Cardiology annual congress in Munich, Germany.
“A 10-second ECG, once a blunt screening tool, may soon become one of the most informative tests in medicine,” said Fu Siong Ng, professor of cardiology at Imperial. Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, the British Heart Foundation’s clinical director, added: “When it comes to the heart, earlier diagnosis and treatment saves lives.”
Image: peakSTOCK
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-1289221241-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
In further promising health news, a new urine test has correctly identified 92% of bladder cancer cases in a UK trial, raising hopes for speedier diagnoses of the disease.
The Galeas urine test was trialled on 964 patients across seven urology departments in England and Scotland. A study, led by the University of Birmingham, showed that it correctly identified 92.2% of cancer cases.
Welcoming the results, experts said the at-home test could spare patients from having an invasive cystoscopy, which involves inserting a small camera up the urethra, while also reducing the burden on health services.
“The results are very significant for clinical practice,” said Prof Richard Bryan, study co-author. “Only 8% of patients in the study were ultimately diagnosed with bladder cancer, which highlights the challenge facing [health] services, where large numbers of patients currently enter the same urgent diagnostic pathway despite most not having cancer.
“Galeas is a promising and less invasive test that can be easier to administer and make testing and screening for bladder cancer far easier.”
The peer-reviewed study was published in the journal European Urology Oncology on Wednesday. Further, larger studies are planned.
Image: Ridofranz
![good news](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/james-tay-ubnm8R49PZQ-unsplash-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
In a win for southeast Asia, Timor-Leste has defeated the world’s leading cause of infectious blindness – the last country in the region to do so.
On Thursday, the World Health Organization (WHO) validated Timor-Leste as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem.
The disease is spread via contaminated fingers or flies that have come into contact with the eyes of an infected person, and is often prevalent in poorer regions. Improvements to sanitation, plus speedier diagnosis and antibiotic rollouts, are among the best tools to tackle the disease.
“The elimination of trachoma from the southeast Asia region is a significant step towards our global target of eliminating trachoma worldwide by 2030,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO director general. “[Timor-Leste] has shown how science and strong health systems can protect people from preventable blindness.”
Image: James Tay
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-1909777407-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
Methane ‘super-emitter’ Turkmenistan has started plugging leaks in its oil and gas facilities to prevent the potent greenhouse gas from escaping, new UN data suggests.
While CO2 is synonymous with global warming, methane is a stronger, albeit shorter lived, greenhouse gas – one released via leaks on a massive scale around the world. In 2022, first-of-its kind satellite data pinpointed the sources of more than 1,000 such leaks (chiefly oil and gas fields), with Turkmenistan the main offender.
However, according to the Guardian, which first reported on methane super emitters, Turkmenistan has now plugged eight major leaks. The work was an “incredible first step”, the UN told the newspaper.
Repairing methane leaks is one of the most obvious climate solutions. The UN Methane Alert and Response System (Mars) sends alerts to counties about their leaks. Turkmenistan received the most (192) last year and responded to 20%, including with plans to fix them. The US, by contrast, was sent 138 but responded to none.
Despite the progress, there’s much work to be done with methane responsible for around a quarter of global emissions.
Image: Joost Potma
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/romane-gautun-5nTz84qV7Vg-unsplash-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
The French, renowned for setting trends, started a new one on Monday – imposing fees on garments that don’t meet environmental standards.
French politicians claim the move will address the growing environmental impact of ultra-fast fashion, which churns out cheap, synthetic garments that swiftly end up in landfill. It comes as a report reveals that the fashion industry’s already substantial emissions ballooned 14% in just two years.
However, the Chinese government has cried foul, claiming the legislation is designed to target Chinese e-commerce retailers, such as Shein and Temu, while letting European outlets off the hook.
Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined by three factors: the volume of products available, how much they cost, and their repairability. Fees will range from €0.50 (£0.43) for underwear to €12 (£10.30) for a coat, with the total amount capped at 50% of the product’s sales price.
France is not acting alone in trying to reduce fashion’s footprint. New European Union rules banning the destruction of unsold garments – a common practice in the industry – came into force in August. Brands must now find alternative uses for unsold stock, such as donation and resale.
Related: The preloved pioneers sending secondhand fashion mainstream
Image: Romane Gautun
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-2154320237-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
China’s energy transition passed a key threshold this week as figures showed solar panels overtook coal power plants as the country’s main source of power capacity.
Figures reported by state media on Tuesday suggested that China had 1,288 GW of solar capacity at the end of July, surpassing coal’s 1,285 GW for the first time.
There’s a catch, however. Despite its growing dominance in China, solar generates less energy than coal because the panels don’t work at night. According to official figures, wind and solar met 24.6% of China’s electricity needs in the first half of 2026, compared to 49.7% for coal.
That’s a lot of coal going up in smoke, but it’s also the first time coal dipped below the 50% mark since records began.
Image: Zhudifeng
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-468138225-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
Around half a million more pupils in England are now eligible for free school meals thanks to a rule change described as a “landmark” moment for children.
Under the new rules, all pupils in England whose parents receive Universal Credit – a means-tested welfare benefit – will be eligible for free school dinners.
The Food Foundation, a charity that long campaigned for the change, said the move “will ease pressure on families struggling with the cost of living”.
It comes amid a major overhaul of food standards in England’s schools, which aims to take processed, deep-fried and sugary foods off the menu, while increasing pupils’ intake of grains, pulses and vegetables.
Image: Monkey Business Images
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/yuma-solar-oZ4IhVjyFwk-unsplash-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
The benefits of solar power are available to more people than ever in the UK after plug-in panels went on sale there for the first time.
The UK government recently relaxed the rules on plug-in panels, which have long been available in the European Union. The devices offer households a way of generating electricity without installing conventional rooftop arrays, meaning renters and people living in flats can also take advantage.
Unlike traditional arrays, the smaller, off-the-shelf systems can be positioned in a garden or, where rules permit, on a balcony. They feed electricity into the home via plug sockets.
According to the government, the panels could save households up to £150 a year on energy bills. The cheapest devices cost £599, meaning a four-year pay-back period. Prices are expected to fall.
“The arrival of plug-in solar panels represents a significant milestone in expanding access to clean energy,” said Joanna O’Loan from the Energy Saving Trust. “Plug-in solar panels will give more people greater control over their energy use and costs.”
Image: Yuma Solar
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Kakapo_Sirocco_1-1-scaled-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
The population of a critically endangered parrot found only in New Zealand has reached a 75-year high.
Kākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were common across New Zealand, until invasive cats and stoats pushed them to the brink of extinction in the 1900s.
A recovery programme launched in 1995 on the South Island, where predator-free habitats have been created. At the time, the population of the bird was just 51, but this week it was revealed that 90 chicks had been born this year, pushing the population to a recovery-era high of 325 birds.
“There is still a long road of recovery ahead, but 90 chicks in a single season is a record,” said Deidre Vercoe from the New Zealand department for conservation. “In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks. It’s a significant milestone for the species.”
Image: Department of Conservation
![](https://www.positive.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/vinicius-amnx-amano-aANIrjIFRKE-unsplash-1-512x512-c-center.jpg) 
While tech-moguls pour billions into trying to live longer, the answer might well lie in Brazil.
Recent research suggests that the country has one of the highest concentrations of supercentenarians in the world – a striking fact in a nation better known for inequality, patchy healthcare and economic and social volatility.
New research – reported by Positive News this week – aims to find out what Brazil’s supercentenarians can teach the rest of the world about living longer, healthier lives.
“We are still collecting, still trying to understand,” one researcher told Positive News. “But already we see some very interesting patterns.”
Read the full story here.
Image: Vinicius Amano
Main image: Dusanpetkovic
Get your weekly fix of good news delivered to your inbox every Saturday, by signing up to the Positive News email newsletter
Be part of the solution
At Positive News, we’re not chasing clicks or profits for media moguls – we’re here to serve you and have a positive social impact. We can’t do this unless enough people like you choose to support our journalism.
Give once from just £1, or join 1,800+ others who contribute an average of £3 or more per month. Together, we can build a healthier form of media – one that focuses on solutions, progress and possibilities, and empowers people to create positive change.
summary: Recent positive global developments include the introduction of advanced diagnostic medical tools, major environmental policy shifts, and successful conservation milestones. Notable highlights feature a new ECG software for heart disease, France's fees on ultra-fast fashion, and a record-high population for New Zealand's endangered kākāpō parrot. Additionally, renewable energy milestones, such as solar capacity surpassing coal in China, demonstrate ongoing global progress.
key_points: A new ECG software developed by Imperial College London successfully identified up to 81% of heart failure cases and 90% of heart valve disease cases in trials.
France implemented new fees on ultra-fast fashion garments that fail to meet environmental standards.
Timor-Leste was validated by the WHO for eliminating trachoma as a public health problem.
China's solar power capacity surpassed coal power plants for the first time.
The population of New Zealand's critically endangered kākāpō parrot reached a 75-year high of 325 birds.

title: My dog has better tick protection than I do. That could change soon
author: Brianna Abbott
content:
My dog has better tick protection than I do. That could change soon
![Getty Images A dog tick as seen under a scanning electron microscope (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p6r9qp.jpg.webp) Getty Images
Lyme disease is on the rise. But scientists are searching for ways to prevent it.
Each time I pull out a wriggling tick from my dog's fur, I flash back to my own brush with Lyme disease – a bacterial infection spread via tick bites. I never found the deer tick that bit me, but I remember the flu-like chills, the body aches and signature bullseye rash that ran up and down my arm. A month of intense antibiotics cleared the infection and I haven’t had any further problems, but other people aren't so lucky.
In addition to an oval or circular rash, Lyme disease can cause flu-like symptoms. Infections that go untreated in the short term can lead to potentially debilitating issues in the months and years that follow, such as fatigue, body aches or nerve damage.
Meanwhile, there are an estimated 476,000 cases of Lyme disease diagnosed in the US every year – and as ticks expand their territory, that risk is growing. In the US, there are currently no licensed vaccines to prevent Lyme disease in people – but that might be about to change. And scientists are developing other strategies to help prevent infections, too. This is the battle against a group of particularly resilient bacteria and their spider-like host – and it's heating up.
"We are seeing many more patients, many more people actually getting infected," says Thomas Hart, assistant professor of molecular microbiology and immunology at Johns Hopkins Lyme and Tickborne Diseases Research and Education Institute, Maryland. "It's a good time for there to be a new preventative."
A public health threat on the rise
Tick populations are expanding their range throughout Europe and the US, thanks to expanding forest and deer populations and climate change creating milder winters. And while tick season usually stretches from spring to autumn in many places, climate change is now increasingly leading to longer, sometimes year-round tick activity.
Ticks carry a number of pathogens that can infect people, leading to diseases that include encephalitis, anaplasmosis and babesiosis, among others. But Lyme disease, caused by some types of Borrelia bacteria, is the most common tick-related illness in Europe and North America.
To this day my labrador Walter continues bounding around in long grass, unscathed by the illnesses ticks carry. He is vaccinated against Lyme disease and eats his monthly chewable tablet, smothered in spray cheese, to ward off fleas, ticks and heartworm – a disease spread via mosquito bites.
Currently there are several anti-tick treatments for dogs and cats, which often rely on chemicals that kill ticks once they start to feed. Typically these are either applied directly to the skin as a "spot-on" treatment, disseminated via a collar, or delivered as a tablet.
Developing preventative drugs for humans, on the other hand, is no easy task. Studies in people are harder and more costly to run than those in animals. For trials in people, scientists often need to recruit a large number of participants and follow them over time as they go about their lives. That's because only a small fraction of them will get bitten and develop a tick-borne disease, and there need to be enough infections to show if the vaccine or drug works.
In animal trials, meanwhile, researchers often put infected ticks directly on them, almost ensuring that they will get infected with a given tick-borne pathogen, making the trials easier to do. But scientists hesitate to use so-called challenge trials for Lyme disease in people, in part because they don't want to risk giving people lingering, long-term symptoms from the disease.
"I don't think anyone would sign up for Lyme," says Linden Hu, professor of immunology at Tufts University School of Medicine in Massachusetts, who has worked with several companies on anti-tick strategies for humans. He explains this is why it's hard to get them approved.
There was, however, a human Lyme disease vaccine approved in the US in 1998, called LYMErix. The shot was tested in a trial with more than 10,000 participants and had 76% efficacy in preventing the disease. But demand was low, partly because of reports and lawsuits over side effects, namely arthritis. Health officials reviewed the data in 2002 and didn't find evidence of a safety risk. Still, the vaccine's maker discontinued the shot the same year, citing a lack of demand.
![Getty Images Ticks thrive in long grass, where they climb to the ends of stalks and wait for a host to latch onto (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p6r9lc.jpg.webp) Getty Images
The push for a vaccine
Now, the growing number of people at risk of tick-borne diseases has spurred a newfound investment in prevention. In particular, the search for another vaccine against Lyme disease is gathering pace – and starting to yield results.
So far, the vaccine candidate that's the furthest along is PF-07307405, by Pfizer and Valneva. It shares a similar target with the old LYMErix vaccine and the shots designed for dogs – a piece of a protein called OspA on the surface of the Lyme disease-causing Borrelia burgdorferi bacterium.
The shot prompts a person's immune system to create antibodies against six common versions of OspA found in the US and Europe. Then, when an infected tick bites the person and feeds on blood, it also takes in the person's antibodies. Inside the tick, the antibodies latch onto OspA, blocking the bacteria from leaving the critter.
"Your antibodies are able to fight off the bacteria when it's still inside of the tick, preventing infection in the first place," Hart says.
Earlier this year, Pfizer announced the results from a phase 3 trial – where scientists test how a new intervention compares with existing ones or a placebo and check its safety. In this case, the trial involved more than 9,400 people, revealing that a four-dose regimen was more than 70% effective in preventing Lyme disease. Fewer participants developed Lyme disease during the trial than expected, however, which meant results wasn’t quite as conclusive as the team had hoped.
No major safety concerns were detected, and Pfizer said in a press release that it is confident in the vaccine's potential and plans on submitting it to US government regulators for potential approval.
"I will definitely get it as soon as it's available," says Laura Goodman, an assistant professor and emerging infectious diseases researcher at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, New York.
Similarly, Moderna is testing two Lyme disease vaccines that target OspA. Both are in phase 2 trials – where an intervention is tested on a larger group of people than in phase 1, to see if it's safe and how well it might work. Meanwhile, researchers at Yale University are investigating a shot that prompts the immune system to respond to tick saliva. This one has not yet been trialled in humans.
Antibodies and other drugs
Another option is to skip the vaccine altogether. For more than a decade, Mark Klempner, a professor of medicine at UMass Chan Medical School, Massachusetts, has been developing an injection designed to target OspA. While a vaccine works by triggering the immune system to create antibodies, this delivers pre-made antibodies directly into a person. It takes just two days to absorb enough to be protected for four months.
Lyme disease is not found everywhere that there are ticks. It's rare to catch it in the southeastern US, for example, where ticks prefer to bite lizards over mammals. The idea behind the injection is that people who live, work or travel in areas with Lyme disease could get it at the beginning of tick season, Klempner says, plus a second dose later on.
The product is known as TNX-4800, and has already made it through phase 1 clinical trials, where an intervention is tested to find a safe dose and identify potential side effects. Tonix Pharmaceuticals licensed it in 2025 and plans on launching a phase 2 clinical trial next year, according to the company website.
More like this:
Another pharmaceutical company, Tarsus Pharmaceuticals, meanwhile, is working on a pill that deploys the same ingredient as an anti-tick medication for dogs. The drug TP-05 interferes with the ticks' nervous systems and kills them quickly, hopefully before they have time to transmit Lyme disease-causing bacteria and other pathogens.
In canines, the drug comes in the form of a chewable tablet, but in people it will be a pill. In March this year, Tarsus announced that it had started a phase 2 clinical trial in people, with results expected in the first half of next year.
"I think it's going to be a game-changer," says Durland Fish, a professor emeritus of epidemiology at Yale School of Public Health, Connecticut, who has researched vector-borne diseases including Lyme disease for decades. The pill could also prevent other rising tick-borne diseases including babesiosis and anaplasmosis, he says.
But it's unclear when and if these options will become available. In the meantime, the best prevention is to stop tick bites in the first place. That means staying out of tall grass, wearing protective clothing, and showering and checking for ticks after coming inside. Those tried-and-true methods really work, Hu says, but they can be hard for people to do.
"People get tired or are out late at night, the kids are cranky," Hu says. That's where a vaccine or pill that people can take – but don't have to remember every time they go outside – could "really be a public health benefit," he says.
–
For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.
summary: Lyme disease cases are rising in the US and Europe due to expanding tick populations and climate change, yet human preventative options remain limited compared to treatments available for dogs. Researchers are currently developing new interventions, including vaccines from Pfizer and Valneva as well as Moderna, pre-made antibody injections, and preventative pills. While human clinical trials are more challenging and costly to run than animal trials, these emerging preventative strategies could soon offer a much-needed public health solution.
key_points: Lyme disease is the most common tick-related illness in Europe and North America, with an estimated 476,000 cases diagnosed annually in the US.
Climate change and growing forest and deer populations are expanding tick ranges and lengthening their active seasons.
Pfizer and Valneva's vaccine candidate (PF-07307405) targets the OspA protein on the surface of the bacteria and showed over 70% efficacy in phase 3 trials.
Moderna is testing two OspA-targeting vaccines in phase 2 trials, while other researchers are developing pre-made antibody injections and preventative pills.
Unlike animal trials, human trials for tick-borne diseases are more complex because researchers cannot ethically use challenge trials that risk giving participants long-term symptoms.

title: Meningitis symptoms to watch out for as two Suffolk teenagers catch infection
author: Emily Goodwin
content:
With two Suffolk teenagers testing positive for Meningitis B, searches for symptoms to watch out for have skyrocketed.
Nearly 50 teens across the region who were in contact with the pair have been offered emergency antibiotics as a precaution, as the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) launches an investigation.
The UKHSA has confirmed that the two teens with meningitis are both from Framlingham and are currently receiving treatment in hospital.
Meningitis B is a potentially life-threatening bacterial infection that can cause inflammation of the lining around the brain and spinal cord, and can rapidly lead to blood poisoning.
Early symptoms include vomiting, fever, aches, muscle pain, cold hands and feet and headaches, making it tough to spot as it can look similar to common illnesses like colds or flu.
But someone with meningitis or septicaemia will usually become seriously ill in just a matter of hours, which is why it’s important to check on someone with these symptoms regularly to monitor the situation.
Meningitis B is a different strain from Meningitis A, which is more common across Africa. This is why it is important to understand the difference in the symptoms before calling a healthcare professional.
Early recognition of meningitis symptoms can greatly improve the outcome of the disease, and so anyone concerned about any of these symptoms, at any time, should contact their GP, call NHS 111 or 999 in an emergency.
summary: Two teenagers from Framlingham in Suffolk have tested positive for Meningitis B and are receiving hospital treatment. In response, the UK Health Security Agency has launched an investigation and offered emergency antibiotics to nearly 50 close contacts. The bacterial infection can rapidly cause severe illness, making early recognition of its flu-like symptoms crucial.
key_points: Two teenagers from Suffolk have tested positive for Meningitis B and are hospitalized.
The UKHSA is investigating and has provided emergency antibiotics to nearly 50 contacts.
Meningitis B causes inflammation around the brain and spinal cord and can lead to blood poisoning.
Early symptoms include fever, vomiting, aches, and headaches, which can resemble a cold or flu.
Anyone concerned about symptoms should contact their GP, call NHS 111, or dial 999 in an emergency.

title: Do people really smell different as they get older? The truth behind ‘old person smell’
author: Jillian Pretzel
content:
Last week, my mom complained that she’s starting to smell “like an old person”.
She had grabbed her favorite sweater and draped it over herself at the movie theater. “It smelled like my grandmother,” she said, almost whispering. “I thought someone must have borrowed the jacket. But it was just me.”
My mom, who’s in her 60s, has a ton of energy. Her hair is thick and still naturally chestnut. She’s healthy and strong; she likes to hike and go to rock concerts.
“I don’t feel like an old person. Why do I smell like one?” she whined.
I told her, truthfully, that I didn’t notice any new aroma. I thought she smelled the same as always: a mix of lotion and gardenia. But I immediately knew what she was talking about.
Experts say that we do smell different as we age. “It’s one of the most universal, least talked-about parts of being human,” says Dr Roya Javid, a dermatologist in Monterey, California. “It’s just biology, unfolding on schedule, the same way we grow taller, then our hair goes gray. Every single person on the planet goes through these same transitions.”
What causes us to smell different as we age?
The musty odor that people sometimes call “old person smell” comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal. 2-nonenal is produced when certain skin oils oxidize and break down, says Javid.
It’s a normal – and unavoidable – change.
“Our skin is coated in a thin layer of natural oils called skin lipids. They keep skin soft, waterproof and protected,” she says.
